speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In introducing the constitutional (amendment) Bill, my speech will cover the Government's long-standing position on marriage and family, what the Bill is and why we are taking this approach, and our unique approach to manage diversity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The PAP Government has been consistent in its strong support for the institution of marriage and the family, through its policies and legislation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One of the first laws enacted by the PAP Government when it came to power was the Women's Charter 1961, which defined and regulated civil marriages.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This was a landmark piece of legislation that protected the rights of women by legalising only monogamous marriages between a man and a woman.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Similarly, the Administration of Muslim Law Act (AMLA) enacted soon after Independence in 1966 provided for the practice of Muslim law to regulate marriages between Muslims.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Under AMLA, marriages must meet the requirements of Muslim law, including being between man and woman.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There is strong consensus in society that marriage is between a man and a woman; and children should be born and raised within such families.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is the view taken by many Singaporeans, whether religious or not.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is also the view that the Government believes in.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It undergirds the shared values that we adopted in 1991.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The family is the foundation on which our society is built and sustained, with each generation raising the next to take its place.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Without strong families, Singapore cannot thrive and society cannot perpetuate itself.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In his book from "Third World to First", Mr Lee Kuan Yew wrote, "Singapore depends on the strength and influence of the family to keep society orderly".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The family is the source of values not only for its members but for society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A 2015 Washington Post article aptly suggests that family values are what makes Singapore strong.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It captures Mr Lee's view that when we break away from tested norms, such as the family unit, there is grave disquiet.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The family is the building block of society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, this is wisdom and precisely why we need to be extremely careful to change the construct of the family.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To further quote Mr Lee's words in a 1994 interview, "The family is the basic concept of our civilisation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have made these clear in Parliament on multiple occasions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have also taken steps to defend our pro-family policies when they are challenged.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, in the adoption case of UKM vs AG, the Court did not agree with the Government that an adoption order should not be made if it resulted in the formation of a same-sex family unit.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Thereafter, the Government made clear its policy position, that it does not support same-sex family formation, surrogacy and planned and deliberate single parenthood, including through ART and/or surrogacy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: More recently, Parliament re-enacted the Adoption of Children Act 2022 to make clear that joint adoption applications can only be made by couples whose marriage is recognised in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Only a man and a woman who are married to each other can apply together.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Among other things, this public policy has long been embodied in section 12(1) of the Women's Charter, which invalidates same-sex marriages.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Consistent with this policy, an overseas same-sex marriage will, generally, not be accorded legal recognition in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our policies clearly reflect the value society places on family formation through marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, we also recognise that there are single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our focus is on their child's well-being and on supporting them in their caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, we extend Government benefits that support the growth and development of their children.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These include subsidies for education, healthcare, childcare and infant care, the foreign domestic worker levy concession and the Child Development Account.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: HDB also assesses their requests for housing holistically, based on their individual circumstances.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We make a distinction between support and incentive.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Thus, we do not provide the Baby Bonus Cash Grant to single unwed parents because this is an incentive for married couples to have children.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our policies support individuals to get married and have children within marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our public libraries also do not carry books which depict such family units for very young children.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Beyond laws and policies, MSF has also been actively promoting, educating and emphasising the importance of families, through our public education programmes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These programmes inculcate family values, such as love, care and concern, respect and commitment to each other in the family.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To support parents, the Families for Life Council has rolled out parenting programmes in preschools, schools and the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We also dedicated 2022 as the Year of Celebrating SG Families, in which the Prime Minister announced an annual National Family Week.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Most recently, we had launched the Singapore Made for Families 2025.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This plan will create a Singapore where families are valued and supported across different chapters of their lives.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These efforts reflect the Government's deep and abiding commitment to the institution of marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and to the formation of families within marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Now I turn to this Bill, which will make it possible to continue with these pro-family policies and the approach embedded in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land and our other laws must not conflict with it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Overall, the Constitution is like the "operating system" for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The four key functions of the Singapore Constitution are: it establishes the key Organs of State like the President, the Parliament, the Government, the Judiciary, the Public Service and regulates their powers with a system of checks and balances; it protects the sovereignty of Singapore; it provides for citizenship; and it protects the fundamental liberties of individuals.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Specific to the fundamental liberties, they are found in Part 4 of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are Articles 9 to 16 and include, among others, liberty of the person and freedom of speech, assembly and association.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many of these rights are not absolute rights.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are subject to exceptions such as the maintenance of public order, morality and national security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If an individual considers that their constitutional rights have been infringed by a law or by the actions of a public body, he or she may bring a legal challenge in Court.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, it is possible for individuals to argue that our existing laws and policies on marriage are unconstitutional and seek a ruling from the Court to that effect.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Just as there have been challenges on the constitutionality of section 377A, there can also be challenges to laws and policies related to marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The experiences of other jurisdictions show the perils of court-led change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Most recently, in August 2022, the Indian Supreme Court observed that the definition of a family unit should be expanded to include homosexual relationships as well as unmarried partnerships or same-sex relationships.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This did not even arise from a challenge of definition of family per se.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It arose from a case where an employer denied a nurse her application for maternity leave because she had already taken leave to care for her husband's children from a previous marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Before this, in 2018, the Indian Supreme Court also struck down section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, which similarly criminalised male homosexual acts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We also see the same trend in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the US for instance, controversial issues such as abortion are litigated and relitigated in the courts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will allow the Government to continue to make laws and policies, which depend on heterosexual marriage as its foundation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There have been questions on why the Government is intervening now.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Perhaps we should leave things as they are, let the Courts decide when there is a challenge.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Why do this now, when there are other issues of concern, such as the cost of living?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We acknowledge that there are indeed other issues of concern to Singaporeans, such as cost of living.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have the mandate and the responsibility to govern, and we must put forward what we think is best for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes making changes in a calibrated and careful manner that may not please everyone.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We appreciate our Courts for exercising wisdom and restraint on this matter.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But a responsible government should not leave the courts to grapple with controversial social issues.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The role of the Courts is to interpret and apply the law.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not their constitutional function to settle political questions or rule on social norms and values.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not their function to engage with the political, social, ethical and other dimensions of the issues.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Nor do the Courts wish to do so.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Litigation is a zero-sum, adversarial process with win-lose outcomes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is unlike a political process, where the interests of stakeholders can be considered, accommodation can be sought to reach consensus.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Courts also recognise that controversial social issues are best dealt with within the sphere of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This Bill is what a responsible government carrying out its duty to the people of Singapore would introduce.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, today, the Women’s Charter and AMLA define civil and Muslim marriages respectively and make clear that same-sex marriages are not valid.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This clause empowers Parliament to continue to make and amend laws for these purposes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The interpretation of other constitutional provisions must recognise this.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, in applying the reasonable classification test under Article 12(1), the Courts must recognise that the promotion and safeguarding of heterosexual marriage are legitimate and permissible legislative objects.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Clause 2 of the Article applies to the Government and any public authority.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It allows them to exercise their functions to protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes, but is not limited to, the following situations: (a) HDB can implement public housing policies that give preference to married couples to support, foster and promote marriage; (b) MSF, when they evaluate adoption applications, can recognise and take into account the public policy goal to foster and promote the formation of families within the context of marriage as defined in the Women’s Charter and AMLA; (c) Curricula for preschools and MOE schools centre on the values that reflect Singapore’s mainstream society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is, marriage as being a union between a man and a woman; and children being born within marriage and raised within such a family construct; (d) In the context of sexuality education, content will be age-appropriate.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This means, for example, in preschools and Primary schools, our curriculum will not feature same-sex parents or same-sex romantic relationships.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At older ages, if introduced, we will focus on educating our young to treat everyone with respect and empathy but will not promote same-sex relationships; and (e) IMDA, in regulating media content, is guided by principles that include prevailing social norms and values that are generally acceptable to members of the public and protecting younger audiences from age-inappropriate content.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Clause 3(b) and clause 4 respectively provides that laws and executive actions cannot be invalidated by Part 4 just because they are based on a heterosexual definition of marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some may ask why specify all the other fundamental liberties in Part 4, and not just Article 12.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Minister Desmond Lee will explain but broadly, we need Article 156 to cover all of Part 4 so that it can apply to other radical legal arguments that may be brought in the future, and based on other articles in Part 4, Article 156 will provide a “strong shield”.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, the shield is also precise, where it only protects the heterosexual definition of marriage and the laws and policies that rely on this definition.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In effect, Article 156 is an exception to the fundamental liberties.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, Article 39A empowers the Legislature to create Group Representation Constituencies (GRCs) to ensure minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Article 39A(3) of the Constitution exempts any law regarding GRCs from being invalidated on the ground of inconsistency with Article 12.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Article 149(1) prevents the Internal Security Act from being invalidated by Articles 9, 11, 12, 13 or 14.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Article 9(6) creates exceptions from Article 9 for the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act and for rehabilitative detention for drug addicts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Article 14(2) also has limits on Article 14, where one’s rights to freedom of speech, assembly and association is subject to public order, morality or security of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Article 12(3) makes clear that the right to equal protection does not apply to laws that regulate personal law, or to laws and practices that restrict office or employment connected with affairs of any religion.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Each case involves a balance between the fundamental liberties and countervailing interests.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This reflects the importance of heterosexual marriage in our society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some have commented that this is an "ouster clause" and could be subject to legal challenges.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To be clear, the nature of Article 156 is not an “ouster clause”.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Instead, it provides exceptions or limits to the fundamental liberties.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have been wide ranging, and we have heard from Singaporeans across various walks of life.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I first want to take the opportunity to appreciate the different groups of Singaporeans who have written in and whom we have engaged before and after the Prime Minister's announcement.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These engagements include those with religious leaders, grassroot leaders, union leaders, LGBT groups, social sector professionals, youth groups and members of the public.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many have written to share their views on this matter.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singaporeans have generally understood the need to respect, graciously and mutually accommodate each other’s views and support the Government’s approach.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Gay people appreciate the repeal of section 377A but express some apprehension of the implications of the constitutional amendments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Those in favour of the status quo have constructively shared their views and emphasised the need to safeguard the institution of marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Others whom we have engaged, such as leaders from the community, also support the proposed approach to keep the heterosexual definition of marriage, while repealing section 377A.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many are concerned about cancel culture, religious freedom, discrimination faced by those with differing views on this issue and the narrowing public space to speak openly about it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These are important feedback and concerns that Minister Desmond Lee will also address when he speaks.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some expressed the wish to go further than what we are proposing, protecting the definition of marriage in our current laws.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They want the definition of marriage to be enshrined in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We understand that these calls come from a sincere belief in the sanctity of marriage and reflect a genuine worry that the institution of marriage might be changed in the future to include same-sex marriages.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But the Government has to govern with principle.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As explained earlier, the Constitution should be for functions such as sovereignty and our system of governance.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The institution of marriage and family is the bedrock of society, but to elevate it to the same level as fundamental rights would fundamentally change the whole complexion and schema of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There are many important laws and principles that are not in the Constitution but are in Acts of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, National Service is in the Enlistment Act; Corruption is in the Prevention of Corruption Act; zero-tolerance to drugs is in the Misuse of Drugs Act; and home ownership is in the HDB Act.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But what we want to be clear about is that the definition of marriage and related policies should not be determined by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, this constitutional amendment provides greater protection than today, not just for the definition of marriage, but also related policies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Prime Minister has said that this Government has no intention of changing the definition of marriage, nor the policies that rely on this definition.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ultimately, whether marriage in Singapore will remain as a union between a man and a woman depends on the consensus in society, shaped by the values we all hold.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So long as society strongly supports the current definition of marriage, no Government will change the definition.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If society's support erodes, no amount of legislation or constitutional entrenchment will prevent change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On our part, the Government is doing all it can to promote social norms and values aligned to the current definition of marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But it is not something the Government can accomplish on its own.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The transmission of social values to the next generation is something Singaporeans practise within their own families and with their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore is a secular state, but a multi-religious and a multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are one of the most diverse societies in the world.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There are different ethnic and religious groups, each with their own practices, customs, norms, convictions and beliefs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This diversity and harmony make Singapore unique and is a key part of our Singaporean identity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not easy to hold such a diverse society together.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are a young nation and all of us have taken great care and effort to preserve the harmony and peace that we have.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have been able to live together peacefully because we learn to understand, go beyond our own perspectives and graciously accommodate one another.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This has been the Singapore way because we recognise what is best for our society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some may wish to maximise their own positions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But when this happens, it unsettles others and causes resistance which would lead to further pushback and split our society apart.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore will not come out well in the end.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is therefore important that certain groups do not push beyond what is acceptable to our society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In most cases, society needs time to adjust to change, especially on issues that can polarise us.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We may have different ideals and perspectives, but we are all Singaporeans and I hope this is an identity we continue to be proud of.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We forge a majority based on what we share in common and what unites us.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why the Government has consistently emphasised the importance of preserving our common space, fostering good citizens and upholding the principle of equality, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Only then can we be united as Singaporeans to achieve progress as a nation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are fortunate that our religious leaders understand the context of our diverse society and their communities trust the Government to treat all faiths completely impartially.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: While they are honest and constructive in providing their views on matters of concern in their religious communities, they trust that laws and policies are in the national interest and not to favour one religion over another.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This approach works because the Government on its part is fair and considers all perspectives, including those who are religious as well as those who are not religious.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: No one can act only for the interests of a few segments of the society without regard for the rest.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Maintaining this approach requires wisdom and courage from everyone.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As we see in other societies, it is very easy to yield to sectarian or tribalist views.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even if you do not win, you will be popular with them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We also continue to protect all from scorn or harm.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes homosexuals who are members of our society, our kith and our kin.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Homosexuals have a place in our society and space to live their lives in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In our families, we should not exclude our loved ones who are homosexuals.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In our communities, they, like other Singaporeans, have access to education and employment, to healthcare and social services, to protection from violence and harassment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Workplace discrimination against homosexuals for reasons unrelated to their ability to do the job is a breach of the principle of fair and merit-based employment outlined in the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But on marriage and family, most Singaporeans wish to retain current norms.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As I have mentioned before, it is the Government's view as well.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As a society, regardless of your views on marriage, family or homosexuality, no one should feel unsafe expressing your views or fear being cancelled, bullied or discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is dangerous for our society if we do not learn to respect others who hold differing views from us.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This threatens the common space and Singapore will not be able to progress as a cohesive society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes religious leaders, asatizah as well as community leaders and Malay/Muslim organisations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many were initially worried that it would result in sudden changes to other policies such as the definition of marriage, adoption, regulation of media content and educational curriculum as well as the overall approach on the issue.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will enable the Government to continue upholding the definition of marriage and the policies that depend on it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In all the discussions, I am pleased with the attitude of our community leaders who were able to discuss these issues in a calm and rational manner.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the same time, the Mufti also explained that the homosexual lifestyle does not remove a person from his faith.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They must still be treated with kindness and compassion, particularly by their own families.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The openness of community leaders and the wisdom of our religious scholars have prevented a situation where emotions of the community on this matter can be intentionally inflamed.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: (In English): Sir, I believe that many of us appreciate this secular approach that has provided Singaporeans security and safety living together and the freedom to practise our religion.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Religious groups can continue to preach about homosexuality according to their religious beliefs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, for all the diverse groups that may be for or against homosexuality, no one can violate the laws of the land or instigate violence or intimidation towards others or a particular group.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are protected by the constitutional right to be free to profess, practise and propagate our religion.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is subject to considerations of public order, public health or morality.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is one that we share in common as Singaporeans and what this Government believes in and stands for.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is how we have come so far and will enable our society to perpetuate and flourish in the future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is in the public interest and not the narrow interest of a specific religious group.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our community leaders, many of whom we have engaged on this issue, also support our pro-family approach and have helped families over the years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They will continue to have a critical role in maintaining social cohesion and rallying support for our family values.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Such is the system that ensures the safety, survival and success of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: No one group can have everything they want all the time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must also redouble our efforts to sustain this system that has brought about peace and harmony in our multi-religious and multi-ethnic society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As we advocate for what we believe in, let us also do it respectfully and in the knowledge that we are united by our Singaporean identity.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Minister Masagos has explained the reasons for the constitutional amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the past year, we have engaged extensively with various groups, some, several times.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those we spoke with include religious leaders, LGBT groups, community leaders, people who want heterosexual marriage as a social norm, youth groups, members of the public who had written to us and many others.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For many who did not believe that section 377A should be repealed, their main concerns were about the consequences of the repeal of section 377A, what will happen after the section is repealed and not because they thought gay sex between men should in itself be criminalised.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In considering whether we should repeal section 377A, I will cover three areas.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, the political compromise that has been struck in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And third, the reasons for now moving on the repeal.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Why do we have to look at the history?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need to understand why and how section 377A became part of the law, whether it was a deliberate, considered decision or perhaps more of happenstance.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The term "gross indecency" can include both non-penetrative and penetrative sex acts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Attorney General Howell moved the Bill in 1938.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He said that section 377A was being introduced to bring our law in line with the UK criminal law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, to understand the genesis of section 377A, we would need to look at the original UK law passed 137 years ago, which is section 11 of the UK Criminal Law Amendment Act (UKCL).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 377A is an almost a word-for-word copy of section 11 of the UKCL.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 11 of the UKCL was passed in 1885.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Its origin is quite obscure and we have not been able to find any background, which explains why this section was introduced and made into law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The unrelated bill was meant to protect women and girls and for the suppression of brothels.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At that point, that unrelated bill on protection of women and girls had already been through a four-year long process, it had endured a long debate in parliament and it had passed the House of Lords without the amendment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The unrelated amendment on male homosexuality was introduced by a member of parliament, Mr Henry Labouchere.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: His motives for introducing section 11 into the bill on protection of women and girls are unclear.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One school of thought is that Mr Labouchere had intended it to be a "wrecking amendment", to derail and discredit the entire bill on protection of women and girls.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In fact, he had introduced another amendment to the same bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another member of parliament said that Mr Labouchere "couldn't have been serious in introducing that other amendment." Academics who have studied the matter have pointed to Mr Labouchere's habitual parliamentary obstructionist technique.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He would make spoiling amendments to discredit bills that have been introduced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another school of thought is that Mr Labouchere was fiercely homophobic and so he introduced the amendment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Labouchere himself gave an explanation in parliament for why he introduced section 11 and his explanation raises more questions than it answered.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He said that his amendment was to protect any person from an assault of "the kind dealt with" under section 11, whether the person was above, or under, the age of 13 years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After that short explanation, he said that he did not think it was necessary to discuss the proposal at any length because the government was willing to accept it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we take at face value what Mr Labouchere said in parliament in 1885, then the purpose of section 11 was to prevent an indecent assault by one male against another male.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The provision here introduced, which was passed into law, was however much wider than that, including those where the sex acts were done between consenting male adults.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, the amendment that was introduced was quite different from the explanation that was given.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Indeed, the explanation he gave is somewhat contrary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The amendment was dealt with in parliament for less than four minutes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There was no discussion about the fact that the provision criminalises consenting male homosexual behaviour even though the stated purpose was to criminalise sexual assaults.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People have spent time trying to work out the motives of Mr Labouchere and the reasons that the UK parliament passed the amendment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some have suggested that the members were fatigued by the late hour – it was 2.30 am – and that the members had been worn out by the long debate on the bill to protect women and girls which, as I said earlier, had taken four years and that the members had just wanted to get on with it, to let the amendment through.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is the genesis, the background to the law passed in 1885 which has gone on to impact the lives of tens of thousands of people and has caused much controversy and intense debate in many countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members may also access the Annexes through the SG Parl Mobile App.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sodomy was first criminalised under the Buggery Act 1533 during the reign of King Henry VIII.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason this law was passed is linked to a specific, important, historical event in British history and not because there was any specific intention to make sodomy a crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have in Annex 1, set out the background and context to how and why the Buggery Act was passed into law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prior to 1533, sodomy was considered an offence punished by the church.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was only tried in the Ecclesiastical Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In other words, not a crime as defined by the state; it was an offence in a religious context to be dealt with by the church.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members would know that Henry VIII broke with the church in Rome, started the Church of England, with him as the head of the church.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He wanted to reduce the power of the church and one of the ways he did that was to reduce the power of the Ecclesiastical Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He did that by converting many of the church's canon laws into secular laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Buggery Act was one such law that was brought over from the canon laws and made into secular criminal law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That way, the King's courts would deal with the matter and the churches' jurisdiction was removed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What happened thereafter is also useful to note.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When she became Queen in 1553, she abolished the Buggery Act and moved it back to the Ecclesiastical Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Queen Elizabeth, another of Henry's daughter, succeeded Queen Mary five years later in 1558.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were questions on her legitimacy and her claims to the throne.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She took several steps to establish her legitimacy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And one of the steps she took was to reduce the role of the church by moving the laws out of canon laws and making them secular laws to show that she was following in her father's footsteps.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Buggery Act became secular criminal law again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am setting out the historical context factually, not suggesting that sodomy ought or ought not to have been criminalised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second Act that was used to prosecute homosexual conduct was the offence of solicitating or importuning in public places for immoral purposes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was first introduced under the Vagrancy Act 1898.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was initially intended to target pimps, men who lived off the earnings of female prostitutes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In practice, however, the legislation was used almost exclusively to prosecute men who engaged in homosexual conduct in public, though male homosexuality was not discussed in parliament when the bill was first introduced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third offence was the offence of indecent assault against males.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was first introduced in under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The offence criminalised homosexual acts committed against males without consent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was introduced as a part of a wider omnibus bill consolidating all offences against the person and was included in the same provision as an offence of attempting to commit sodomy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Unfortunately, the provision and its overlap with existing homosexual offences and even male homosexuality were not discussed at all during the parliamentary debates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we see is that these provisions, when they were first introduced, there was no substantive deliberation on whether there was indeed a need to criminalise homosexual behaviour and it looks more like happenstance than a deliberate decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Regardless, the criminal provisions were retained as part of the UK's criminal law until the 1960s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee stated that it was not charged to enter into matters of private moral conduct except insofar as they directly affect the public good.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee was only concerned with whether homosexual behaviour should be dealt with under the criminal law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee concluded that the function of criminal law was three-fold: one, to preserve public order and decency; two, to protect the citizen from what is offensive and injurious; and three, to provide sufficient safeguards against the exploitation and corruption of others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In their view, it was not the function of criminal law to intervene in the private lives of citizens or to seek to enforce any particular pattern of behaviour, further than it was necessary to carry out these three functions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee stated that: "Unless a deliberate attempt be made by society through the agency of the law to equate the sphere of crime with that of sin, there must remain a realm of private morality and immorality which is not the law's business.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To say this, is not to condone or encourage private immorality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Moral conviction or instinctive feeling, however strong, is not a valid basis for over-riding the individual's privacy and for bringing within the ambit of the criminal law private sexual behaviour of this kind." The committee accepted that homosexual behaviour between males could have a damaging effect on family life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think many Singaporeans believe this as well and we must acknowledge these feelings and beliefs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee, however, emphasised that this damage was no greater than many other activities which were sins and may be considered immoral but were not otherwise criminal offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The debate continued through the late 1950s and early 1960s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Law students may recall the well-known debate between Lord Devlin and Professor Hart on the Wolfenden report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For Members' reference, I have summarised the points they made in Annex 7.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Eventually, Lord Devlin, who had argued for the criminalisation of shared morality, also said that private consensual homosexual sex between adults should be decriminalised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By that time, religious groups such as the Church of England and the Methodist Conference, and members of both houses had publicly expressed support for a change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The members of the House of Lords who spoke in support of decriminalisation included the Lord Chancellor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was the Speaker of the House of Lords and the Head of the Judiciary, as well as the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, who was the leader of the Church of England and the head of the global Anglican Union as well as various other bishops.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He stated upfront that he believed that homosexual acts were wrong, he went on to say that the case for amending the law rested on reason and justice, and on considerations of the good of the community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, to amend the law was not to condone the "wrongness" of the act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It, however, put such acts in the realm of private moral responsibility.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He believed that the law, as it stood, gave a sense of injustice and bitterness, which helped morality no more than would a law which made fornication a crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He further agreed with his predecessor that having such a law created fear, secretiveness and despair in gay persons who did not dare to seek help, lest they expose themselves and their friends to criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would add that not all religious groups were in favour of the change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some, such as the Church of Scotland and the Church of Ireland and the Baptist Church, objected to the reform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before I move on from the UK, I would like to highlight the context of Northern Ireland.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Northern Ireland was and is part of the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, the partial decriminalisation of homosexual conduct in the UK in 1967 only applied to the mainland and did not apply to Northern Ireland.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Northern Ireland’s path to decriminalisation started instead from the courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, at that time, Northern Ireland’s society was deeply religious, largely conservative and the majority of the population on Northern Ireland opposed the decriminalisation, including most of the Protestant Churches as well as the Roman Catholic Church.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill was opposed by all 12 of the Northern Ireland members of parliament in the UK parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, nonetheless, it passed through both Houses by majority vote.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Northern Ireland’s experience shows how a court decision can force a change even though a society is not ready for such a change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, homosexuality remains a deeply divisive issue around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is true even within more religiously homogenous communities, such as the Church of England and the Global Anglican Church.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we look at the Anglican Communion, it comprises 42 member churches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is the third largest Christian communion after the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For decades, there has been a strong difference of views within the Anglican Communion on whether same-sex unions can be legitimised and blessed and whether persons living in same-sex relationships can be ordained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Anglican churches in the Global North, such as in the US and Canada, are increasingly supportive of homosexuality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They allow same-sex marriages and ordain persons in same-sex relationships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, several Anglican Churches from the Global South do not agree with this approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This has resulted in the creation of the Global Anglican Future Conference, or GAFCON, in 2008, led by the more conservative Anglican bishops and leaders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the Church of England, LGBT issues have also been the subject of intense debate for decades.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mentioned earlier that the Church of England had supported the partial decriminalisation of homosexual conduct in the UK in 1967.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But actually, within the Church of England, there was no consensus.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Church was more or less equally split on the issue when it was put to a vote.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of its 735 members, 155 voted in favour, 138 voted against, and the rest either absented themselves or abstained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there continues to be strong differences in viewpoints on this issue, as Members may have seen from recent media reports.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, that even within a single religious community, it is difficult to agree on the “right” answer, assuming there is one, on the issue of homosexuality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, that homosexuality is a topic that continues to raise strong viewpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, that if we do not handle this carefully, homosexuality can be a deeply divisive issue even among those who share a common belief.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the international media outlets that report on these issues often gloss over these differences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They gloss over the problems their societies face, and do not understand the need to deal with these issues sensitively, with understanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They present views as if they are settled and that anyone who has a negative view of male homosexuality is a bigot and is wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the US, it is considered more accepting of LGBT rights than many other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the country is internally split over this issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, in the Republican states of Florida and Texas, there remain strong objections to LGBT rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They state, and I quote: “Homosexuality is an abnormal lifestyle choice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We believe there should be no granting of special legal entitlements or creation of special status for homosexual behaviour, regardless of state of origin, and we oppose any criminal or civil penalties against those who oppose homosexuality out of faith, conviction or belief in traditional values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one should be granted special legal status based on their LGBTQ+ identification.” But other Republicans have different views on homosexuality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These were persons who identified themselves as Republicans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at, say, Italy – I will not go through in detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have in set out what has been happening in Italy in Annex 2.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have laid out examples of how, within the same religion, the same denomination, the same churches within the denomination and in wider society, within some Western countries, even those who are often described as "liberal", the issues remain deeply divisive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To be clear, it is not the exact same issue in all these communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some, the division is about homosexuality in itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some, it is about the roles of LGBT people, for example, in church ordination.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In others, it is other related issues like same-sex unions that are divisive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Around the world, in several countries, as well as in jurisdictions and territories which are not quite countries, several have decriminalised their version of section 377A, including Commonwealth and Southeast Asian countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some have decriminalised it through the parliamentary process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some have had their section 377A equivalent struck down by the courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But there are also some countries which continue to keep the criminal laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Slides 1 and 2 of Annex 3 show the countries, territories and jurisdictions that have decriminalised homosexuality and those which have not done so, because not all the places in these two slides are countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Slide 3 shows the same for Asian states, places and jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can see that across the world there are different approaches, even though there is a trend towards decriminalisation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, we look carefully at international trends, but we do not simply follow such trends.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We chart our own path based on what we believe is in our own best interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we are very clear to foreign governments and companies that these are political, social and moral choices for Singaporeans to decide and that they should not interfere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MFA spoke to the embassy to remind them not to interfere in our domestic politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: More recently, in August this year, US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi issued a statement when she was in Singapore asking business groups to support the LGBT community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MHA issued a statement reminding foreign businesses to be careful about advocating on socially divisive issues in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We would also say to US politicians who feel very strongly about these issues that perhaps they should first try and persuade the people in Texas and other such places before they issue statements in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, section 377A was substantively debated in Parliament 15 years ago in 2007, during the Second Reading of the Penal Code (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the course of two days, 16 Members of Parliament and Nominated Members of Parliament rose to speak on section 377A, to argue for, and against, its retention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have summarised the different positions taken by the Members of Parliament and Nominated Members of Parliament in Annex 4.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister spoke and stated the Government's position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that Singaporeans as a whole remained largely conservative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The majority wanted to keep Singapore a conservative society with heterosexual stable families.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But at the same time, there was growing science-based evidence that sexual orientation was substantially inborn.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Gay people must have a place in society and they are entitled to their private lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But there were still very different views among Singaporeans on whether homosexuality was acceptable or morally right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, LGBT advocacy should not set the tone for the rest of Singapore society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was a very Singaporean way of dealing with the situation, which best fitted with the way our society was.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister also reminded Members that section 377A was inherited from the British and that Asian societies which were similar to ours did not have such laws – not in Japan, not in China and not in Taiwan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if we forced the issue, it would divide and polarise our society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would lead to even less space for the gay community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, it was better to let the situation evolve gradually.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was better and it has worked for Singapore in the past 15 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We managed to maintain some harmony while many other societies have become deeply divided on these issues over the same period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, it is the right thing to do and society is more ready now for the repeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some religions, homosexuality is considered a sin.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Members heard earlier, some sins are crimes, but not every sin is a crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our position in Singapore is, for a conduct to be a crime, there should, generally, be a public order or public interest issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is broadly similar to the position set out by the Wolfenden Committee, which I referred to earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The basic function of criminal law is to preserve public order and decency, to protect citizens from what is offensive and injurious, and to provide sufficient safeguards against exploitation and corruption of others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, like in many other places, it is, generally, not the function of criminal law to intervene in the private lives of citizens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As we consider this question, it is also important to understand what will remain criminalised, even if section 377A is repealed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, non-consensual sexual assault by males against other males will obviously be an offence, and it is a serious offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, sexual acts committed by males against young persons, again, a serious offence regardless of consent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three, sexual acts between two males committed in public that offend public decency will remain an offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The maximum penalty for the first two offences is, in fact, more severe than the maximum penalty under section 377A and rightly so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Government takes an extremely stern view against all non-consensual sexual offences and in respect of sexual offences against minors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most gay people do not cause harm to others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They just want to live peacefully and quietly and be accepted as part of society – the same as any other Singaporean.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are our family, our friends, our colleagues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They do not deserve to be stigmatised because of their sexual orientation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To a gay person, even if section 377A is not enforced, it is there, memorialised in the law, a sword hanging over his head, a daily reminder that every time he engages in private sexual activity, behind closed doors, in the sanctity of his bedroom, he is, nevertheless, a criminal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to ask, is it fair that gays have to live in this way?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is not something we should accept, even if we personally disagree with homosexuality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I will say – let us start to deal with these divides, heal these divides, remove their pain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Repealing section 377A makes it clear that gay people are not criminals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Compared to 2007, we are now at a stage where our society can accept the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From our engagements, we see that most Singaporeans accept that sex between men should not be a crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even those who want to retain section 377A, do not want to see it actively enforced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as has been stated, in and out of Parliament, we must, and we will take steps at the same time to deal with the possible consequences of the repeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because some consequences would be unacceptable to a significant section of our society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government has explained its position about dealing with consequences, Members can refer to Annex 5 for a summary of what the Prime Minister, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, various Ministries, as well as I, have said on the matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts may strike down section 377A in the future and if the Courts strike down section 377A, it will be a binary process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts cannot deal with all the legitimate concerns about the consequential effects of the repeal, which many are concerned about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why do we say there is a significant legal risk of section 377A being struck down?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts of Appeal has dealt with section 377A twice in the last 10 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, in Lim Meng Suang vs Attorney-General, decided in 2014; and second, in Tan Seng Kee vs Attorney-General, decided earlier this year in 2022.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Both decisions took quite different approaches on two issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, a procedural issue; and second, a substantive issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Lim Meng Suang, the Court made a procedural decision in 2012 and the substantive decision in 2014.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The procedural decision was on standing – whether the applicants had locus standi, or standing, whether they were entitled to make the application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal said that the applicants did have locus standi because there was a real and credible threat of future prosecution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal further added that even if no prosecution was contemplated, the applicants could bring their action, they had standing, because of the very existence of a law which is unconstitutional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members should note the Court of Appeal in 2012 said the very existence of 377A gave locus standi, for an applicant to make an application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On Article 12, the Court of Appeal applied a legal test, known as a "reasonable classification" test, to come to that conclusion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It said that section 377A satisfied that test and did not violate Article 12.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal, therefore, dismissed the application in Lim Meng Suang, on the substantive basis that section 377A was not unconstitutional, even though the applicants had locus standi to bring the challenge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 377A was then challenged again in the Courts in Tan Seng Kee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was again argued that section 377A contravened Articles 9 and 12.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, section 377A was also challenged, on the grounds that it contravened Article 14 of the Constitution, which guaranteed the right of freedom of speech and expression.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Court deliberately did not rule on one of the substantive grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, on the procedural issue, the Court of Appeal reversed itself on the locus standi point and took a different view from its earlier decision in Lim Meng Suang.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, according to the Court of Appeal, the applicants did not face any real or credible threat of prosecution under 377A and so, they did not have standing to bring the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Lim Meng Suang, the Court of Appeal had said that the very existence of 377A was enough to give locus standi.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Tan Seng Kee, the Court took a diametrically opposite view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will note one Court of Appeal can disagree with another Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is also significant to see what the Court of Appeal had to say in Tan Seng Kee on the substantive issue, as to whether section 377A was unconstitutional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal actually did not need to give any view on the substantive merits of the challenge because it had already said that the applicants could not bring the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it, nevertheless, went on to give its views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal first considered the arguments in relation to Article 9 of the Constitution, on life and personal liberty, and said, quite clearly, that section 377A did not violate Article 9.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court, then, considered whether section 377A contravened Article 14 on freedom of speech and expression, and it said no, there was no contravention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, it considered Article 12, the equal protection clause, on this, the Court of Appeal took a different view from its previous decision in Lim Meng Suang.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal said that there were two ways to apply the "reasonable classification" test: one is the approach adopted in Lim Meng Suang in 2014; and the second was the approach adopted in a 2021 case in Syed Suhail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal went into a detailed comparison between the two approaches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court said that if the Syed Suhail approach is taken, then section 377A might fall afoul of the "reasonable classification" test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even though the Court of Appeal was careful to say section 377A might be unconstitutional if the test in Syed Suhail was applied, lawyers would know – at least some lawyers would know – that the Court of Appeal has, in fact, in subsequent cases applied the Syed Suhail test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the decision in Tan Seng Kee, the Court of Appeal has applied the Syed Suhail test and approach in two other cases, in May and August of this year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In May 2022, in Datchinamurthy a/l Kataiah vs Attorney-General; and in August 2022, in Terry Xu's case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What does all of this mean, in plain language?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Members could say, "Well, we accept what the Court of Appeal has said".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Taking such a view, I can give an analogy; it is like letting a small boat sail in choppy waters surrounded by rocks and hoping that the boat would not crash into the rocks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are two major risks in taking this view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, just because the applicants in Tan Seng Kee did not have standing, does not mean that no one else will have standing in a future case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But such persons may well have a case for standing by arguing that their rights had been violated and, therefore, that they have sufficient interest to challenge the constitutionality of section 377A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will not be able to directly reopen their convictions, but they can ask for section 377A to be struck down on the basis that this will give them vindication.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the very fact that they have been convicted under an unconstitutional legislation gives them the standing and to allow them to redress the hurt of their conviction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Tan Seng Kee, the Court of Appeal was very careful to circumscribe what it said about who had locus standi.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It expressly stated that its decision on locus standi will not, for example, prevent the Police from investigating conduct under section 377A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In reality, there is a broad universe of cases where the Police may have to investigate, because before investigating, they might not know exactly what the facts are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you cannot rule out the possibility that in some situations, a person involved in the investigations brings a challenge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you cannot rule out there a future Court could find this to be sufficient grounds for a person to have locus standi to challenge section 377A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, of course, there is the other risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal can always change its mind on locus standi, just as it did between Lim Meng Suang and Tan Seng Kee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It changed its mind precisely on this point of locus standi.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we cannot proceed in the belief that the Court of Appeal will certainly not change its views in the future.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In September this year, I took part in a law forum organised by the Singapore Academy of Law and the Law Society, which discussed the implications of Tan Seng Kee and the legal risks surrounding section 377A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was a panel discussion moderated by the Dean of the SMU law school.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The panel and audience included the Dean of SUSS law school, legal scholars from our law faculties, past and present presidents of the Law Society, Senior Counsel and distinguished senior legal experts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The panel and the audience were pretty unanimous on the legal risks surrounding section 377A, in light of Tan Seng Kee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can refer to Annex 6 for key points and views that were shared at the law forum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will be just wishful thinking, and wishful thinking is no substitute for careful legal analysis or proper policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we engage in wishful thinking and if section 377A is struck down in the Courts, that could lead to a whole series of consequences, which would be very damaging to our Singaporean society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But before I do that, it is useful to look at what happened in India, as an illustration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In India, their section 377 was challenged on grounds broadly similar to those used to challenge our section 377A in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2009, the Delhi high court ruled that their section 377 was unconstitutional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The court then said that its decision would apply only until parliament repealed section 377 as per the recommendations made by a law commission in 2000, nine years before the decision of the court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the judgment, however, the Indian parliament did not do anything about the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The government also did not appeal the high court judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, an appeal was brought by some organisations and individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On appeal in 2013, the Indian supreme court overturned the high court decision, saying there was no "constitutional infirmity".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, section 377 was held to be constitutional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nonetheless, the court emphasised that parliament was still free to consider the desirability and propriety of deleting section 377 from the Indian Penal Code or amending it to exclude private acts between consenting adults.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2016, a fresh application was filed in the Indian supreme court to again challenge the constitutionality of section 377.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2018, the Indian supreme court ruled section 377 to be unconstitutional with regard to consensual acts between adults.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It reversed its 2013 decision on the grounds that section 377 violated the right to life and liberty, which is Article 9 of our Constitution, that it violated the right to equal protection, which is Article 12 of our Constitution, and that it violated the right to freedom of expression, which is Article 14 of our Constitution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the court found that section 377 did punish homosexuals arbitrarily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The court said that a subjective notion of public or societal morality which discriminated against LGBT persons and subjected them to criminal sanctions, simply on the basis of an innate characteristic ran counter to the Indian constitution and could not form the basis of legitimate state interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The court held that parliament's failure to delete section 377 was not, in any way, a good reason for the court not to strike down section 377.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When a provision violated the constitution, the courts must strike it down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fast forward to this year, 2022, as Minister Masagos had mentioned in his speech, the Indian supreme court has expanded the definition of family to include same-sex relationships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The court held that such atypical manifestations of the family unit are equally deserving of protection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When Parliament does not act when it should act, then we may leave the courts with no choice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If fundamental constitutional rights have been violated and, yet, Parliament abdicates its duties, then the Courts may have no choice but to act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be argued that equal protection means we cannot discriminate against same-sex couples, in the same way that section 377A can be said to discriminate against gay persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be asked: why should a marriage only be between a man and a woman?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why can a marriage between two men or between two women not be considered a marriage?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some places, jurisdictions like Taiwan and some countries like the US, have ended up legalising same-sex marriage through court challenges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As mentioned earlier, India's supreme court also recently said that "family" will include same-sex relationships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, so far, the Courts have recognised that Parliament, as the elected branch of Government, is better suited to resolve such difficult societal issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Parliament, there can be consultation, discussion and debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Considerations going well beyond the law can be taken into account, whereas Courts can only consider the legal issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Consensus can be forged in Parliament to bridge divergent viewpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Open-ended resolutions are possible, instead of binary, win-lose outcomes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some who have said, since our Courts have recognised what belongs to the political process and what belongs to the judicial process, it is unlikely that the Courts will ever strike down section 377A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In other words, we can just take the easy way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But such an approach would be irresponsible and wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we should not assume that the Courts will never strike down section 377A just because the Government chooses to retain it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our system has only worked well all these years because all three branches of the state – Parliament, the Executive and the Judiciary – work within their respective boundaries and have fulfilled their respective roles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if Parliament does not do its duty, if Parliament does not deal with the law which is likely unconstitutional, then, you may leave the Courts with no choice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Parliament does not do what it has to do, then the Courts will have to do what they do not want to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I emphasise: Parliament has a duty to deal squarely with laws which are unconstitutional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Parliament abdicates its duty and does not do what it has to do, then the Courts may have to do what they do not want to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would be much easier for us, as Members of Parliament, to leave this to the Courts – "leave the question to the wisdom of the honourable Court", as the Indian government did.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we left it to the Courts, the Government would bear no blame.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we approached this purely as politicians, concerned only with votes, and not making anyone unhappy or making as few people unhappy as possible, then, that road of leaving it to the Court would have been easier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Pretend that these issues do not exist, need not have been talked about after the Court of Appeal's decision in Tan Seng Kee, leave it to the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this Government will not take that approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As elected representatives of the people, we cannot do that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, the Court processes are adversarial by nature.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no middle ground, no balancing of competing interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts cannot consider competing social norms and social consequences of their decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Going further, if the definition of marriage is changed through a Court challenge, there can be a cascading effect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could impact questions relating to same-sex marriage, media content, housing policies and various other policies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be asked: why should we only give housing benefits to heterosexual married couples?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be argued that that is unequal under Article 12.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should we impose higher ratings for content on movies and Netflix that depict same-sex family units?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be argued that this curtails some producers' freedom of expression under Article 9.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such changes through the Court are not in our interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we want to act in the best interests of Singapore, then, we have to move on this, given the legal analysis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can look at the United States to see how Court decisions on such issues can seriously affect the fabric of society, divide the society, unleash partisan views on both sides of the divide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we have that in Singapore, our social fabric will fray.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Government and Parliament do not take responsibility and, instead, stand by and do nothing, then, litigation could change our societal norms very quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
