text: I have given two reasons for proposing the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, we should do so because there are no public order issues that are raised from such conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I accept that Members of Parliament (MPs) and others may disagree with that, that even though there are no public order issues, they may feel that there are other reasons for keeping the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I accept that people can and do legitimately have such views and it is reasonable to hold such views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the second reason I have given, the legal consequences, that is not a matter of conscience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires each of us to think carefully and apply our minds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second question is a matter of considering the consequences for Singapore, given that there is a clear legal risk that section 377A could be struck down and given that, having heard me, you know what the consequential legal risks are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, this has been talked about in public – what the consequential legal risks are to the heterosexual family, housing, education, other policies, that they could all be at risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Knowing all these risks and refusing to take a position or be clear in how we will deal with it, is avoiding our responsibilities as MPs, basically, passing it on to the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is easier politically, but it is also worse for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, to put it bluntly, that will be an abdication of duty and it will be cynical if we, as MPs, did that, because we would be putting, if we take this as a deliberate decision, political capital over doing what is good for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Speaker, I believe that, in this House, if we proceed in good faith, there are matters of conscience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But ultimately, there is also the question of what is in Singapore's interest and what is in the interest of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the law here and the legal consequences here, go beyond matters of conscience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Section 377A of the Penal Code	– which I will henceforth refer to as 377A – that criminalises homosexual conduct in private, is such an issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some Singaporeans, it is a very difficult subject.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For others, especially younger Singaporeans, they wonder why it has to be a difficult subject and why people of a different sexual orientation cannot be treated as equal Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In recent years, the issue has caused growing tensions between groups who identify themselves for and against the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans have formed organisations and groups on the issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the personal level, the conversations can be uncomfortable and discussing the subject without measure and consideration can quickly pull people apart.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In normal circumstances, I would not lift the whip for Parliamentary debates, given the party political structure that overlays elected MPs in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, 377A is unique in that it is conceived through a religious lens by many in Singapore, in addition to being a matter of conscience for a no less significant number.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The People's Action Party has announced that it is not lifting the whip for this debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Given the very public opinion on the impending repeal of 377A, there is a risk that the democratic value of the Parliament could be diluted if the views of Singaporeans on this subject are not adequately ventilated in the House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In doing so, I have also asked all who will speak to carefully reflect on the position they take and to envision a set of principles or perspectives from which society as a whole, with its different views, can move forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How can we mitigate this and contribute to lowering temperatures and ensuring Singapore is a home for everyone?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The other Workers' Party MPs will state their positions on the matter in the course of their speeches.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2019, in my first term as Secretary-General of the Workers' Party, I stated the Workers' Party's position on 377A in a speech to the National University of Singapore Political Association.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The party position I advanced was similar to that of Singapore as a whole – it was varied and diverse, with no consensus as to whether 377A should be repealed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The depth of the impasse in Singapore society at that time was stark and encapsulated somewhat in a panel discussion between Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam and Prof Tommy Koh on the Institute of Policy Studies' 30th anniversary in late 2018.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prof Koh said, "A mutual friend of ours was recently invited by one of our religious organisations to speak at a conference on a secular topic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He accepted, prepared the paper and then he was disinvited.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because he signed the petition to repeal 377A." Such has been the divisiveness over 377A.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my 2019 speech, I said that the LGBTQ+ community should not be exploited for political points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At that time, I believe there was more to consider than deciding which was the right side in this matter, particularly in a society which generally eschews from posting open and frank conversations on difficult matters in the public realm.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Against this political culture and background, the Workers' Party neither took up the cause of LGBTQ+ rights, nor stood against it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I still believe that had the Workers' Party openly supported a repeal of 377A, it would not have been good for Singapore politics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More crucially, it would have not served the interest of the LGBTQ+ community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On issues of great social division and contending values, we do not need politicians to be seen as siding with particular groups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From my vantage point as the Leader of the Opposition, my personal belief is that the repeal of 377A does not in any way signal the state's hostility towards the family unit or religious freedom.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Rest assured, the family remains and, I dare say, will always be at the core of our social norms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to reiterate that defending the Singaporean family also means doing more to protect its different forms, including families with single, widowed and divorced mothers and fathers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must do more to help caregivers who perform the labour of caring for aged parents and those with special needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What the repeal of 377A certainly does not signal is Singapore becoming a more liberal or permissive society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What it does is make room in our shared public space for members of our common Singaporean family to not be discriminated against due to their sexual orientation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Religious Singaporeans are free to maintain their beliefs about homosexuality, but this should not interfere with what is legal in our public sphere.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Likewise, supporters of the repeal have no business interfering with the private beliefs of religious Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In any secular society, sin and crime are separate categories.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, we have laws prohibiting crimes such as murder that are also considered wrong in many belief systems.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But we also do not outlaw many activities considered sinful in some religious communities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Consuming alcohol and pork are legal but not permissible to Muslims.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are also no laws against eating meat, though this is not an option for Jains and some Hindus and Buddhists.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In singling homosexuality between men in particular, the decision to keep 377A appears to the LGBTQ+ community and not a small number of Singaporeans, to be unjust and unequal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An important reality is that the political compromise in place since 2007 undermined the sense of belonging of Singapore's LGBTQ+ community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Though unenforced, one should not underestimate its symbolic message that they are outsiders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, this so-called compromise is not binding on future governments who could choose to enforce the law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet, repealing 377A will no doubt cause anxiety, if not outrage, amongst Singaporeans who believe that our laws must also reflect cultural or religious attitudes towards homosexuality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are Singaporeans who see this as an erosion of the family as a basic unit of Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality of our political culture, which leans towards conservatism on social issues, is that such concerns cannot be summarily ignored or dismissed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the stark reality before this House and Singaporeans today is that there were never any good options before the Government that could please everybody with regard to managing the tensions of 377A.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Keeping to the status quo indefinitely would only shine an ever brighter spotlight on the issue, particularly as social mores regionally and locally continue a steady shift towards greater acceptance and accommodation of LGBTQ+ individuals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like many Singaporeans, I could understand why the uneasy compromise set out by the Prime Minister in 2007 was deemed to be a midpoint that would keep any excessive social cleavage in check.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also represents a balancing exercise to ensure that society does not fray over the decision to repeal 377A.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope Singaporeans who are against the repeal of 377A approach this issue – in spite of their personal beliefs and religious convictions, which I and my colleagues respect, and I suggest everyone in this House respects – through this lens of compromise and accommodation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Equality and justice, both stars in our flag, are plenty and bountiful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike finite resources, we do not have less of either by extending it to our fellow citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We all gain from a more just and equal society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We can also look to some of the timeless principles shared amongst all great faiths.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The blessed irony here is that religion plays a huge part in inspiring our best qualities as human beings – to be generous, to love our neighbour and to be merciful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These qualities do not weaken but strengthen our faith.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Wherever you stand on this decision, I hope Singaporeans approach our LGBTQ+ community, who are a small minority of the population, like they are anywhere in the world, with these qualities in mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More than ever, with the impending repeal of 377A, Singaporeans on all sides must come together in good faith and mutual trust to not let this issue further tear our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am certain the decision of this House is not a panacea that repairs the tension between camps.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should anticipate that new battle lines will be drawn.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the LGBTQ+ community, the march towards greater equality has not ended.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some conservatives are likely to mobilise to try and stop any further expansion of LGBTQ+ rights.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the socially divisive nature of 377A, I would suggest three points that could help in keeping things from boiling over.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope Singaporeans can consider these as guideposts should they deem them useful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, any conversation must recognise that there is a distinction between public and private perspectives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just because one group has a position on an issue does not mean it can impose that position as a public expectation on everyone else.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because in Singapore, there must be a place for everyone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public space is for all to share and where we encourage a "live and let live", "give and take" attitude towards our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public space is where we create conditions for all Singaporeans to succeed and certainly, not to feel marginalised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public space is where we are tolerant of Singaporeans who are different, insofar as the law allows.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, the fact that we are a secular society does not stop religious Singaporeans from holding views that are reflective of their religious norms and values.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is fully understandable that the faithful wish to propagate their religious convictions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The heavy correspondence that I received and numerous meetings that I had with my constituents on this matter reflect that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am sure I am not alone in this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should these Bills be passed, it does not mean that the underlying issues will simply go away.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, the fact that we are considering these Bills, does signify a potential for this House to express its collective will and I heard the hon Opposition Leader say "collective values" as well, across party lines, and decide on the basis of what is in the greater good of our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members of Parliament deciding on matters based on national interest and public good, not their personal interests.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The well-known politician and philosopher, Sir Edmund Burke, said that parliament is not a congress of ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members of parliament will have to decide based on national interests and not just based on the opinions of their constituents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is where our involvement here becomes all the more important, because we cannot decide just on the basis of our personal views.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have to decide on the basis of what is the national interest, how best can we take Singapore forward and ensure that the future of Singaporeans will always remain bright.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is my view with respect to this issue?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand from the Leader of the Opposition that he has decided to lift the whip.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I just want to clarify that while the whip is not lifted for the People's Action Party, it does not prevent any Member of Parliament from my party to speak his views and I will shortly speak my views too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The whip is basically a system to deal with voting and that is separate and distinct from clearly and honestly expressing our views.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On my view, I can be relatively brief.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I said that anyone, regardless of his sexual orientation, is deserving of equal treatment, dignity and respect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: No one should be treated as social outcasts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Repealing section 377A is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Homosexual males in consenting relationships will no longer be viewed as criminals and we would have taken a decisive step in removing the stigma that they previously faced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the main principle underlying the repeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am indebted to the hon Minister Shanmugam for painstakingly reviewing the provision based on materials stretching back to the 16th century.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Listening to him, it seems to me that the legislative objective behind the equivalents of section 377A is also rather obscure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is in accord with the views of a significant majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are important lessons that can be drawn from the Government's approach in this House to deal with this issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, it is about ensuring that our nation for now and I hope, for at least the next 20 years, will continue to be united and stable and not fail to hold because of this divisive issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So much of what we do as a country depends on our unity and stability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We do this by making the political accommodation that these Bills collectively represent, something that the hon Prime Minister spoke about at some length during his National Day Rally 2022.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we need to guard against is the spectre of identity politics with the emphasis on a "all or nothing mindset".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If that happens in Singapore, I fear that it may be the beginning of the end of Singapore's cohesive social compact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, it is about acknowledging that our laws reflect the changing realities of our times.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This includes respecting the voices of all sections of society, including those of our youths – their voices on their vision and aspirations for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our youths shape the future of our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to forge an inter-generational understanding to keep us together as a society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our founding Prime Minister, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, pithily put this across in a speech he delivered way back in 1966, about the importance of working with our youths to create an enduring future in the context of multiracial harmony.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our values, our attitudes are fixed but the minds of the young are flexible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They come out with innocent minds…And we must give them the values of tolerance, understanding, togetherness and a society which gives everybody a meaningful life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in that way, we will secure an enduring future for ourselves".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, we have an opportunity as, currently, based on the same TODAY Youth Survey, three out of five youths support the importance of upholding the definition of marriage as between one man and a woman.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was reportedly attributed to our youths internalising the traditional definition of marriage as a norm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In our Westminster-styled Government, our judiciary is an independent Organ of State that is vested with the judicial power to decide on legal issues without interference from this House or the Executive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Being an unelected body, it is not directly accountable to our people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have seen examples in other countries where judges are accused of playing politics when deciding on legal issues that have major socio-political ramifications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Based on a September 2022 Pew Research Centre survey, Americans' ratings of the supreme court are now as negative as – and more politically polarised than – at any point in time, during the three decades of polling on the nation's highest court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such sentiments, undermine the confidence in and the legitimacy of the judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This in turn, this can affect the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And the way to do it is to ensure that the policy issues that have socio-political ramifications are dealt with firmly in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We, in this House, have a much better ability to deal with such thorny issues, as compared to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As elected representatives, we have a much better pulse on what our people think and what is needed to ensure our nation's cohesiveness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also have a unique ability to accommodate divergent views and reach a consensus that allows our society to march on and make progress.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In discussing this case in this House in January 2019, the hon Minister Mr Desmond Lee in a carefully worded statement, acknowledged that the decision has "evoked a diverse range of emotions and reactions amongst Singaporeans, and raised questions about its implications".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, it is best that we, in this House, continue to take the lead to set policies that have socio-political ramifications to preserve the legitimacy of our system of Government, particularly our judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have a query in relation to the proposed Article 156(3) and (4) of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Part 4 of the Constitution lists the fundamental liberties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are described in the 1957 Report of the Federation of Malaya Constitutional Commission, from which our Singapore Constitution was modelled on, as "fundamental individual rights which are generally regarded as essential conditions for a free and democratic way of life".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are eight rights enumerated in Part 4.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They include safeguards against liberty of a person, slavery, forced labour, protection against retrospective criminal laws, equal protection of all persons before the law, prohibition of banishment and freedom of movement, freedom of speech, religion and education.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, when it comes to laws against subversion and emergency powers, Article 149(1) of the Constitution specifically identifies five provisions that are to be excluded from Part 4.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I hope we see the difference in approach here – on matters of national security, we are careful enough to pick out specific exclusions because there are at least three individual rights that are so important so as to be able to stand up against issues pertaining to national security.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Why then, is there a need to adopt a blunderbuss approach in preserving legislation or Government action dealing with the definition of marriage as between a man and a woman?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be possible for the Government to identify specific provisions just as what was done for Article 149, and as the hon Minister said, Article 39(a), which deals with GRCs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I heard the hon Minister as saying that, the reason why he wants to have such a shield is because we may not know of an argument that can be raised in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But we are dealing with fundamental liberties and one of the reasons for having fundamental liberties is to curb excess of power, or have a situation whereby there will be an irrational use of power.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a matter of principle, we should be careful in providing for derogations to fundamental liberties of an individual as it would ordinarily be inimical to the concept of democracy and rule of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, may I ask whether it is intended that the Court's powers of judicial review of Government action on the traditional grounds of illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety be ousted?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I heard the hon Minister, he mentioned that that is not the intent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But then, maybe to articulate my point, let me give an illustration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Say, for example, a government in the future decides to banish a citizen, that is a fundamental liberty under Article 13, on the basis that he does not subscribe to a marriage between a man and a woman, or he enters into a marriage, which falls outside the definition in the Women's Charter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How can we then protect such a person from being banished?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Can the Courts exercise its judicial powers to provide a solution for such a person?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is due to the likely unconstitutionality of section 377A for violating Article 12, especially in the light of recent legal developments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish now to focus on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill now before the House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe it is important to study the various parts of Article 156 in detail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first half of Article 156, namely sub-articles (1) and (2), state that laws and policies concerning the promotion of the institution of marriage lie within the province of Parliament and the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The repeal of section 377A is concerning to many Singaporeans who are not supportive of the repeal and who fear that the removal of the offence would mainstream gay lifestyles in further spheres of life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is therefore appropriate to consider what the actual effect of Article 156 is.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I intend to look at each of the four sub-articles in turn.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is stated that Parliament may pass laws which define, regulate, safeguard, support, foster and promote the institution of marriage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, that sounds like a clear statement of what Parliament can do.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, with due respect, I am not sure what this sub-article actually achieves, apart from stating the obvious.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is indisputable that under Article 38 of the Constitution, legislative power has already been vested in the Legislature consisting of the President and Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In what way then is Article 156(1) meaningful?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, for Article 156(2), it states that the Government and any public authority may exercise their executive authority to protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote the institution of marriage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Again, is there a need to state that the Government and any public authority may exercise their executive authority?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It already is the position that under Article 23 of the Constitution, executive authority is vested in the President and exercisable by Cabinet Ministers and other bodies as authorised by law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is arguable then, that Article 156(1) and (2) do not add anything new to the current position.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I next move to the second half of the proposed Article 156.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The latter two sub-articles seek to prohibit challenges under Part 4 of the Constitution to laws and policies based on the current definition of marriage as between a man and a woman.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish to record my concern about the implications of sub-articles (3) and (4) on judicial oversight of the actions of Parliament and the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It bears stating here that Part 4 is the part of the Constitution entitled "fundamental liberties".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is Part 4 that grants individuals critical protections against abuse of state power, such as ensuring freedom from arbitrary arrest and freedom of religion, and the right to equal protection under the law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are enshrined in the Constitution for a reason.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, these fundamental liberties may not all be absolute, and some of them have been qualified in the Constitution itself.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But if one looks at the existing qualifications, they tend to be scoped tightly and justified on the grounds of national emergencies, security, public order and public health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was a point that Member Mr Murali touched on earlier as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To clarify, I am not advocating for gay marriages here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My concern is purely about whether it is justified to exclude judicial scrutiny on this topic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From a governance standpoint, I find this position very difficult to accept.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under Article 93 of the Constitution, judicial power has been vested in our Courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Article 4 provides that the Constitution is the supreme law of the land, a point recognised by Minister Masagos earlier.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Article 4 provides that laws passed by Parliament that are inconsistent with the Constitution shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Constitution is the fundamental legal safeguard of citizens, to protect them against illegal laws and policies that violate the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And it is the job of the Courts to assess whether any law is constitutional or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, I heard Minister Masagos in his Second Reading speech, and I would humbly submit that it is not the same thing to say that when the Courts is assessing a law for constitutionality, it is intervening in a political space.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is the Court's job to ensure that laws and policies conform with the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Quite apart from the decision being taken today, I am concerned about what this carve out means for the future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government, present or future, come up with other areas of life, where the Courts are to be excluded from reviewing laws and policies for constitutionality?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will Parliament in the future be looking at Article 157, 158 or 159?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, as far as sub-articles (1) and (2) are concerned, it does not seem to me that these provisions add anything to the current position.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, Sir, I appreciate the difficulties the Government has in navigating this issue of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not easy to arrive at a solution that addresses the concerns of society which is divided on the matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I understand the signal the Government wishes to send through the proposed Article 156.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, my concerns about safeguarding the Courts in doing their constitutional duty remain.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many Members in this House have known my long-standing support for the institutions of marriage and family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And two, how can I ensure that the carrying out of that duty works to the best for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My speech today will answer both those questions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For this, my starting point is to go back to 1962 and quote Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 1962, Mr Lee Kuan Yew gave a speech to an audience from the University of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Lee said that the phrase should be modified – it should read "Order and Law".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because Mr Lee's view – and I think it is a correct view – is that without order, then laws become useless.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to quote Mr Lee: "Those of you who are just embarking on the study of the law will learn the phrase 'law and order'".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a settled and established society, law appears to be a precursor of order.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Good laws lead to good order, that is the form that you will learn.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the hard realities of keeping the peace between man and man and between authority and the individual can be more accurately described if the phrase were inverted to 'order and law', for without order the operation of law is impossible." Minister Mentor inverted the phrase "law and order" to become "order and law".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By inverting the phrase, he showed how one must establish order first before laws can work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because what we are debating today is the order of things and the order from which all relevant laws and policies should be construed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some use the phrase societal norms, some use the phrase social mores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would use the term "the order of things".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as we are debating removing a law, we are also debating strengthening the order of things by virtue of an amendment to the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are coupling the removal of a law with an amendment to the Constitution to protect the order of things.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, what more, the Constitution is not just another law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is the beacon from which all laws take their bearing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It sets the tone – it is the backbone of the order of things.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do I believe that there is a significant risk that section 377A will be struck down by the Courts in a future legal challenge?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the question to ask next is: do we wait or do we move first by shouldering the legislative responsibility of making hard decisions and deciding on what needs to be protected?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is clear in my mind that we must do the latter.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must analyse, deliberate, look into our own selves and make the hard legislative decisions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Members of this House, we have a duty to decide on and reinforce what we desire to protect given the significant risk that section 377A may be struck down.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For this, I now turn to the amendments of the Constitution before the House today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The amendment to the Constitution is clear as to what it seeks to protect.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Marriage is the union of a man and a woman.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For centuries, this union has been the foundation of societies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Children and society, as a whole, flourish when marriages are supported and the resulting family unit is strong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Prime Minister has said in 2007, 2013 and 2016 that the traditional family unit should form the "basic building block of our society".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Prime Minister stated as recently as three months ago, "we have upheld and reinforced the importance of families through many national policies and we will continue to do so." Mr Speaker, the amendment to the Constitution strengthens this foundation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It states clearly that marriage is between a man and a woman; and it follows that this is the basis on which family is built.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By constitutionalising this, we are entrenching our values on what is the core, the base, the order of things from which all other relevant laws and policies in our society take bearing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is the beacon – the guiding light.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a legislator, I see this inclusion and amendment to the Constitution as a deliberate and positive step.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By making this amendment to the Constitution, it means that we are also protecting all our social policies that flow from this definition.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a position has been echoed by various Ministries in press statements or by Ministers in response to press questions since the National Day Rally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, the only form of marriage that is recognised in Singapore is the union between one man and one woman.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No other form of marriage is recognised in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A religious teacher – an ustaz, imam, priest, pastor, bishop, rabbi or men and women of any religion – cannot be prevented from teaching what their faith teaches about marriage and about homosexuality.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If practising homosexuality is not condoned in a particular faith, the religious leader can state so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, spousal rights can only be granted within the context of a heterosexual marriage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, education in school, particularly sex education, should affirm heterosexual marriage as the norm and the bedrock of family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is no room to argue that because section 377A is being repealed that this somehow provides a gateway or a licence to teachers to promote or normalise homosexuality in schools in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The repeal does not provide such a licence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Advertising content should not affirm homosexual unions in any way.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Seven, as for adoption, there cannot be a case where a civil union recognised overseas gives a couple in the civil union the ability to adopt under our laws.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have spoken with people who want section 377A to be retained at all costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have spoken with people who want to do away with section 377A and open the gates to changes for all institutions – marriage, adoption, the works.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They too have the right to hold those views.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But in the final analysis, I have to make my own decision on this difficult issue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I, too, have close friends who have same-sex attraction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To take a public position on such a difficult issue is not easy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I cannot shy away from facing difficult issues – and what I have shared in this speech is my position for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, in this struggle is where I belong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We, all of us here, have to make a deep effort to make the right choices in Singapore and for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we are debating today in this House, on Singapore soil, is squarely a domestic issue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other countries can choose how they want to shape their societies, but other countries should not impose their choices on us, no matter how well-meaning they perceive themselves to be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Speaking plainly, let us guard against covert and overt foreign influence in our domestic affairs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me, Sir, to end with the need for unity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unity has been a powerful force in modern Singapore's unprecedented history.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It must remain a part of our future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Why, in my view, is the aspect of unity so important today?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, there are people in our society who hold strong views on these issues.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, there is a potential here for Singapore to be torn apart by discord.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, my hope is that Singaporeans can discuss our views on these issues peacefully.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Where we disagree, let us express such disagreement respectfully and politely.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we are doing today, in this House, is to entrench what we seek to protect and remove a law that has a significant risk of being struck down.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, by choosing to deal with this in Parliament, we are taking a deliberate and considered approach.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Parliament, being made up of elected Members, has the requisite mandate to deal with these issues.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No other institution can carry through such a legislative manoeuvre.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is hoped that the choice of deploying Parliament to deal with this issue is the best path for unity for our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, let the decorum, tone and respect that we display during this debate in this House set a good example to all Singaporeans of how to deal with such difficult and sensitive issues in future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My prayer is that we will not be torn apart by discord but, instead, stay united as one nation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In all our deliberations – present and future, In all our debates – present and future, In all our decisions – present and future, Let not the unity of our nation be lost.  .

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I last spoke in Parliament on this issue at the query of Minister Shanmugam, I said that there were two different views within PSP and we had no consensus at that time, similar to the situation in our society at large.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whilst there is a big group that does not feel very strongly about this issue, there is also a significant group that holds very strong and opposing views, and they are not easily persuaded.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We were of the view that any attempts to forcefully reach a single position at that point would be divisive.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that while we strive to establish common ground in core areas for unity, we also need to leave room for diverse viewpoints in other areas.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, we believe that this is one issue where we should allow Members to hold on to their personal beliefs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Societal values evolve with time and laws evolve accordingly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let society at large determine when is the right time to change this law.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since then, we have held more rounds of lengthy discussions in yet another attempt to seek common ground.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We recognise the unfairness of 377A on the gay community, but we also recognise the fears of many on the subsequent effect on families and the difficulties they face in reconciling with their religious beliefs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our concern is again whether this issue would damage social harmony in Singapore, which is something that we value.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any society, contentious issues will always arise.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recognising that no one single person can have his way all the time and that taking turns to compromise is part and parcel of democracy, it is a sign of maturity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The willingness to compromise is not a sign of weakness, but instead one of maturity, resilience and community spirit.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans are concerned about the effect such a repeal will have on the institution of marriage.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The path towards political maturity is filled with gives-and-takes from all sides.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP is confident that Singaporeans can do it and we will strive towards that direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, I have met with groups such as Young Out Here, Greenhouse, Oogachaga, Sayoni, T Project and others who run support groups to help LGBTQ+ individuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It also hangs like the Sword of Damocles over them, since the law exists and reminds them that they are criminals even when what they are engaging in is a private, consensual act between two adults.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: LGBTQ+ individuals may also suffer from stigma, discrimination and be disproportionately impacted by mental health concerns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At T Project’s shelter for their community, I saw how a small shelter for six persons was stacked with suitcases and personal items of about another 10 individuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The owners of these items have no permanent abode and move from place to place as their life is often complicated by mental stress, poverty and unemployment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In conversations with Greenhouse, which runs a support group for 200-plus gay individuals, some shared that they have struggled since young to find acceptance from their family but love and acceptance were not forthcoming.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This has consequences on their physical and mental health, ability to find and hold a job and increases their risk of committing offences and suffering from substance addiction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They shared that substance addiction becomes a coping mechanism for them when they are unable to find acceptance in society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We understand their concerns and are working with social service agencies to be open and sensitive to the diverse needs of clients and to provide social support, regardless of their backgrounds and sexual orientations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, I have also spoken to many individuals who are worried about where our society is headed should section 377A be repealed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In an engagement with over 100 members of the public who had written to their Members of Parliament, some youths recounted how they had experienced being ostracised or “cancelled” in schools and Universities because they were seen to be “conservative” and not advocating gay rights.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Others spoke about how they were singled out at their workplaces because they are religious and, by default, seen to be homophobic and, therefore, at odds with the company’s diversity and inclusion policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I saw a grandmother’s hand trembling, as she spoke about her grave concerns should Singapore go down the slippery slope as some other countries have after decriminalising gay sex.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MOM is also looking at enacting workplace fairness legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On being “cancelled” for one’s beliefs, the Government is looking into policy solutions to preserve space for persons of different views to share what they think, safely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But ultimately, what is important is that we maintain mutual respect when we engage with one another and not tear each other down.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I also met with leaders of religious groups, some of them four to five times.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They have been steadfast partners in our nation-building.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They have worked tirelessly to bring Singaporeans from different races and religions together to build common spaces and common values.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The religious leaders shared views from their communities on section 377A – views anchored on hopes for Singapore to continue to be strong and stable and a place for families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many of their congregants have a great sense of gratitude and pride in how far our nation has come and wish for nothing more than for our children and future generations to thrive and prosper and they see the heterosexual family unit as the bedrock of our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And I want to thank them for being considered in their approach and for sharing the views of their communities in a constructive manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have heard their views and will continue to work with them to navigate a way forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The issue that stands before us is one of public policy, as to whether gay sex in the context of private sexual behaviour between consenting adults, should remain a crime under Singapore laws.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Though the Bills are voted on separately, they should be seen holistically because this is not a zero-sum game, where one side wins and the other side loses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And in the spirit of how the two Bills are drafted, we hope that Singaporeans, with all their varied views on the issue, can be united in our desire to find common ground so that we can move forward together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Let us be united in wanting Singapore to be a home for all, a tolerant and inclusive society, where all Singaporeans feel a sense of dignity and have collective confidence in our future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The decision was made on the basis of feedback from society at that time and was a temporary compromise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, without repealing section 377A, legislation and law enforcement will not be fully consistent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Over the past few months, the Government and people from all walks of life have held many exchanges on the section 377A issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Judging from the feedback from various quarters, most people support the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Of course, there are also some polarised views in the exchanges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, some see homosexuality as immoral, while others want more rights for the gay community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is not necessarily a bad thing that there are opposing views in society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore is a multi-racial, multi-religious and multi-cultural society, but we are proud of our harmonious co-existence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Each of us has a different family background, culture and education and there may be different views on a particular issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some people are worried that homosexuals will cause social problems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we can also see that some of them are in need of understanding and assistance from society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I have visited a mutual aid society that provides assistance to homosexuals, and some of them were not accepted by their families since young.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Later, they encountered various problems in life, such as bullying, mental health problems, financial problems, and some felt that they had no way out when facing a crisis in life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We do not have to live in the same way as others, but we do not have to force others to live in the same way as us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Do not do unto others what we do not what for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the sensitive issue of homosexuality, we hope that groups with opposing views will be tolerant, understanding of each other, put aside their differences and seek a consensus.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the process of interacting with the Chinese community, I understand that many people attach great importance to the traditional family-centric values and do not want to change the family values of Singaporeans just because section 377A is repealed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Only when families are stable can our society be stable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: One of the first laws enacted by the PAP Government since it took office was the Women's Charter in 1961.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is a landmark piece of legislation that protects women's rights, allowing only monogamous marriages between men and women to be legalised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Since then, the Government has been supporting families in Singapore through various policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, married households have always had priority in access to public housing and related subsidies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Baby Bonus is also meant to encourage marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MSF has also been actively promoting, educating and stressing the importance of the family through public education programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We also understand the challenges faced by different types of families, such as single parent families and divorced families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MSF will do our best to help them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As far as the institution of marriage is concerned, we have to uphold it, not subvert it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Only then will we be able to ensure the continuity of policies and stability of society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Otherwise, current policies and laws relating to marriage, including policies such as the Baby Bonus and HDB flats, may face Court challenges in the future, which will complicate the issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some people may ask, people are more concerned about bread-and-butter issues such as rising prices and housing, so why are we discussing the issue of section 377A now?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Even as the Government solves these important bread-and-butter issues, it must also solve other problems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Repealing section 377A and safeguarding the marriage system also affect the lives of Singaporeans, who also need our attention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have to solve not only macro problems, but also micro problems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Letting every Singaporean live with dignity and hope.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: One important reason for the global inflation is because the current international situation is unstable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Sino-US relations continue to be tense, and the Russian-Ukraine war has continued for more than half a year, causing the prices of oil and other raw materials to soar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At a time when the international environment is unstable, Singapore must maintain its internal stability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Today, we are moving two Bills at the same time, and I hope people can see the good intentions of the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The two Bills are one legislative package and cannot be separated, so as to preserve the balance and stability of the society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the one hand, repealing section 377A will better protect the freedom and rights of individuals and reduce social pressure on homosexuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the other hand, upholding the institution of marriage will help to maintain the stability of the relevant laws and policies and reduce the worries of various ethnic groups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, I hope that everyone will adopt an inclusive and balanced attitude towards the two Bills and move forward together as one united people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, I would like to thank the Chinese community for their understanding towards many social problems and for always emphasising mutual respect and compromise, seeking common ground and harmony, when facing different social issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: With regard to social mores, it is inappropriate to be overly intimate in public, whether between men and women or between people of the same sex.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Social mores also are not dependent solely based on the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They require the concerted efforts of society, families and education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Each of us need to play a part.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It has not been easy to come up with these two proposals today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore is a multi-religious, multi-racial and multi-cultural society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Every racial and religious group has its own practices, customs, norms and beliefs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is not easy to bring together such a diverse society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Hence, the Government has always stressed the importance of safeguarding the common space, nurturing good citizens and upholding the principle of equality, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Only then can we unite and work for the progress of our country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Even if we do our best to find a solution that will bring about a more balanced and harmonious society as a whole, there will still be people who are not satisfied with the outcome.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The two Bills strike a balance between freedom and stability, just like the two ends of the scale, which cannot be separated from each other, so as to achieve a balance and harmony in society as a whole.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I hope you will see that the Government has put in a lot of effort into this issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I also urge everyone to continue to respect one another, put aside their differences, seek consensus and be inclusive of one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will continue to work hand in hand with Singaporeans to stay united and maintain our social harmony and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   I will touch on the need for the repeal of section 377A in the Penal Code, given the recent development of our Court of Appeal decisions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By way of explanation, our Constitution is the supreme law of the land.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If there is any Bill that contradicts the Constitution, then it is invalid and will expire.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In recent years, there have been many Court challenges and appeals about the constitutional status of section 377A.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The argument is that this section violates the country's Constitution.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because section 377A only criminalises homosexual conduct between men and not in general.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This may breach the Reasonable Classification Test in the interpretation of Article 12 in our Constitution in the case of Syed Suhail.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, based on the assurance given by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong in 2007 and the Attorney-General in 2018 that this section will not be enforced, the Court of Appeal is of the opinion that it does not need to make a decision on the constitutionality of section 377A this time and the appellant has no locus standi or right to bring it to Court.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is due to the doctrine of legitimate expectations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the Court of Appeal recognises that the Attorney-General presently, or in the future, is able to change the policy at any time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This means that the Court's opinion on the issue of locus standi or the doctrine of legitimate expectations can also change at any time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, it is not a question of "if" but "when" section 377A will be struck down by the Courts when other cases are brought to Court.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I agree with the Government's approach to debate this issue in Parliament and not allow the Court to make a decision in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although our Singaporean society remains conservative when it comes to marriage and family, most of us do not want a person to be jailed simply because of his conduct under the section.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although we still differ in terms of religion, race, values or way of life, we are all human beings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And each of us has the same right to be protected under the auspices of fair and equitable laws for all citizens.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The amendment to the Constitution proposed today is important because it aims to protect the laws and policies of the Government based on the definition of family and marriage between men and women.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With this protection, no case can be brought to Court to challenge the constitutionality of the law that defines marriage between a man and a woman as well as Government policies that are based on the definition of marriage, including public housing, education and media policies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, this Bill sends a signal that everyone must be equally protected under the law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, the amendment to the Constitution clarifies the Parliament's role to protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote the institution of marriage.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding this, I have met many residents in Keat Hong and Chua Chu Kang and members from various organisations and charities, including Malay/Muslim organisations, who are uncertain as to what future changes these amendments will bring.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think it is important to actively engage families and parents on this issue and provide them with various avenues of counselling or parenting support.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The same goes for our teachers and educators too.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For the Muslim community, the common feedback from mosque or organisation leaders is that there is a need for clearer guidelines or capability training.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The new Article 156(2) states that the Government and public authorities may, in the exercise of their executive authority, promote the institution of marriage through public housing, education and media policies that promote and safeguard the institution of marriage.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, such parenting support or counselling should also provide for a faith- or value-based support, if such is available, so that the individuals would choose what suits them best.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Also, it is important to preserve the freedom of conscience in our schools, businesses and religious institutions so that our fellow Singaporeans are free to practise their belief, their faith or otherwise, without any fear of cancellation or reprisals against them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the announcement by Minister Shanmugam and also by Minister of State Sun Xueling just now that the Ministries and agencies are looking into this.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us not let this issue divide us but instead unite us.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For the record, I still agree with the previous position of the Government in not enforcing section 377A.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Since the Government announced that it will be repealing section 377A of the Penal Code and after the subsequent announcement of the proposed constitutional law amendments, I have received feedback and spoken to many residents and Singaporeans of different races, religions and ages.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have heard and read the views of members of the LGBTQ+ community, particularly, their unhappiness with perceived discrimination and different rights as compared to heterosexual couples in the areas of marriage, owning BTOs, rights of child adoption and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also heard much feedback from residents and Singaporeans of their concerns on the repeal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many were concerned that we would be removing a symbolic social marker with such a repeal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: People are also concerned with the societal changes they have seen in many countries in the areas of gender identity, sex education, marriage laws and public policy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With the repeal, some will press for more changes in law and policy after the repeal, like what is seen in other countries, for example, in Australia and the US.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They wonder to what extent the proposed amendments to the Constitution can prevent such changes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many express concern that the removal of such a marker may make it difficult for parents in setting down their family and social values at home.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many are also concerned they will be stopped from expressing their contrary views on sexuality after the repeal, including the fear of being cancelled.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some are concerned that there will be name calling because of the view they take on sexuality in their workplace or for young people and children in their schools.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: People are also concerned that more changes will make society more divided.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Singaporeans I have spoken to or who have written to me with their reservations include those whose views may not be influenced by any religious views and also those of a wide age range.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The proposed repeal presents a number of difficult issues for different groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The symbolism of section 337A is different to different groups, their differing views and even the experiences of individuals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As a Member of Parliament (MP), in considering all issues, I am also guided by my own conscience in arriving at a position that I feel is right for our society and our people, even if some may disagree.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am personally troubled by the removal of the marker that it represents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, I made this decision with a heavy heart.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is both a most difficult decision and is the most difficult speech I have to make to date, given the divided issues at play for different segments of my constituents and for Singaporeans; being very careful not to cause hurt or offence and yet, having to be principled with my own beliefs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is also not made easier because, like many fellow MPs and Singaporeans, I also have many friends and good friends who are from the LGBTQ community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
