text: Some have over time shared with me some of their difficult circumstances and experiences in life which makes my decision today even more difficult and humbling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My colleague and my hon friend, Ms Sylvia Lim, has raised some concerns regarding the implications of the proposed carve-outs in the proposed Article 153 to exclude the Courts' role in ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The position I take today does not change how I treat all my constituents and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will continue to serve all my constituents to the best of my ability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moving forward, I hope for greater understanding between those who share different views on LGBTQ and greater tolerance of different views.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We may not always agree with each other on every issue, but we can, and should, agree to disagree.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should still love and respect each other no less as fellow human beings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And I hope that there will be more dialogue between those who share different views, so that there may be a better understanding and less polarisation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Each individual functions within a society, so there is a place for public debate about the laws and institutions which we would want to have in order to regulate life within that society.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: At one level, I believe that this debate is about whether the family, defined as a marriage between a heterosexual couple, and their parenthood is the unit that forms the basic structure of a well-ordered society.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Children are born into families and develop their complete lives, with the investment of their parents, who gave birth to them.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If we view the family, as just defined, as part of the basic structure of society, then we would want to have laws and institutions that support that family.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: We would want to strengthen this social norm and support the public commitment made by a man and a woman to be married to each other and to raise their children within the safety of their wedding vows.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Playing their complementary roles, fathers and mothers raise their children, who contribute to the orderly formation and further reproduction of society, over many generations.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Research shows that the cognitive and the socio-emotional skills that are acquired in early childhood and their development is very much shaped by the family environment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Society can, then, uplift the quality of life for future generations of citizens by supporting the husband and wife in their child-rearing activities.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has made a transition from an economy built around factories that produce standard labour-intensive goods for sale into the world market, to one that is more service-oriented and where the fourth industrial revolution will require workers to exercise a wide range of both cognitive and non-cognitive skills.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In such an economy, I believe the family remains the bedrock of society, where children learn complementary lessons from their fathers and their mothers, so that they develop the skills needed to become well-functioning future workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: We take for granted that as our parents have invested in our lives, it is our responsibility to provide care for them when they become old.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Even when there are failures in particular cases, we hold as examples those who inspire us with their devotion to duty, to the care of their ageing parents.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government, through its public programmes provides assistance in various forms, much of the glue that holds a society together, comes from the constituent members within the family.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: We should, in instituting our laws, convey through all means possible, the gratitude we feel for the complementary roles that our fathers and mothers play in raising us to become well-functioning adults.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In many historical cases around the world, where the structure of the family has been changed from the norm that the Government has reaffirmed, legislative changes have indeed taken place sequentially.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Beginning with the decriminalisation, similar to the repeal of the law we are discussing today, to subsequently defining the family in a very different way from the basic structure of the family just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   Having engaged with residents within my constituency and the Malay/Muslim community and organisations, as well as being part of the NTUC and the Labour Movement in Singapore who regularly engages fellow leaders and workers, I appreciate their constructive feedback and concerns.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As such, I would like to raise three concerns relating to the repeal of section 377A, which I hope would be addressed henceforth.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These three concerns relate to workplaces, family and education, specifically madrasah education in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One the key tenets of good working experience for any workers is to have good workplace harmony.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Employers should ensure that their policies and practices provide an inclusive workspace that respects and is sensitive to different personal beliefs and values of all employees.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: They should not promote activities that may potentially give rise to bullying or discrimination.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To better support both employers and workers in navigating workplaces in the future, I call upon the Government to consider setting guidelines or advisories that will provide clear guidance towards such activities at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, the family unit has been a critical pillar of society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many policies, such as housing, are centred around the family unit or nucleus.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am heartened that the Government will continue to uphold the traditional family in its policies and in the law, as it works with stakeholders to chart a way forward.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, there is a pressing need to create a safe space for families to openly discuss matters pertaining to sexuality.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, parents and children ought to be able to freely discuss matters pertaining to sexuality without fearing stigmatization.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Parents who do not concur with the gay and homosexual community’s view of sexuality should not be publicly shamed.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: They should be free to share their beliefs with their children, underpinned by religious teachings or their worldview.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Parents should be given the space to protect their children from any content they deem inappropriate, including matters pertaining to the gay and homosexual community.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I call upon the Government to further fortify the traditional family unit to ensure that it remains a safe space for families to discuss matters pertaining to sexuality.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Last year, in response to a Parliamentary Question raised by Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Masagos Zulkifli, Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs and Minister for Social and Family Development, mentioned, “Our madrasahs incorporate sexuality education in their existing curriculum for both male and female students.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While this is not a standalone subject, it is covered substantially within the syllabus through topics like boy-girl relationships, gender, sexuality, and managing issues relating to self-image, puberty and adolescence, as well as managing peer pressure.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These topics are targeted at students aged 13 to 16.” With the passing of this Bill, there is a concern over how it will affect sexuality education taught in madrasahs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Furthermore, it is unknown if additional training will be provided to equip asatizah with the skills required to address sensitive matters pertaining to sexuality and how such issues should be brought across to students.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, the extent to which this Bill would influence sexuality education in madrasahs ought to be studied further.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore is a diverse nation and would continue to be more diverse.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Despite our differences, we are able to come together and build consensus on national issues.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I am in favour of this Bill as we are one big family and the beliefs of every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What if you were born into a world where your actions marked you out as being in minority because most people do not want to do what you do?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What if you were able to live your life in the society you were born into, but at the back of your mind, you could never get over this niggling fear, this fear that one day, the majority might turn against you, might bully you, might discriminate against you or worse?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Each of us can close our eyes and imagine that we live in such a world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And then imagine a different world, a different situation imagine that you hold dearly to a viewpoint as a matter of conscience, a viewpoint that others believe is deeply offensive and hurtful, even though to you it is a view that does not call for hurt towards any other human being.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rather, it is a view about what sorts of behaviours should be held up as moral markers in our society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Imagine that you cannot speak about that point of view that you hold, on pain of being cancelled, abused, or attacked on social media or worse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Each of us can close our eyes and imagine that we live in such a world too.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That is what is at stake in this debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are we to be divided between people who cherish the freedom to act in a certain way versus those who cherish the freedom to espouse views that are deep matters of conscience and never the twain shall meet?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will this be an unbridgeable chasm in our Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have seen what such divisions about values can do in other countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can look at the culture wars in the USA, for example, an oft-quoted example, where differences in values, often with the religious dimension have become political and polarising.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Another example, possibly is Turkey, where differences in values with the religious dimension have had huge political ramifications in the past and still do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Politics is and should be about the contest of ideas, robust respectful debate about what is best for the country is a good thing, as most Singaporeans would probably agree these days.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The truth, what is best for our country in our time emerges from such disagreement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Other things are needed for political progress, but there can be no progress without respectful, robust political debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But major political divides around values or on matters of conscience and religion are a different matter, to some extent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such debates are often impossible to settle with reference to an agreed set of facts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, as we chart a path forward on these issues before the House today, before the country today, it is worth recalling a few truths that almost no one would disagree with on either side of the questions before us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us recall a few things that unite us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The touchstone in our hearts should be what is best for and what is possible in this country we love, not some other country we know about.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I know that this is the case for my colleagues in the Workers' Party, who have a different view from mine on 377A and with whom I have had many lively and meaningful discussions from which I have learned a great deal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I suspect that this would be the case for all other Members of this House, who can be taken to represent the political mainstream.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us stop and reflect on that for a second.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No one is saying discrimination is okay; no one is saying bullying is okay; no one is saying violence is okay.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some on the fringe on either side may not agree but no one in the mainstream disagrees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, what then is at stake, if it is not practical enforcement?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In explaining my own vote today, I would like to address both these issues in turn.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I do so, I would like to record my thanks to the Leader of the Opposition for lifting the whip in this debate and thus allowing Workers' Party Members of Parliament (MPs) to speak and vote according to their conscience and deeply held values.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Workers' Party MPs do have a majority view but I support the right of each MP to vote according to their conscience on retaining or repealing 377A as a moral marker.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Yet, as I said earlier, no one in the Workers' Party is calling for 377A to be actively enforced.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, I would like to talk about the rightful place of the law in policing private acts between consenting adults.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, we have the offence of statutory rape where sex with the minor is criminalised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The minor may have consented, but the law recognises that the minor does not have the maturity to meaningfully consent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But my own view is that the law has no place to intervene in private behaviour among truly consenting adults, provided there is no other public consequence thrown up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we retain 377A as a symbolic marker, should we also introduce other laws into the statute books as symbolic markers without enforcement such as, for example, for illustrative purposes, laws encouraging healthier sexual behaviour, or laws encouraging Singaporeans to have enough children to lift our total fertility rate?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not think we should and I do not believe anyone is calling for this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, by the same token, there is a case to repeal 377A as unnecessary because symbolic markers are not inserted into our body of laws for other issues of importance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And also, because free and respectful conversation about symbolic markers can and should continue completely independently of the law and criminal penalties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I shall return to this in the later part of my speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are other better ways to register our views on matters of conscience, ways that are pursued outside of the realm of laws and criminal penalties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, such an approach to the law, in my mind, places too much power in the hands of the Government and the AGC to decide what laws should be enforced and what laws should absolutely not be enforced.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It leaves too much to prosecutorial discretion and too little to the rightful province of Parliament in making these laws and the Courts to interpret them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Markers can be created and conveyed respectfully in other ways without incorporating them into our laws.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Which brings me to the last part of my speech on 377A, the part that addresses the subtext.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will removing 377A mean that in the wider society, those of a religious persuasion or who are otherwise persuaded, cannot express their views freely about LGBTQ+ relationships, which may be prescribed in religious faith?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Article 15 protects the right of each Singaporean to profess, practise and propagate their religion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Freedom of speech is also protected by Article 14(1) of our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Making these arguments about 377A – I also want to make another argument – those who question LGBTQ relationships on the grounds of religion or other considerations rooted in personal conviction should be free to express their views respectfully.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As I said earlier, the mainstream of opinion among Singaporeans who want to retain 377A is not to call for its active enforcement and not to condone bullying and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals of any kind.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a huge point in favour of the common ground, the strong middle in this debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I would argue that as the mirror image of that, those who questioned LGBTQ relationships on the grounds of religious faith or deep personal conviction should have the freedom to espouse their views respectfully, making clear that they regard everyone equally as a citizen, but they hew to their deep personal convictions on this matter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To criticise a choice someone makes in their personal life is not tantamount to criticising, denigrating or disenfranchising that person.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But this depends, of course, on how that criticism is made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Already, as it stands, some religious teachings do constitute criticisms of certain acts not deemed illegal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Likewise, those of a different persuasion, those who believe in LGBTQ equality have the right to respectfully criticise opposing views.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is such respectful speech where we agree to disagree even possible?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will return to this topic in the last part of my speech today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I leave the subject of repealing 377A, Mr Speaker, Sir, I must say that it is my personal conviction that every individual should be treated equally regardless of sexual orientation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I personally believe that the principles of equality and fairness demand this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I say that as those are rational principles, but I also say that as a human being with the emotional make-up that that entails.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a human being, I close my eyes and imagine if I lived in a world, where what I deeply feel and who I love are held to be fundamentally wrong by many or most of my fellow human beings, are at odds with the social mores I see everywhere around me, reflected in the media, culture, education, religion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The pain that comes from that sharp disconnect between the inner life and the outer reality cannot be described in words easily.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I see no reason to disagree with this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On a matter such as the definition of marriage, which is deeply cultural, the law should be made democratically by the people of Singapore, whose voice Parliament reflects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such laws should be made by the legislature, which is accountable to the people directly, and not by the Courts, which have no such direct accountability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I agree with the points she has made, which come from a good lawyer's understanding of constitutional law; and I say this as a non-lawyer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, as a legislator, I believe that the amendment does signify a correct principle, one I agree with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I believe that it is a useful signifier to establish, however imperfect the mechanism and wording of it may be on grounds of legal scholarship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How can we move forward as one united people, as a democratic society?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, in this House we debated the issue of hiking GST versus alternative revenue-raising mechanisms that the Workers' Party put forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We did not find consensus but there were points of agreement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But in that GST debate, the debate turned on rational argument and ultimately philosophic considerations of a secular nature.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Here, the debate comes down to matters of deep personal conviction that is less easily resolved with reference to agreed facts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will we succeed in cultivating the ability to respectfully disagree on such matters where much of the rest of the world has failed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will we succeed in preserving our unity and not allowing these disagreements, that are so hard to resolve by debate, to become political rifts?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we hold different views that may never be reconciled and have those views respectfully played out in civil discourse, bearing in mind the place of our laws and the place of freedom of speech and religion in a healthy balance, bearing in mind that we are all citizens, equal before the law?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we move forward by respectfully agreeing to disagree without demonising the one we disagree with but embracing him and her as our fellow citizen, our colleague, our brother and our sister?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not know for a fact that we can or will.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I argued that Parliament should make laws to reflect the public morality of our times.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The messaging by the Government is important – that Singapore is a society whereby the family unit is still seen as the basic structure of society.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Further, the Government had indicated that there will not be proactive enforcement of those who are gays.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At that time, Prime Minister Lee had said that the Government had decided to keep the status quo despite the legal untidiness and the ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What is the intended signal by the Government when it announced its intention to repeal this law?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How do we explain to the many Singaporeans who are still pro-family and worried about the decline in family values?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I spoke to many Singaporeans who had expressed their concern about the repeal.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of them said that they do not wish to see homosexuals being prosecuted as criminals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But yet, they are concerned whether the repeal would lead to an erosion of family values and an increased number of gay people.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And I believe that many Members of Parliament (MPs) in this House have received letters from concerned residents who expressed similar concerns.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To keep an open mind about this issue, I also spoke to different groups of citizens who felt that we should allow those who are homosexuals to live the lifestyle that they wish.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They opine that is not the Government's business to tell our citizens, especially those who are gays, how to lead their lives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: While some expressed concern about the open expression of homosexual relationship like hands holding and public kissing, they felt that there is no need to make this behaviour a criminal offence.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, it appears that the advocacy by the homosexual community over the years has made our citizens more accepting of gay people.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are also a number of citizens who felt very neutral about the matter.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They have no views on the issue at all.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In other words, it is not their concern.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Nor do they wish to criminalise a homosexual." Minister Indranee Rajah, when she was a backbencher, had also, in her speech said, "I think we do not want to have a situation where we demonise homosexuals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We certainly do not want to regard them as anything less than Singaporeans."  The Government's stand at that time was articulated by Prime Minister Lee when he said, "There are gay bars and clubs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Government does not act as moral policemen.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And we do not proactively enforce section 377A on them."  Since the Government does not actively enforce section 377A on homosexuals, the question is whether is it time for Singapore to repeal section 377A today?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is the Singapore society more accepting of homosexuals in our midst?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many Singaporeans have accepted that homosexuals are fellow Singaporeans living in our midst and doing their part to contribute to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In particular, many of the younger generation are accepting of the homosexual people.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And similar to the position of many Singaporeans, which I alluded to 15 years ago, we do not wish to see homosexuals being criminalised.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But the message that I heard from many Singaporeans is that we need to protect marriage as a union between man and woman, that we need to support values that promote the role of the family as the basic building block of society, that we need to protect Singaporeans from being intimidated or harassed simply because they disagree with the lifestyle of the gay community.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many within the religious community are also concerned whether the repeal of section 377A would lead to a situation whereby the religious leaders cannot tell their congregation that they do not agree with the practice of homosexuality.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The religious leaders are concerned that they cannot pray for someone who is homosexual to reflect on God's command.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In other words, the religious leaders lose their freedom to preach on what is acceptable or wrong based on their faith.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are many who expressed concern about the intolerant views of some gays who attack anyone who disagree with their homosexual views.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are fears about the activism of some of the LGBT community who push their ideology that their world view should be seen as the norm and acceptable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Therefore, anyone who disagrees with their world view should be condemned and ostracised.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In Australia, when the Government held a postal ballot on same-sex marriage, it resulted in vitriolic abuse against people holding views in opposition to the legalisation of same-sex marriage.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: An Australian politician said, "A culture has developed whereby it is acceptable to vilify, mock, abuse and shame anyone who stands in the way, or even raises questions, about whether we should legalise same-sex marriage.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have been called a homophobe, a bigot and been told that my views are disgusting." So, said the Australian politician.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And when such strong and intimidating language is used, it is impossible to hold a civil debate or respectful discussion about any topic regarding the gay community.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They told me that their townhall meeting was almost cancelled because of complaints and threats by the gay community.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They complain that the minority in the gay movement are refusing to allow anyone to have a conversation about their concerns regarding homosexuality.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And I have deep respect for such people because their sexual preference is really not an issue to me.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But because of this small minority of militant homosexuals, they give the others a bad name by being bullies and by being difficult in their conduct.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, it seems like there is a reversal of role.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is not the gays who are being discriminated in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: On the contrary, if you do not agree with the pro-gay movement, you may be penalised at work or face discrimination.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There should be no space for people to propagate hate messages within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.30 pm until 4.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since this plan was first revealed, many Aljunied GRC residents have reached out to me to express their views about this issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Residents spoke to me during my house visits, came to my Meet-the-People Sessions, sent me WhatsApp messages, emails and petitions, and wrote detailed letters explaining their arguments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Several invited me to their homes, where they gathered their friends and family to passionately express their concerns and urge me to raise them in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This included representation from members of the LGBT community who see section 377A as a law that discriminates against them and victimises them and who support its repeal.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge these sentiments as they cut to the core of how members of the LGBT community see themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My constituents' feedback can be grouped into several, sometimes, overlapping, categories.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They worried about getting cancelled or suffering discrimination in school or at the workplace because of their beliefs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, some have expressed concerns that the higher health risks of some types of sexual practices are not being adequately communicated to young people for fear of sounding discriminatory.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fifth, others are worried that the disruption to the current equilibrium will lead to an increase in advocacy by groups on both sides and spark the type of culture wars seen in other nations, which will present challenges to Singapore's national cohesion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Sixth, some have argued that the LGBT community is already disadvantaged by the laws that support the heteronormative family and that repealing section 377A does not confer any tangible disadvantages on those who oppose the change.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These residents are of the view that section 377A should be repealed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Seventh, residents on both sides of the debate have cited the need to live and let live and call for greater tolerance of different views.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are diverse and often opposing positions on what is clearly a very controversial issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those at one end of the spectrum rue the day that this marker is removed while those on the other see it as one of the many social changes they wish to see in our country.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have also noticed a large middle ground which does not have strong opinions on this issue and is more concerned about bread and butter issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is in fact some agreement on both sides of the divide.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Both agree that section 377A bears significant symbolic weight in our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They both also anticipate that the repeal of section 377A will open the door to many more challenges to the prevailing norms in our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are all valid concerns and sincere feedback expressed by Singaporeans, all of whom have the interest of our nation at heart.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Listening to constituents on both sides of this contentious debate presented challenges for me on how to raise them both in this House.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I see it as my responsibility as a Member of Parliament to reflect the feedback and concerns of my constituents in this House.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, as an elected representative, I will also need to take a stand and vote on these Bills.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My vote will be based, first and foremost, on what I believe is in the best long-term interests of our nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will take into consideration the viewpoints of my constituents and my own conscience.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have come to agree with what the Prime Minister said in Parliament on 23 October 2007 when he explained that the Government was retaining section 377A but not proactively enforcing it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was, to quote the Court of Appeal, a "political compromise" that was "conceived with the express intention of accommodating divergent interests, avoiding polarisation and facilitating incremental change".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Attorney-General Lucien Wong took further steps in 2018 by noting that the Police will not proactively enforce section 377A, for instance, by conducting enforcement raids.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Section 377A is, therefore, no longer a Sword of Damocles hanging over men in same-sex relationships.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They will not be prosecuted or convicted under section 377A for consensual sexual acts done in private.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, section 377A has never criminalised same-sex attraction between men or same-sex relations between women.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is important to me and the example that I have set for my children that I hold fast to the values that I have established to be true, without wavering because of political headwinds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Whilst some, especially those in the LGBT community and many of my friends, residents, party members and volunteers, may strongly disagree with my position, I hope that they will accept that these are my sincerely held values which I am trying my best to uphold.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My vote is not an attack on their values nor a diminishing of their humanity in any way.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some have criticised me for allowing my faith to inform my vote in Parliament, arguing that the two should be kept separate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I hope Singaporeans will consider the broader issues at hand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are too many important issues that affect the lives of Singaporeans for one's vote to be decided based on this single issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I was worried I might come across as prejudiced against members of the LGBT community.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: LGBT persons are human beings worthy of the same amount of love and respect that we accord to any other person.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many are our family members, friends, colleagues and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Disagreeing with LGBT positions is not an attack on LGBT persons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, I hope that my speech will open up a platform for more difficult but respectful conversations on this issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, we must recognise that LGBT issues are sensitive issues, just like race and religion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: People who subscribe to one faith do not force their belief on others.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Religious beliefs are also not taught as facts in our school curriculum that students are expected to accept without question.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, we should treat LGBT issues as sensitive topics, just like religion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should not force people to accept one view or another, with the risk of being labelled as bigoted or immoral.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is not to say that the issue should not be discussed at all.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the contrary, discussion should be encouraged, but as a balanced discussion on different viewpoints, not as a lesson on facts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is inherent in a society as diverse as Singapore's that there will be fundamental differences in values and world views among our people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This need not be a source of conflict.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While we may disagree on some issues, there are so many other issues that we agree on and can work together to advance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We do not need to descend into labelling, name-calling or questioning the worth of our fellow human beings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead, we need to open up spaces for our people to hold different views at work, in schools and even within families.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By looking beyond our differences and working together on what we have in common, we will build that better society we all aspire towards.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These examples do not mean any direct correlation between their sexual orientation and their talent or achievements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There are many people, who just happened to be gay, who have made contributions to society in their own way, whether in their profession or just as individuals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These are people who walk among us every day.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They are our friends, our family members, our colleagues and our peers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They should not be treated any lesser for what they would like to do in private.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We need to be inclusive of different lifestyles, just as we like to have the choice and freedom to lead our private lives in peace.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I spoke in 2007 in support of a repeal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: That was 23 years after the last review of the Penal Code.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I said then that I hope we would not take another 23 years to address this again.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I am glad that our Government made that decision today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the last 15 years, public sentiment has evolved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There is a shift away from our previous views, especially more evident among the young, who feel that there is injustice that there are penalties targeted specifically at sexual acts between men.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It signals the pro-family stance of the current Government and population.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It is also the right thing to allow the definition of marriage to continue be covered by the Women’s Charter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: If and when the majority of our population or Parliament feels that the current definition needs to change, that should be for our future generation to decide.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It is important that the provisions and any amendments to the Constitution are carefully considered, otherwise it loses its value through capriciousness and constant changes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In Mandarin):   Older Singaporeans should have seen or heard of the movie "Cousin Wan Jun".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It is a 1965 movie adapted from the novel "Chasing” in Qiong Yao's “Six Streams" series.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The movie tells the love stories of Wan Jun and her three cousins as they grew up.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This reflects the olden days when people like to strengthen family ties by marrying relatives, whether through matchmakers or even arranged marriages before birth.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Now, people have better knowledge of genetic science and understand that marriage between relatives will significantly increase the incidence of genetic disorders and children born with deformity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Bai Ju Yi said in his poem, “With 3,000 concubines in the palace, their love is only concentrated on one person”.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In ancient times when polygamy was the norm, the emperor had multiple wives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In fact, we do not have to go back to the imperial era.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Although my grandfather and maternal grandfather were neither officials nor come from rich families, both of them had two wives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These two examples remind us that many customs and even laws change with the progress of society and science.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, the current definition of marriage between men and women will continue to be covered by the Women's Charter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In other words, if, one day, more than half of the Members of Parliament or population agree to amend the Women's Charter and expand the definition of marriage, it would be a new law and need not garner two-thirds of votes as required for an amendment to the Constitution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our generation should not and does not have the right to set a higher bar on the issue involving someone's lifetime happiness, depriving the next generation of the chance to make a decision for themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They include professionals from all walks of life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some have been living with the same-sex partner for decades and are faithful.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some are also public-spirited, contributing to society and the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some Singaporeans may not have known or come into contact with homosexuals directly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But I think you would have heard of these names: Taiwanese writer Pai Hsien-yung, Golden Horse award-winning director Tsai Ming-liang, Hong Kong director Stanley Kwan, founder of Cloud Gate Dance Theatre Lin Hwai-min, Hong Kong singers Anthony Wong and Leslie Cheung, lyric writer Lin Xi, and Cantonese Opera singer Ren Jian-hui.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These are household names in the Chinese arts, culture and entertainment scene.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Their talent has provided us with much spiritual food and entertainment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They have countless loyal readers, audience and fans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They live in a more conservative and traditional oriental society and have probably gone through a lot of struggles, from knowing their sexuality and accepting that they like same-sex relationships, to coming out of closet and accepting public scrutiny, or even criticism.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In English): People's views and social norms do change over time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In the past, it was unusual for men to wear earrings, remove body hair, or perm their hair.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For women to wear skirts that do not extend below their knees, or for anyone besides gangsters to have tattoos.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Now we see these expressions of individuality frequently in our everyday lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We should not tie our future generations to be restricted by today's traditions and norms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Instead, we should advocate for more freedom for them to decide how they want to live their lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Today, we are addressing an act of intimacy, in this case for men with men.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Just like every other kind of relationship, let us continue to maintain discretion in the public display of affections.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Therefore, the advocacy of specific rights before our society is ready may do more harm than good.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We aim to be more progressive, but we must ensure that our direction and steps are carefully considered.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Sustainability and Environment and Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We are debating on the issue of the freedom to love.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is an issue close to my heart and also to many conservative Singaporeans at large.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Section 377A has been a key flash point of debate on societal norms, traditional values, freedom, equality any many other topics.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This very House has also seen many a fiery and passionate debate over the last two decades on this issue.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our Courts, it has witnessed a share of constitutional challenges as no other law, perhaps, has seen.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And it is with the most recent challenge in the Courts that has brought us here today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For many, 377A represents a bulwark against a perceived counter-cultural tide that may engulf society should the law be done away.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At this point it is worth noting that for most conservatives, opposition to the repeal of 377A is premised not on the act nor the actors itself, but what the repeal may lead to – what I alluded to earlier, of that tide, or slippery slope of what they view as same-sex unions, adoptions and surrogacy by same-sex couples becoming the norm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Recent interviews with apex religious leaders in the media show that it remains a complex issue.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, they do acknowledge that the prerogative of repeal lies with Parliament, as long as the rights of the religious are protected, what they believe in and what they can preach.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a parliamentarian, my public duty is to make laws that are for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As other Members have mentioned, we are guided by our culture, our faith and the environment that we grow up in.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am a Catholic by faith, guided by the teachings of my faith to discern with justice decisions that are moral.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am also a father and a husband, whose moral duty it is to ensure stability and well-being for my children and family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, I arrive at today’s debate having wrestled with all my roles and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also arrive having had the opportunity over the last few months to have robust, intense and passionate discussions with fellow legislators on this topic, and many constituents and Singaporeans who have corresponded with me and feel passionately about this issue – on both sides.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am deeply appreciative of the willingness of all sides of the debate to have listened rationally and respectfully to each other to arrive at a common ground.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I will state what I believe marriage to be.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Marriage is a bond that draws a man and woman together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a natural relationship framed not just by love but promises of commitment and responsibility.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Marriage aligns with the way in which men and women live interdependently and bring out the best of each other.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Marriage is a faithful, exclusive, lifelong union of a man and a woman, joined in an intimate community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is the bedrock of families and conversely, society as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A man and a woman commit themselves to each other, for better or for worst, to the wondrous responsibility of bringing children into the world and caring for them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The call to marriage is also woven deeply into how society works, into the human spirit itself.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Man and woman of course, are equal, however, are created differently but made for each other.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This sexual difference draws them together in a mutually loving union that should be always open to family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, erasing the connection between gender and marriage changes the fundamental nature of a marital union, which is to nurture society’s next generation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unlike other relationships, marriage has the potential to create and nurture new lives, making it a unique institution.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For these reasons, states recognise the marriage of a man and woman as a public institution in its laws.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Marriage is protected and honoured because it makes an exclusive and indispensable influence over the common good of society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The real problem today is a view that marriage as simply a formality or a fad with no social obligations, that it is just a private and personal decision between two persons with nothing to do with wider society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But marriage is not just a religious or cultural institution.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In a heterosexual marriage, by bringing children into the society, the state has an obligation towards the couple and their children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For this reason, marriage requires the state to intervene and regulate it because of the social implications.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If it is just a relationship between two ordinary people, we do not regulate ordinary friendship or even platonic friendships.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That those of us who hold on to the traditional definition of marriage are conservative and old-fashioned – out of touch with reality.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Those who share these sentiments are called out online and accused of blind prejudice, of being bigots.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, I accept, as many Members have alluded to, that in taking a stand about this, I and other Members open ourselves to disagreement by others; strong disagreement at times.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I appreciate, therefore, this opportunity for a respectful debate in this House.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, I acknowledge that that same high bar for a constitutional amendment in the future would apply to defining marriage in the Constitution right now.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In as much as the current amendment would not be considered equivalent to enshrining marriage, it offers a clear definition of marriage as it currently stands, as a union between a man and a woman.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hold the Government to its word that under its watch that no redefinition of marriage will take place.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And even if a future government does so, it will perhaps require a repeal of Article 156 that we are introducing, as it would be made redundant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore seek the Government’s continued affirmation that this remains its commitment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This being the year of the celebrating family, perhaps all the more apt that we collectively pass this amendment and affirm marriage and the family and their place in our society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the passing of the constitutional amendment, the task is not complete.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The task ahead will require a whole of society effort to emphasise the importance of marriage and the family – not just on the part of Government but for every individual and group that believes in the importance of marriage and family, and to champion it collectively.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our laws that uphold the family and marriage, especially on spousal rights, must be re-emphasised.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Education, the key leveller for society, that is widely available for all in Singapore, must continue to ensure that our curricula continue to uphold the definition of marriage and family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And in the media space, print and in broadcast, must also help to shape the norms as currently established.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What I hope the Government will help to clarify is the protection of non-government entities from legal challenges over the issue of marriage in the public sphere.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Rightfully, our Government is secular and must remain so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It does not base its laws or policies on religion or faith.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But Singapore is also a multi-religious and multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We built this city on our Asian values, cultures and traditions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many citizens’ beliefs and way of life are shaped in line with their religious and cultural beliefs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, if a religious institution declines to conduct a ceremony for a transgender or same-sex couple, will they be subject to a lawsuit?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are many other implications and I hope that the Government would be able to clarify this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a decision that I struggled deeply over the last few months, personally and professionally.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I made the point earlier on the role that section 377A as a bulwark.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we do pass Article 156, and pass it we must, I am of the belief that a new gate, perhaps not as robust as what many perceive 377A itself to be, but a gate nonetheless, will now be in place.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As I have made clear earlier, the non-enforcement of 377A had made the law itself redundant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Parliament alone should be responsible for the passing, amendment and repeal of all laws, and she states this right clearly today rather than wait for the Courts to strike it down.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I must also emphasise that I am not unsympathetic to the experiences of rejection, violence and vilification that the LGBTQ+ community faces.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I know many of them and I am honoured to enjoy the friendship of many as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am also aware of the targeting of religious and social conservatives online by trolls and those opposed to their views on traditional marriage and family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must therefore come down hard on discrimination in all its form in the workplace, in schools, in the public sphere.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should treat bullying and harassment seriously, be they in physical or virtual spaces, for all parties in this debate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must endeavour to build a more equal society for all, not just for one, because whatever the label applied to each of us, we must first acknowledge the wholeness and dignity of each person as an individual being.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I acknowledge as well the passion and drive that the LGBTQ+ community has displayed over the years in their effort to repeal section 377A.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many members of the community and their allies are measured, responsible and aware of the complexity of the issue in our society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we break down this barrier for what is in the private sphere, I continue to believe strongly that this must not lead to the breakdown of the institution of marriage in the public sphere.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I fully acknowledge as well that the view may evolve in the distant future, but for now, we have an opportunity in this House to ensure that the institution of marriage endures and is championed and celebrated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the basis of the passage of Article 156, I also give my support for the repeal of 377A.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After the conclusion of all our debates, we must return to working together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unity is not the absence of disagreement but a consensus to agree to work together in spite of those disagreements.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I am the proud parent of four children and four grandchildren, so this was a debate which I saw the opportunity to share some personal perspectives and that of my residents.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Traditional marriage has been venerated in all societies, all civilisations since time immemorial – first point.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, a marriage is far more than a legally binding contract between two consenting adults.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third, the rights of children, in fact, are paramount and, in fact, triumph even the mutual happiness of parents.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, I start off with these three propositions for your consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: My life was transformed the first moment I held my daughter in my arms.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For the first time in my life, I held a precious, new, unique human being – utterly dependent on my wife and me.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: She may have been delivered by my wife but my daughter and now, her children – my grandchildren – have a future that goes, hopefully, far beyond me.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That moment was also the time when I realised just how much my parents love me and, with some guilt, I realised that actually all of us cannot possibly love our parents as much as our parents love us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Every single one of you here who has been a parent, I think, has had that experience.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What it shows is that love flows down the generations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, parental love is about paying it forward.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is this focus on forward and the future that drives us – drives all parents – to give the best possible start to their children.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is what makes us so focused on leaving the world in a better state for our children to inherit.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: You see, it is this focus on the future, on protecting, nurturing, saving, investing, building; it is this future-oriented focus that affects the tone of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Frankly, even in Parliament, it is why, for me, there is no such thing as saving too much for the future – because it is for them and not for us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Even as we do that, we are simply, in fact, replicating what our parents and grandparents did for us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is why I believe all societies, all religions, have always conferred a sacred status on the institution of marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is why this is a key pillar, a key prescription, for human progress in societies everywhere since time immemorial.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The second point is that a marriage is far more than a legally binding contract between two consenting adults for the sake of their mutual happiness.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: My wife has often reminded me of an aphorism – the best gift you can give your children is to love their mother.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Initially, I found this advice bemusing, but the more I thought about it, actually, this advice makes perfect sense.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because, you see, children – in fact, think back to your own childhood – children need that reassurance, that sense of stability of knowing that both parents are in a committed, loving relationship for the long term and that both parents, will always be there for them.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, the way we approach our marriage is not and should not be about just optimising the happiness of two adults but really for the sake of our children and their future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because if we are successful and if we are blessed, then, we are good role models for our children.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But our mistakes or, sometimes, our wrong choices, have profound impact and implications on our children.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: My third point is that every child has a biological father and mother.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is not just a matter of biology and genes and chromosomes, but think back to your own childhood – our mothers and our fathers played essential, complementary but not identical roles.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When I served as the Minister in the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports, I studied the problem of children in juvenile homes or with dysfunctional social circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The single, most important factor I often found recurring was an absent father.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, some children, especially those in less ideal circumstances, deserve and need additional support, which this House agrees with, I am sure.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Some of my friends whom I have known for the longest time are gay.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: My generation came of age in the early 1980s.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The AIDS epidemic had not yet been named or discovered but it had started.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many of us were not quite aware of the threat.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The veil of ignorance, the fear of embarrassment, in fact, contributed tragically to the cutting short of lives of some of my friends.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But beyond that, in fact, I am sure if you all speak to every single one of your gay friends, every single one of them has suffered the pain of rejection, of discrimination, sometimes, of violence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They have suffered that at home, in schools and in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They crave our understanding, our empathy, our support and our protection.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First, to protect the traditional family, which frankly is under considerable stress in modern days.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But equally important, there is also a duty to protect our gay brothers from victimisation and the fear and the pain, the dejection and the rejection.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There are no simple answers to such apparently contradictory social imperatives.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann, Deputy Speaker Christopher de Souza, Mr Edward Chia and I represent the GRC of Holland-Bukit Timah.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To be frank with all of you, the majority of the feedback that we have received online and face-to-face, the majority has expressed great anxiety about families, anxiety about the repeal and a deeper anxiety about the future of families.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It may not be all of us in the future; it will be a different House, but it will be decided through the political process, with all the engagement, discussion, debate, negotiation and compromises which are needed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That is the way we need to move forward.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Similarly, to my residents who have asked for it to be entrenched, two-third majority and lock it up.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have to tell them that actually, these are issues which no amount of legal and constitutional lock-ups will decide for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The values, the mores, the attitudes of our children and grandchildren – we can all do our best to instil values in them, but we have got to trust them.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We trust them and entrust them with the power and the authority to make decisions in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, I also accept this amendment which makes it clear that the current definition and if there is going to be any future amendment, will be decided in this House and not in a court of law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We do all these in full appreciation of the fact that difficult issues that go to the heart of identity, deeply held values and lived experience are best settled through careful, respectful, sincere discussions – without polemics, without win-lose outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And so, it is in this spirit that I support the amendments moved today.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have to find ways to continue to protect this precious and fragile institution of the traditional family and marriage and we have to remember that the welfare and the rights of our children are paramount.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It also means our public messaging, our education, in schools, the mass media must continue to uphold these traditional family ideals.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Having said that, in my earlier versions of the speech I tried to say we can do all these without discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But actually, in life, if you uplift one form, if you prioritise one type of social arrangements, inevitably it means you have to choose and it cannot be completely equal.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Having said that, I believe a spirit of mutual respect and perhaps more important than anything else, compassion, can allow us to find that hopefully safe landing zone where we can protect our families and protect our gay brothers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On that note, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the amendments standing before the House today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
