text: Most prefer to preserve the existing social norms on marriage and family that have served us well as a stable and prosperous society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, there is a small yet increasingly expanding segment, that feels differently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of them are youths, who had a different kind of exposure and experience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They have their own views on this matter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On the part of the Government, we have sought to take a calibrated position and try to balance various aspects in this sensitive and difficult issue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is a position that most in society can accept, even if it does not fulfil all their wishes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, it is important for us to hear different voices from all segments of Singaporeans, including the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I have been involved in several dialogue sessions involving the Malay/Muslim organisations on this issue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Personally, I have also engaged a wide range of groups and many individuals from the Malay/Muslim community on this issue in small and informal discussions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some from the gay community shared with me their stories of being discriminated, ostracised and even threatened by those closest to them, including family and friends.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: No one should be treated this way, especially in a society such as ours, where family and community play such pivotal roles in our daily lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: That is why some individuals, even though they do not practice the homosexual lifestyle, feel that we should not ostracise this group of people.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They feel that we need to be open, despite having different views, so that the gay community can lead their own lives in a safe manner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At the same time, there are others who do not accept the homosexual lifestyle but want to have a discussion on the basis of compassion for their fellow Muslims who are struggling with difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Yet often, they find it difficult to speak up, because they are concerned about the repercussions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They worry about the criticisms and negative and extreme responses that could arise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They are worried that they will be accused of being too conservative if they were to share their views or too liberal for wanting to engage the gay community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have seen for ourselves some of the online reactions that are very harsh and unpleasant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I have also spoken to our youths on this issue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many are sympathetic of the difficulties that their gay friends and family members face.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They care deeply about their mental well-being and their access to social support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Yet, there are still differences of opinion among these youths regarding the repeal to section 377A and the constitutional amendment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some see the repeal as an overdue issue and question the need to amend the Constitution.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Others, whether religious or non-religious, worry about the impact of this repeal on our cherished social norms and traditional family structure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There is no single narrative or perspective that can fully reflect the reality that we live in.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: And only by acknowledging these complexities, we can finally begin to move forward together as a community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We want a community that shows kindness and compassion to all, regardless of their background or circumstance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This includes even those who do not adhere to religious teachings on homosexuality.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To quote the Mufti in his religious guidance that provided wise counsel to us on this matter, “There are many factors that define a person as a human being, not just sexual orientation alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are individual Muslims that face struggles as they seek to reconcile their sexuality with religious guidance and obligations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As long as one proclaims and practices the basic tenets of the religion, that person is still a member of the Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Every Muslim deserve to have their dignity and respect preserved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must ensure that every Muslim does not feel that they are turned away from their faith due to our attitude towards them.” We must be prepared to face future challenges together as one people: difficult economic conditions; societal norms that continue to evolve; new issues that will challenge our traditional values; and many more.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The nature and integrity of our society will be tested.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is our chance to set the norms for our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We may have differing views, but we must find a way to resolve the differences and find the best way forward for our country.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am confident that if we can learn to navigate sensitive and crucial issues constructively, we can form a clearer vision for ourselves and future generations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: May this lead us to a brighter future for all of us as a nation.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important step towards respecting and acknowledging gay Singaporeans as an integral part of the Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The colonial origin law is outdated and it ignores the objective reality that Singapore is home to many gay citizens and residents who are also contributing members of the Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To retain a law that criminalises a legitimate community of fellow Singaporeans in order to preserve traditional values is at best a stretched logic.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: There are other better ways to promote traditional values.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I recognise that a significant segment of the Singapore society is still very conservative.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Some fear the repeal will lead to a flood of changes to the complexion of our society.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I also recognise that there is an appropriate time and place for all things.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, amending some public policies to fairly include gay Singaporeans does not equate to an erosion of the family as society's building block.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Like all Singaporeans, gay citizens have everyday concerns about life and livelihoods that public policies can address without threatening the current definition of marriage.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We also should be mindful that social norms change and evolve.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, we must not forget that gay Singaporeans contribute economically and socially to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They should be treated as full members of our society and be accorded the respect and support like any Singapore Citizen.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we should be careful to ensure that our public polices do not marginalise or pervade stigmatisation or discrimination against them.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In the public discourse on the repeal of section 377A so far, I am heartened to see a lot more restraint exhibited, in comparison to what we saw back in 2007 when the repeal was first debated.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is a positive sign that our society has evolved and we are able to discuss difficult issues without being inflammatory.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the forward discourse will continue to be balanced, considered and secular.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In a diverse and multi-faceted society like ours, fault lines exist everywhere.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Some are deep and old, others are new and emergent.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We only need to look around the world to see many examples of how once inclusive and tolerant societies could suddenly become severely polarised and fractured.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: As Singaporeans, we must remember to always demonstrate a high level of respect and willingness to engage with fellow citizens who hold different views.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To promote social harmony and cohesion, our national values should promote mutual accommodation and compassion among the different segments of the Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Even if we cannot agree, we must always uphold mutual respect and be prepared to listen and to try to understand each other.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am speaking today on both the Penal Code (Amendment) Bill and the Bill on the amendment to the Constitution as many of my residents have reached out or written to me since the Prime Minister's National Day Rally speech on the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They had asked that I share their concerns and seek clarification to address their apprehensions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is a difficult topic with differing views but an important one for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At this point, I should share my personal views on this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I will say that it took me quite a long time to write the speech.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My speech is not long, do not worry, but it took me a long time to write it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because I had to ask myself where I stood on this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As a parent and also being a Member of Parliament for the last 16 years and seeing my residents when they come to me with issues, I have a very firm belief that the family is the cornerstone of society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I really believe it is the source of strength and it is also the source of weakness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, I do cherish the traditional definition of family.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Being a parent for more than 30 years now, and being married for over 32 years, I will say to you, as much as I think I am a good mother, I have realised that my husband and myself play a very important role for our three children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do want to preserve and protect the definition of a family.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, let me now summarise the apprehensions expressed by my residents and what they centre around.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One, the safeguarding and the definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman and pro-family policies, such as, public housing, education, adoption rules and media standards.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Two, that the repeal of section 377A will encourage gay activists to push the agenda much further and this may cause reactions and divisions in Singapore as we see happening in many countries in the world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The concern of my residents is the divisions and what it may cause.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Three, protecting people from being pressured, bullied or discriminated against when they do not support the same ideas and beliefs whether to retain or repeal section 377A.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many have shared that they feel that section 377A is a unique Singapore compromise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Its non-enforcement means our colleagues, friends, neighbours and family members who identify themselves as homosexuals are able to live out their private lives while protecting gay values from becoming mainstream.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It has worked for Singapore, so, the question is, why the need to make the change now?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Shanmugam has explained the circumstances and that there are real risks that section 377A can be stuck down.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Section 377A has been challenged as unconstitutional and continues to be challenged.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Courts have judged that such matters are sensitive societal issues and that it is for Parliament to decide.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But the point is that if Parliament does nothing, the Courts will have to do what it has to do, when it has to do it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And when that happens, the apprehensions that have been expressed will become real.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is precisely that the Government, hearing the views of the majority, is acting.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is easier for the Government to do nothing – and in fact, politically actually, much easier, especially given how controversial this issue is.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, that would be extremely irresponsible, as there is real risk that the very definition of marriage and the pro-family policies that the majority want to protect will be challenged as we are already seeing in several countries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On the point of why we keep section 377A, I think it is also important that I also share feedback that I have received from residents, that I have friends, colleagues, neighbours and family members, as I have shared, who are gay members.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They, and even those who have asked for the repeal of 377A, do not view it as a crime that what consenting adult gay men have and do in private.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But what it stems more from the fact that of the fear of what it means after that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What the repeal of 377A really does is it removes the stigma and the hurt that the gay people in our community have been feeling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I want to say that gay males are fellow Singaporeans as they are and they can be your neighbour, your co-worker, your friend or even your family member.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They contribute to and are part of our society and they too, deserve dignity and respect.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendment, I feel, is a balanced one, as it protects the traditional definition of marriage and pro-family policies while allowing our future generations to decide on societal norms.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That is the reassurance that has been given.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think that that is a balanced approach and one that does seek to protect, the definition that the majority want to hold.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are hearing strong sentiments and differing views with the debate around the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Youths and working professionals have approached me and expressed fears and anxieties with gay activism.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Some have shared that while they accept their friends and family who identify as gays, they find it difficult to voice their opinions when they do not share their values and ideas, for fear of being labelled, bullied or cancelled in school or at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The fear, real or perceived, is that the repeal of 377A will amplify this activism.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But, similarly, I would like to caution us that with the debate on this repeal, we are also seeing a heightened attention on those that identify as gay.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I also have residents expressing concerns of possible discrimination against those who identify themselves as gay.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is clear is that this is a subject that matters to many, regardless of whether we support the repeal or the retention of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would ask for more to be shared as to what the details of these are and to reassure individuals and groups that there are clear protections from discriminatory pressures, a cancel culture and bullying in society, in schools, and/or at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The societal values and definition of marriage, family and policies affecting our children are important for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we have done before, I do appeal to all, regardless of where we stand on this matter, we must work together and not allow this to divide us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While diversity exists, we have learnt to respect and allow different individuals to practise their faith, believes, traditions and religions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: All these are possible because first, we have intentional policies in place to enhance behaviours which are widely acceptable or discourage certain behaviours which are less accepted.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, we learn to respect one another from the values we are taught in school and at home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Third, we define over time the country we wish to live in and the societal behaviours that most consider as norms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is the basis I believe have bonded us together and enabled us to live in harmony thus far.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But beneath this social model, there still lies frictions and differing views in our country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Some of these frictions or differences are not easily solved or appreciated by different groups as it is not simply an assessment of right or wrong, nor is it about the louder voice triumphs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Especially not so when it comes to one's preferences, liberty of choices and how one can make others understand their views and accept it without having broader societal impact.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If only things were as straightforward, there would be hope of reduced conflicts and more peace today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As it is with any evolving society, when the exposure to different facets of life become wider for most individuals, the reality is we are faced with a gradation of expectations and perceptions from the family, friends, co-workers and society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For us to move forward as a country, there needs to be more ability in us to actively hear different viewpoints, be less biased beginning with a lesser extent of pre-judging people and for activists not to plainly impress one's agenda on others to accept regardless of the other's preferences and values.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How then can we achieve a calibrated balance between one's beliefs and practices without imposing on others?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe this boils down to the values that define each of us and what we are prepared to accept and adopt in our lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There are values which are key tenets of a society's mainstream, those which most can accept and acknowledge as norms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These values are those where people freely express and are naturally accepted without being judged.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, we must also recognise that there are other values which serve some unique groups or serve some purposes or being adopted by some but are not commonly observed amongst our daily lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is where management of social expectations and perceptions play a role.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Personally, I was raised on the values where family centricity is key.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One where marriage is defined as between one man and one woman.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is what I also wish to see remain as the beliefs, teachings and practices in our education system.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While I think many may share this view, we should not be oblivious that our next generation will not have access to information that influences them about homosexuality or sensitive topics; just because it is not taught or spoke about in mainstream schools.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Particularly so for ours, as many pieces of today’s legislation are designed with the family unit being the fundamental social fabric.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But housing demands come from many groups besides those with a family nucleus.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These groups include the unmarried singles, single parents with or without children, lone seniors and more.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: They, too, have a need for basic housing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For a need as basic as housing, this becomes a tricky situation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Whom then should be given access to public housing and in a timely manner?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Similarly, this also does not indicate that those who do not believe or adopt it should ostracise individuals who are different from themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Every family, every community, every individual has the right to choose what is comfortable for their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But as individuals, regardless of our beliefs and inclination, we should not impress upon others that they must embrace our way of living.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With time and ability of individuals to perceive different norms, the values of what define us as a society will naturally surface.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, Sir, let us not allow divisive voices to break us apart but rather for us to consider when and how we want to be inclusive while maintaining our own beliefs and values.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The responses and emotions were mixed – from disappointment that the repeal was not enough, to concern that societal norms and values would be challenged and even, eventually, possibly changed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, in the run up to this Parliamentary Sitting, I have often been asked what my views are on the matter, and one particular question that I was asked, which stuck with me, was if I was “pro-repeal” or “pro-family.” These were terms that made me realise how polarising the issue was for many people who took a binary view of the matter.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For them, it was either one or the other.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, when we use terms like “community” and “society”, we have to acknowledge that these are larger entities that are made up of individuals, they are made up of people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And no one is exactly alike – we look different, we think different, we have different beliefs, we have different cultures, we have different values, we have different lifestyles, and, yes, we have different sexual preferences and practices.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A truly inclusive community and society consists of people who are willing to not just tolerate, but actually accept those who are different from them, and those who are different should not be discriminated against in any way.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, while I understand the legal arguments for the repeal of 377A, I would like to say that it is even more important for us to recognise the need to repeal 377A from the perspective of moral integrity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You might ask how you would define moral integrity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think, simply put, moral integrity is doing the right thing because it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Repealing this law sends a strong signal that we do recognise and respect individual differences, and that different groups are welcome in our community, which brings me to my next point about people, community and conversations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because we now have to look at the issue from the different perspective of how, while a community and society is made up of people, as I mentioned earlier, these people do not live in isolated silos but have to live and function within the larger entity of a community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, the changes that the Government is affirming with the definition of marriage, of what constitutes a family and related social policies are done in the context of what it feels would work for our Singaporean community, having taken into account the various opinions and views on the matter.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Differences in opinion, such as those arising from a topic, such as the repeal of section 377A, can lead different groups to clashing head-on over issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It may lead to our society fracturing over fault lines because of the different hectoring voices that shout others down.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However – and this is my sincere hope – such differences, if looked at rationally, can also be an opportunity for frank and open dialogue to look at the debate and embrace different perspectives and viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These conversations, based on mutual respect, can help us evolve into a more inclusive society, one that is richer through plurality and diversity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Enshrining anything in law is important but, equally important, is the value of open discussion and mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also important not to embrace a "cancel" culture or to automatically rule out someone who holds different views or even someone who decides to look at the topic conservatively.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Worse still, we should not go back to labelling and stereotyping, even though I know I just used the term "conservatively".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My view is that it would be good to allow others their views, even if it may seem more traditional and less progressive – there go the labels again – when viewed through certain lenses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not easy, it is not possible, but it is really my view that we are able to allow others with a different opinion from us to speak, to have their voices heard, for us to have this dialogue.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would now like to move into education and schools, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe it would be good to consider education and consider how the schools can play a part in nurturing open conversations so that this topic is handled sensitively.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our schools must be safe places for students to engage in respectful conversations or debates with others who may hold contrary opinions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the careful management of discussions on controversial issues, schools can help to promote freedom of expression, as well as inclusion and tolerance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In doing so, I believe they would encourage mutual understanding and acceptance.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In many ways, sensitive handling of these challenging issues would be a form of modelling of open discussion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I then made the point that, like any quilt, in time, we do have occasional tears in the fabric and some parts of our quilt are fraying at the edges.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I conclude my speech in support of the Bill and the repeal of 377A.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The concerns and aspirations of every Singaporean should be heard and should be valued, especially on such issues that matter to all of us.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For most of the voices that are speaking up, they have come from a place of love – a love for the future of this country, a love for the future of our people and our society, and a love for this world.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are members of our community who have difficulty accepting the implications that they feared would come with the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The fear is about losing the fundamental values that we have built our society on and the fabric that holds us together.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To me, this fear comes from a position of love, not of hate, as they love the country and community that we have built and are worried about it being damaged.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are also members of our community who feel that the repeal of section 377A has been long overdue, and some of them are also hoping that our societal norms can further evolve and become more liberal towards different types of marriages and families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This set of views also stems from a place of love, where they would like to embrace differences and allow everyone to pursue whatever lifestyle they so desire.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, we have also come across voices who do not come from a place of love but would rather stir hatred and misunderstanding within our society, and these are the ones who are drawing and then exploiting fault lines within our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such views can come from any quarter of society and may even be disguised as supporters of any of the positions that I had mentioned above, but their ultimate aim is to push Singapore to an extreme corner of the spectrum, without consideration as to whether this would be good for us.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of these could also be driven or initiated by foreign elements with an insidious agenda, given the borderless nature of social media and the Internet.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to unite and fight as one to overcome the many difficulties which lie ahead.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to deal with the rising costs of living amid increasing global tensions and geopolitical conflicts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us all be more understanding of and respectful towards one another, so that no one will feel discriminated against.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is one aspect where we individuals have choice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And in Singapore, marriage between a man and woman remains the fundamental building blocks of a family.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we have to consider how, since 2007, when section 377A was last debated, social acceptance for homosexuality has "shifted appreciably" as mentioned by Prime Minister Lee.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Back then, it was decided not to actively enforce section 377A.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It has been unsuccessfully challenged in the past before, but it will be reckless of us to not consider this and the ramifications if it was struck down without any protection on the definition of marriage as how our society values it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it is only right that we consider to repeal section 377A in our Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We acknowledge that we are still a largely conservative society, but our gay citizens have a place in society and should not be treated as criminals.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While, in general, more are accepting of homosexuality now, we are also very concerned about protecting the current social and family norms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the repeal of section 377A, how can we effectively safeguard our social norms and values and, in particular, the institution of marriage which is currently defined as being that between man and woman?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also understand how this definition underpins various national policies, such as housing and education.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it is even more necessary for us to ensure that the current social and family norms are protected.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Undoubtedly, there are strong views for and against the repeal of section 377A and the amendment to the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are concerns that there would be increased activism on both ends of the spectrum, which can potentially be aggressive and, more importantly, divisive to our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think it is necessary for us to accept this as a consensus – the best possible outcome, given the various viewpoints and deliberations with regard to all the various groups of people, religious, non-religious organisations and the gay community, which has been ongoing since 2007 and before.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we should not curtail or suppress social activism for causes that our citizens believe in, we must also caution against extreme views and actions that may prove to be divisive to our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In time to come, should values and norms here in Singapore "appreciably shift" again, then we should be able to come together, sharing our views and reaching a consensus on how we best move forward.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Activists in both camps need not think that they should resort to drastic measures to highlight their cause, nor should any of us be influenced by foreign developments, including pushing values from multinational corporations which are not aligned with our Singaporean values.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore's laws are its own and we need not follow the lead of other countries if it does not suit the values and dispositions of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   We can see how the whole world changes with the passage of time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Section 377A is a piece of legislation that we inherited from the British and has been used as a symbol to define marriage as between a man and a woman.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although previous cases have not succeeded in rejecting section 377A, we cannot take that risk, especially since such a key decision will leave a huge impact on other legislations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For our Muslim community, we have AMLA, which defines marriage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although this ensures that policies in Singapore will continue to prioritise the family and the definition of marriage will not change, we cannot deny that the rest of the world has and will continue to evolve, including the values within their own communities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot be influenced by foreign elements, including multinational corporations that support values which are not aligned with our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The laws in Singapore are our laws and we should not follow in the footsteps of other countries if these are not appropriate for our country.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, it is important for us to define the kind of values we want in Singapore's society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like a Malay proverb which exalts that children should be nurtured from young, it is important for us to build a family based on these values, so that we can instil them in our children.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Regarding homosexuality, we must admit that there are a few in our society who face personal challenges and sometimes, they are ridiculed, condemned and marginalised, or left behind without the support of their families from a young age.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In cultivating family values, we should also cultivate and portray our religious values, such as mercy, compassion and love for each other, so that these individuals do not feel left out and ostracised from our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As each of us provides family support, I urge our community to refer to asatizah and MUIS for help and guidance, if needed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Admittedly, however, this is not the end of our conversation on this topic, just like all the other issues that we face in society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, we must continue to keep future dialogues civil, rational and, most importantly, beneficial for Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We only have to look around us to see how issues can be made very divisive, if everyone insists on their entrenched views and not hear one another out and come to a compromise.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How, then, do we protect the definition of marriage, something which we all value as a society?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the other hand, for those who welcome the repeal and look beyond decriminalisation, there is room for the definitions to change when public opinion, values and norms differ.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think this is a viable compromise for our society to move forward for now.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This could potentially be a divisive issue, but it may not be.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I see it instead as an opportunity to open meaningful conversations about equality and inclusivity within our society.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Equality being one of our nation's ideals, we need to ensure that policies implemented to uphold the equal protection of rights for Singaporeans who do not fit squarely into the definition of a traditional family unit.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: So, for instance, single-parent households and LGBTQ+ Singaporeans, amongst others – after all, these people and many others not mentioned, contribute to the diverse, vibrant, welcoming society that is so admired around the world.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Do our policies recognise this and are we doing enough for them?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to put forward the following suggestions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Other jurisdictions, such as the European Union, have undertaken similar reviews in ensuring that all citizens, regardless of their background, are not unfairly discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This also ties into the ongoing Forward Singapore exercise, as we refresh our social compact to pursue a more equal and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Second, would be on education for our children.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with my Parliamentary colleague here, the hon Member Darryl David, that schools should be a safe space to explore, debate and educate about respect and inclusivity, and we should train our teachers to have productive conversations with students about these.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: So, in conclusion, Mr Speaker, Sir, regardless of where all in this House stand, I think we all agree that we want the best for our country and our people for a prosperous and inclusive and forward-looking Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: During his speech to announce Singapore's Independence from Malaysia on 9 August 1965, our founding father Lee Kuan Yew said: "Everyone will have his place: equal; language, culture, religion." We are, thus, compelled to move in this direction and ensure that every Singaporean can live a joyful, happy and peaceful life and contribute meaningfully to this great nation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is based on these ideals for a better Singapore that were first articulated more than five decades ago that we have built this inclusive global city which we are all proud to call home today.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has, indeed, become a beacon for many and, while conservative in our nature, we are a tolerant, peaceful and harmonious society, where everyone can live in community without fear.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that one day, we will not have to rely on the Constitution to safeguard, respect and celebrate our differences where there is a lot more binding us together as Singaporeans – a love for food, being "kiasu", being "champion grumblers" – than what differentiates us.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We have built a society based on interracial and inter-religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am certain we can establish a similarly harmonious relationship among one another regardless of our differences.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, we can learn to welcome, protect and even celebrate those differences, as one diverse, inclusive harmonious nation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our society's view on section 377A has evolved over time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Part of it can be attributed to our youths today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, I believe I can best contribute to our debate by highlighting their views.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The views of our youths are not solely attributed to the influx of "woke" culture from the West.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And that is, for the past few decades, we have been building a kinder Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our schools have taught our children and youths the value of justice, empathy and kindness.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Naturally, our youths believe the dignity of every Singaporean matters.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, we should not be surprised if our youths think that the provisions of section 377A are innately discriminatory, even if they are not enforced by the Government.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, should we be surprised that our youths can empathise with the lived experience of the gay community, some of whom have experienced real or perceived discrimination?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, while our Singapore youths respect diversity, they also continue to uphold the sensibility of a traditional society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They are pro-family and most believe marriage is best defined as between a man and a woman.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, with regards to family, their views are not that different from the generations of Singaporeans before them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Most of them have grown up with loving parents, grandparents and under the nurturing shade of our family centric policies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They, therefore, intuitively understand the importance of families, not just for themselves, but also for society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, many youths also wonder why it took society so long to repeal section 377A.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, they have now observed the painstaking consensus building effort needed to move Singapore along.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To sum up, our youths do not see the repeal of section 377A, or their belief that all Singaporeans matter, as contradictory to their pro-family stance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Their views are reasonable and we should listen to them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Next, I would like to talk about how we can best support our youths on this issue, especially, on the one hand, our youths who are gay and worried that they will be ostracised and, on the other hand, our youths who are worried about being "cancelled" for voicing, in a respectful manner, their traditional family values.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Indeed, we must take pains to ensure that our schools remain neutral on this issue and support both types of youths in an effective and low-key manner.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I have observed that for a minority of youths, there is a certain fluidity in gender self-identification.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A youth might identify himself as gay at a certain age but have a different take years later.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And the reverse can also be true too.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, our schools should neither celebrate nor ostracise our youths for being gay.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our schools should not let gender become the defining attribute of who a person is, because if this issue gets polarised, we will be robbing them of the opportunity to do an authentic self-evaluation, in their formative years, of who they truly are.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must also remember that for a small country, if our children and youths are fiercely divided along any issue, and then they grow up within the confines of those fault lines, the divide is not just ideological.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Frequently, the divide will have a human face attached to that divide.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And in my discussions with many teachers and school leaders, I believe our Primary, Secondary schools and Junior College (JC) leaders have done a good job in keeping our schools neutral.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They have taken a child-centric approach to providing quiet and effective support to our youths.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Compared to other countries, they have been quite successful in preventing educators from injecting their personal agendas into the classrooms.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But it has been a while since we have last debated on this issue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, it is best if MOE can remind our school leaders and teachers on this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And Singaporeans will also appreciate if MOE can reiterate their firm stance on this matter.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The situation in our tertiary institutes is more complex.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We are, first and foremost, representatives of the people that voted for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, this is our utmost responsibility: to properly capture and reflect the views of our constituents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, we are members of a political party, who were likewise elected to formulate policies for our nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the Workers’ Party, our mandate – as loyal opposition – is to provide alternative views and constructive critique of the ruling party’s ideas and proposals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And third, we are of course individuals who carry our own beliefs and convictions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rarely is there confluence in these three identities, which results in us having to make a reasonable effort at balancing between different preferences and exercising compromise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is not necessarily as difficult as it sounds; for esoteric bills, our electorate often expects us to do our homework and choose what is in the best interests of the country at large.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, they may not hew to strongly-held views of their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At other times, there are bipartisan consensus on how best to proceed and so our interventions in Parliament are limited to flagging points of concern, but the Workers’ Party nevertheless votes alongside the ruling party.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my speech, I wish to explain why I believe that these disparate views can be reconciled and how this leads me to vote the way that I will.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the many letters written to me by the residents of Sengkang, those that have expressed their concern over the repeal of 377A have, almost uniformly, cited their reservation over how such a repeal would open the floodgates to revisions to the traditionalist interpretation of marriage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This concern has not only been limited to those who are more religiously inclined.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have spoken to residents who would otherwise hold no strong views on 377A, nevertheless underscore their wish that the heterosexual definition of marriage be, somehow, protected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this is a prospective fear: one based on how the repeal of 377A is a slippery slope; once the law is removed, the floodgates are open and all manner of permissive laws become possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, 377A is currently on the books and consenting relations between two men is currently a crime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, a man engaged in same-sex sexual relations could be jailed, if the strict letter of the law were to be followed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It seems clear to me that there is not, and cannot, be a genuine equivalence between the two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The usual pushback against claims that 377A constitutes an actual violation of the law, is that 377A is not enforced and – on the basis of court judgments – will not be, unless otherwise instructed by the Attorney-General.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This suggests that the Article is merely a relic, one that has no bite and hence, any fear is similarly ephemeral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is true that the Courts have previously ruled that 377A would not be prosecuted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think about what this means when the status of rule of law in our country if we insist on instituting laws that simultaneously do not matter in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: How many more de jure issues also would not matter, de facto?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we wish to make a slippery slope argument, this strikes me as a far slipperier one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, we should recognise that even an unenforced law can have effects on individuals and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think of the symbolism behind what a law, any law, implies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Suppose, for a moment, there was a law prohibiting relationships between individuals of different races, and further suppose that a similar legal precedent and political compromise exists, in that those who are in such a miscegenated relationship are assured that they will never be prosecuted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is a hypothetical but is it fair to expect those who are in a mixed-race relationship to accept the assurance that such a sword of Damocles hanging over their relationship does not really mean anything?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To take the argument further, should we expect that individuals will feel that they are a fair and equal part of society, when society has deigned it permissible to have a law that, even while unenforced, nevertheless explicitly condemns their behaviour?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We are an Eastern society, with different cultural mores and practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They argue that a repeal of 377A amounts to bringing in the polarisation and cultural wars – so prevalent in the seemingly dysfunctional democracies of the West – back home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our cultural norms skew toward greater social conservatism and society stresses compromise for the sake of harmony, rather than the contentious and often raucous activism favoured by civil society and activism in the West.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But an untenable status quo, however entrenched, does not imply that all is well under the surface.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For those who keenly feel the yoke of discrimination, suggesting that we should keep things the way that they have always been – simply because that is how it has always been – is more than simply benign neglect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is an insult to their plight, to the burden that they have been bearing, perhaps silently, until now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is like telling a prisoner that their desire for freedom is an attempt to stir up unrest while they are in jail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a man attracted to the opposite sex, I can never fully empathise what it means to develop feelings for someone of the same gender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But when I was a hot-blooded teenager, I had a dear friend, who turned out to be gay, explain to me what his world was like.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The analogy has stayed with me ever since.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just imagine, he said, if the way you feel about women – the strong, unrelenting attraction when you first meet, the wish to share one’s most innermost thoughts and feelings with them, the deep desire to be with that person for the rest of your life – imagine if all that was not the natural order of things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Imagine that society deemed my attraction to women as not just abhorrent, but also judged intimate expressions of my love to be criminal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not too far from other historical legacies where the law deemed certain forms of love to be illegal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As recently as the 1960s, interracial relationships were limited in some form in as many as 31 US states, as it was in Nazi Germany and apartheid South Africa.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I am not equating the two, my point is that my own relationship as well as that of my parents – which occurred between two different ethnicities – would have fallen afoul of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The usual retort to such scenarios is that it is contrived; humans are not animals and, after all, we can always exercise self-restraint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some argue that because same-sex attraction is ultimately psychological, it can be overturned, with intervention and counselling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I am not here to question the natural biological order which I respect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, it is a physiological reality that asexual reproduction among mammals is impossible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And hence, the male-female pairing is necessary to ensure the continuation of these species.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, for certain individuals, such attractions are deeply embedded in what may be regarded as innate biologically-led behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, I also cannot really ignore how many in our Asian society continue to equate marriage and partnership to one between a man and a woman.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This view is held not only those who are religious – by which I mean not just by groups that have been more vocal about traditional marriage, such as evangelical Christians and Muslims – but, based on my conversations with residents in Sengkang and beyond, also those who do not strongly profess any faith.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For these Singaporeans, the fact that marriage must involve a union between a man and a woman goes beyond a legally binding contractual relationship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This sense is so deeply ingrained that they are not only are unable to accept the principle of same-sex marriage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For them, were such marriages to become recognised, they – perhaps paradoxically – would feel that society is not only no longer representative of who they are, but some may even go as far as to feel that it has turned against them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is secondary that heterosexual norms remain the firm majority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many will feel a sense of exclusion and victimhood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As it turns out, this worldview is remarkably pervasive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I do not have comprehensive data, I have had many conversations over the course of the past few months and I would be willing to venture that a significant majority of Singaporeans – including those in Sengkang, including otherwise liberal-minded spirits, and even including those who are otherwise sympathetic about the repeal of 377A – carry this perspective close to their hearts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is important that we do not dismiss this worldview as emanating from an oppressive majority, finally receiving their comeuppance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is because I actually believe that such sentiments – even if some may argue are seemingly misplaced – are indeed genuine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When I was a teenager, I took my Christian faith very seriously – to the point where I even harboured ambitions to be a missionary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I am no longer as zealous today as I was, I can fully empathise with how it is like to hold fast to a set of tenets and beliefs that so completely shape one’s worldview that it would be wholly inconceivable to not expect that challenges to it would not be met with visceral resistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To reiterate: this is not a sentiment that is limited to those that are religious.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is one that is accepted by broad segments of Singaporean society, almost to a point where it is regarded as self-evident among these groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To those within this group, their sense of identity and meaning is as much tied to heteronormativity as those who identify as homosexual tie theirs otherwise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He also explained why decisions on the repeal of 377A and – perhaps more importantly, constitutional amendments – should be determined in the legislature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He was articulating, in this specific instance, the principle of de facto parliamentary sovereignty, a notion that others have observed also applies to Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As Workers’ Party chair Sylvia Lim has articulated, there may be potential legal lacunae that passing such constitutional amendment may entail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am also aware that the amendment will continue to discriminate – albeit to a lesser extent – against those who wish to normalise their same-sex relationship, especially in matters of public policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This question of jurisprudence – where I am very sympathetic to the views of Ms Lim – is important and a concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But even accepting this argument, I believe that there remains a strong justification for ensuring that deliberation of matters of broad societal concern occur within the forum designed for such matters, which is this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will also explain why I believe that a social institution such as marriage may reasonably be included in a foundational document, such as the Constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Keeping in mind that representative democracy will always be imperfect, it is nevertheless the closest system we have that reasonably aggregates the preferences of our people at large.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And in our time, the significant majority of Singaporeans have articulated their preference for a clear reassurance that the institution of marriage be protected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: From my perspective, I do not see why not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Constitutions are live documents, meant – as Thomas Jefferson once said – to serve the present generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They embody the rights of nature, of society and of government; these are essential principles of constitutional design.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Consequently, I believe it is reasonable that our Singaporean Constitution captures the key institutions that our society cherishes, which includes this cornerstone institution of marriage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is in this light that I see a vote in favour of a constitutional amendment that codifies the institution of marriage as a reflection of the conversations I have had with my many diverse constituents on this matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is therefore appropriate that such a definition be clarified only in subsidiary legislation, subject to change by the people of the contemporary time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Almost two centuries ago, the French political philosopher Alexis de Tocqueville documented his observations on the then-nascent state of democracy in the United States.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He shared his admiration for the democratic project as it unfolded in America.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, he pointed out an inherent tension in the power of democratic majority opinion, and in particular, he highlighted what he observed to be the "tyranny of the majority".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tocqueville did not much propose a resolution to this conundrum, beyond suggesting, like his contemporary, English philosopher John Stuart Mill, that appropriate respect for individualism and liberty could offer a way out of this conundrum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, these thinkers believed that it was vital for each society to arrive at their own definition of the limits that public opinion would have over individual lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One could argue that democratic republics, of which Singapore is one, are the practical manifestation of this compromise between individual rights and popular opinion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We stand, today, at a similar precipice, albeit in our own Little Red Dot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The way I see it, the repeal of section 377A is the way that our society respects these individual rights, while enshrining the institution of marriage within the Constitution is how we respect the values of the majority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, the decision we make today is not solely about a political compromise, as so many have suggested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is also about striking the balance between the principles of individualism and majoritarianism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a republic, we are required to do right by our people – we have it right there in our Pledge, a commitment to "justice and equality".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Which is why fundamentally discriminatory laws such as section 377A should no longer be allowed to stand.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I worry about how I can inculcate in them the right values, the right tools to be able to dissect tricky situations and to be able to tell right from wrong, even when the world around you sometimes appears to have gone mad.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Today, my sons are still young, and it will be years yet before they are old enough to understand the topics we are debating and to have their own views on these matters, which touch on the very core of what it means to be humans living together in a society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I hope that when they are old enough, they will be able to understand and appreciate what I say here today, as it is my contribution to what I hope will be a healthy and positive debate for a more tolerant and accepting nation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are topics that are fundamental to who we are as individuals, who we are as a society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And because society is a collection of individuals, this necessarily means that we are people who have different views and ways of looking at things.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It comes as no surprise that we have many different viewpoints and that some amongst us do feel extremely passionately about the issues involved.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a good thing in and as of itself, as it shows that we care deeply about the society we live in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When the repeal of section 377A and the amendments to the Constitution were first announced, my thoughts were initially clear-cut – this relates to my conscience and it seemed straightforward.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, as I listened to friends and residents who shared their thoughts with me on the matter, I realised that there was a wide variety of opinion on the matter, each informed by one's own life experiences, their own social or religious value systems.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would also be impossible to find a position that everyone fully agreed on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But whether they are for or against repeal, one thing was clear to me: that everyone is motivated by the same desire to see Singapore move in the right direction, in the direction of the greater good.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think it is crucial that we do not lose sight of this, even as we may debate over what this greater good is.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is important because having many different cultures, values or viewpoints is not new to Singapore and it will not be the last time we face an issue that risks our society being increasingly polarised.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I am reminded that we can face challenges as a nation and can do so soberly in a way that balances the individual's right to hold their own beliefs and practices, with the need to build a cohesive society founded on principles of understanding and acceptance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also not lost on me that I am speaking today not just as an individual, but as a representative of my constituents who have entrusted this privilege to me and my teammates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is something that we will never take for granted, even as we strive each day to be worthy of that trust.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And as interests and viewpoints are split on section 377A, I believe we need to remind ourselves of the same principles of acceptance and understanding that have helped us build a strong ship that can weather difficult storms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe that we must have empathy and put ourselves in the shoes of those who hold different views from us, and to try our very best to understand where their concerns are coming from.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must approach this difference with respect; it does not do anyone favour to dismiss the other as being hysterical, overblown, or wanting to impose corrupt values on others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It sends a signal that one segment of society is so morally reprehensible that their identity should be considered criminal, even if it is only on paper.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It excuses discriminatory behaviour and contradicts the Pledge we take, as citizens of Singapore "to build a democratic society, based on justice and equality".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some residents and concerned citizens have written to me to express concerns about the repeal of section 377A and the deleterious effect that this will have on the next generation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having three young and curious children myself, I fully appreciate where this is coming from.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And indeed, I often find myself worrying about how to teach them to know right from wrong, and to be able to distinguish between good and bad influences.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, we cannot completely insulate them from the outside world and our children will be exposed to many different ideas and arguments which we believe are wrong.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our role as a parent is to educate, to guide them as we think fit and to have a sense of moral values which they can apply to different situations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, our children are also their own people, and we must accept that they too will eventually grow up to have their own views, make their own choices and to deal with the consequences of their actions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while it is true that a country's laws do provide some moral guardrails for what is acceptable to society as a whole, history has shown us that in some instances, this has not always been the case.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, I like to think that if I lived in a time and society where slavery was legal and accepted, I would still teach my children that the very concept of a human owning another human is abhorrent and unacceptable under any circumstances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having said all of this, I have also heard and understand the concerns of those who feel that the repeal of section 377A will be a slippery slope to further shifts in policy that they feel are simply unacceptable, or that its repeal will cause deep faults and divisions in society that are irreparable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But since as early as 2007, the regard for section 377A as a bad law has been growing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Legal personages, including former Judges of the Court of Appeal and a former Chief Justice, have cast doubt on its constitutionality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Similar arguments have been made in this House before as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If not, today, the law would likely have been struck down in the near term.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But we must also not mix legality with morality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The repeal rejects a legal framework of discrimination, but parents remain able to educate our children and impart the moral lessons that we want within our household, shaped by our own beliefs and faiths.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The concerns relating to the silencing of certain groups are also, I believe, understandable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, Article 15 of our Constitution guarantees the freedom of religion in Singapore, specifying that "every person has the right to profess and practise his religion and to propagate it".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This right has been upheld by the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
