text: And if there should be any proposed amendments to remove or water down the right to religious freedom in Singapore, I will not hesitate to oppose it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, this approach is similar to thorny moral questions that are handled differently between religions or communities today, yet our laws are secular and do not attempt to enshrine the moral compass of each group.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our laws seek instead, to provide the protection for each community from discriminatory treatment from another.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The same principle applies here and the protection of religious freedom will remain a core tenet of our democracy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With this in mind, I record my concern about the proposed constitutional amendment before us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I can understand and appreciate that the majority of Singaporeans feel that marriage is between a man and woman and share the concern about a judiciary running roughshod over the will of the people as expressed through Parliament, I note that the Singapore Courts have always been conscious of the concept of parliamentary sovereignty, giving precedence to the lawmaking function of Parliament and are ever cognisant of not overstepping the line into judicial law-making.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps in taking fright at the "phantom menace" of judicial activism, we may be losing sight of a more fundamental principle – that the judiciary should be the ultimate arbiter of the constitutionality of legislation and has an important role in safeguarding the fundamental liberties protected therein.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This concern goes beyond the present issue and I hope we will not lose sight of the bigger picture.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we were to pass this constitutional amendment today that prevents the Courts from determining the constitutionality of a legislative policy, what would stop a future Parliament from passing discriminatory legislation and then shielding it from judicial oversight?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, a future Parliament may decide to pass or entrench laws that prevent the propagation of one's religion and then immunise that from court challenge on the basis of the constitutional protection for religious expression by introducing a carve-out similar to the present amendment as contained in Articles 156(3) and (4).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would additionally urge empathy when debating and passing the constitutional amendment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I applaud removing the divisive thorn of section 377A from the body politic, I worry too that the constitutional amendment may continue to advance the divisiveness that we precisely want to combat.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For a pluralistic society like Singapore, it is in walking together, in conversation with each other, all the while cognisant and respectful of our differences that we are able to move forward.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Sometimes, legislation is not just the imperfect substitute for society's greater good, it can be a barrier to it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note that I have spoken very much in the abstract so far, on principles and ideas.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, allow me the liberty to close with a personal anecdote about a boy I grew up with in this part of the world.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We moved to different cities in our teens and did not see each other for almost a decade.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One day, in our 20s, our paths were fortuitous enough to cross again thousands of miles from home and I remember sitting up late one night, chatting about nothing in particular.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I made a throwaway, teasing comment about whether he would take girls to a particular spot to impress them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: He suddenly grew quiet and paused for a long while, looking away.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I could see that his mind was racing and he swallowed hard a few times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I thought a long time about whether to tell you but decided to do so because I think you'd be okay with it." It was now my turn to be silenced as he started telling me about how a few months ago, he attended his sister's wedding, where he felt compelled to tell lie upon lie to well-meaning relatives asking when it would be his turn to get married.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: He felt like a total charlatan but overriding this was his greatest fear that he did not want to "bring shame upon his parents".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will never forget the fear and anguish and the pain in his eyes and I regret that this was not the first, nor the last time I saw these emotions as someone "came out" to me about their sexual orientation – all because they feared condemnation and disgust for who they were.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a whirlwind of emotions that I will never fully understand and I would not wish this on anyone.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a timely reminder that for the vast majority of us, the topics we discuss today are but academic to our personal situation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will be a start towards better understanding each other and how we can begin to heal any rifts that may have arisen.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Families and spouses who love and value each other and their children will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is what makes us as a nation, as one nation, and I hope we never lose sight of this, nor stop fighting to keep this as our shared future.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Let the lawyers discuss the legal aspects of the implications of such a change.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I look to them to lead the future discussions of what their faith finds permissible.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I speak to you now, as a doctor and as a mother of boys.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I ask about these only to advise on any impact on their medical care.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As a mother of boys, I want for them a world where they can grow safely in.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It was a time to find oneself – your identity and who you are – and I dare say that there are some adults who are still searching or may never find the answer their whole lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We form our identity through multiple factors – our character at birth, be it extro- or introverted, then shaped by family, school and peers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Teenagers explore their sexuality and their gender identity.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In my time, tomboyish girls and effeminate boys were given mocking and even derogatory names.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For those of us who were lucky to never be confused as to whether you liked a boy or girl, it was already not easy.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We still worried and fussed over whether your crush liked you back, collected red saga seeds, folded hearts from bus tickets and listened to heartbreak songs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For those who felt an attraction to someone of the same gender, I can only imagine the fear and anxiety – fear that there’s something wrong with you, that your parents will disown you, that your friends will call you a freak.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: How many have suppressed their feelings and stayed single or went on to have a heterosexual relationship just to fit in?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I look to an environment where each person can grow and explore safely.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As I have said in most of my other speeches, education is key – education by the family, by formal schooling and by the various faiths.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: For those people facing conflicts and stress, there must be safe havens for them to seek fair and balanced counselling without undue influence.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the healthcare profession needs to step up and lead this with paediatricians, psychiatrists, psychologists who are trained and experienced – professional providers who do not impose their personal views.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This will be a guide for parents to use in our own conversations at home with our growing children.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: To fellow parents, if you, like me, grew up without any knowledge of LGBT terms, let us educate ourselves.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Only then we are equipped to guide our children as they grow and explore.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This is when we can meaningfully share our personal beliefs, our religious convictions and allow the child to find his or her own way, with love and support.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I urge everyone to stay calm and be kind.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is the fact that the debate that we are having yesterday and today in this House is a milestone – a huge milestone – for our evolving democracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It reflects the political leadership of a government and a parliamentary majority who have resolved to rise to our duty, not abdicate from our responsibilities and find the political courage and gumption to confront the difficult issues head on and do what is right even if there is no political favour to be gained and, indeed, every chance of a political cost to bear.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Once the prospects of the Courts striking down section 377A in a future challenge became clear, this Government of the day did not choose to "unsee" what it had seen.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government did not look the other way.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Instead, we sprang into action, put it squarely on the agenda as our duty required us to and set out to find a way forward for all Singaporeans, difficult as it may be.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I say – especially to the youths who desire a more robust democracy in Singapore – I say let us celebrate this moment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I listened to my colleagues yesterday – Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Alex Yam, Minister Vivian Balakrishnan, Ms Jessica Tan, for example – who hold very strong beliefs on the family unit and want the institution of marriage to be protected and strengthened.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, eventually, by the end of their speeches, they have also expressed their strong support for repeal in this debate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, there was Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng, for example, who has been advocating strongly for repeal, indeed, since 2007.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, in this debate, eventually, by the end of his speech, he has also expressed strong support for protecting the institution of marriage.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, very different starting points – repeal on the one hand, protecting the institution of marriage on the other – and a broad tent of views, a broad tent of starting points, even amongst PAP Members of Parliament representing various parts of our society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, we have found mutual accommodation and we have found convergence in support of both Bills.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we have closed ranks and come together to try and bring all Singaporeans along on the way forward, together, in the national interest, our personal views notwithstanding, as my colleague Mr Murali Pillai has so eloquently put it.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is how a responsible governing party works.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I am glad that Opposition Members and Nominated Members have all joined us in seizing this moment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We owe it to Singaporeans to do right by our democracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We discuss the difficult issues directly, and above all, we stand for unity and compassion as one people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I once asked two friends – husband and wife, in their 30s, young parents to two kids and we were talking about their expectations of their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I asked them, what if their son turns out to be gay, and wishes to bring his partner home to meet them, what would they think?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Without missing a beat, they replied to me, they cannot even begin to contemplate and imagine such a scenario.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I do not think they belong to a minority of young parents today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, if their son does turn out to be gay, I would make a guess that they will: one, love him all the same; and two, they will certainly not want their son, and his acts of intimacy with his partner, consensual, in private, to be labelled as criminal.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Why should their son be labelled a criminal?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This, I think, is the crux of the section 377A issue.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Regardless of our views on homosexuality, I think we can generally agree that we know a gay friend or even family member, and we love and respect him like we do any other friend or family member, and we have very little reason, really, to see him as a criminal.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe this is the prevailing morality of our society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And because our laws ought to reflect the morality of our society, repealing section 377A and decriminalising gay sex is really the right thing for us to do.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Going back to the story of my two friends, the young parents.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yes, if their son does turn out to be gay, they will certainly not want their son's private activities to be criminal, but I think it will be much less certain if they will accept the notion of a son-in-law, or of a grandchild, or grandchildren, within the context of such a marriage between their son and his gay partner.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I think they would also completely understand if their friends were to turn to them and say: look, we really will not agree to allowing your son to marry here in Singapore, because it runs against our beliefs and it runs against what we would like our children and grandchildren to believe about marriage, or at least, what we would like our children and grandchildren to see and hear for themselves before forming their own conclusions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On marriage, I think, this is the prevailing morality of our society, and our laws and policies should also protect this, even as we repeal the law on gay sex.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, it seems, from a survey conducted by TODAY just two months ago, that younger Singaporeans generally think this way too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Some have commented that where we are today is effectively one step forward and two steps back for the gay community.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we are coming together as a society and coming to terms with the reality that a majority of us are not yet ready to give up our fundamental beliefs including on marriage and so, let us find a balance, let us find mutual accommodation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a mark of our maturing society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Some, on the other hand, have characterised the repeal as a capitulation by the Government – and society at large – to the relentless campaigns and militant advocacy of some gay rights activists.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe, instead, that this change is about all of us, our society as a whole, maturing, progressing organically.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Change takes time – and this has taken quite some time – but this change has not been precipitated by the narrow words or actions or deeds of a few.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think this change represents part of our broader progress towards becoming a more inclusive society, in various other dimensions like wage level, age, disabilities, mental health and yes, we have become more inclusive on the dimension of sexual orientation, too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, sir, try to imagine as a parent that one day your son tells you, “Mom and Dad, I am gay.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I want to bring him to see you”.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It may be a difficult problem and I do not wish any parent to go through this test.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But, if this is the reality, then I guess that our first response should be that our love for our children remains the same.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In addition, we would not wish the son to be considered a criminal because of his sexual orientation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This second point is the crux of section 377A of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Regardless our attitude towards homosexuality, we would have homosexual friends or even family members in life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Like anyone else, they deserve to be loved and respected.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is what we should do as an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Of course, I fully understand that many Singaporeans are worried about the consequences of repealing section 377A.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: What will LGBT and gay rights group advocate next?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yesterday, Minister of State Sun Xueling pointed out that the Government has put in a lot of efforts to address the issue of section 377A and the concerns of various groups in society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Although the section 377A issue is difficult, we did not abdicate from our responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There is an ancient saying that “the policies of the country must benefit the people, and the key to political education is for the policies to be implemented smoothly”.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has faced the issue squarely and found a compromise.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Through these two Bills, the Government has achieved this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In English): So, where else do we go from here?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My hope is that all sides will continue engaging with each other and do so with ever greater depths of mutual respect, understanding and empathy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For one, gays and lesbians are not a monolith.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Not all homosexuals are judicial activists; and judicial activists do not speak for all homosexuals.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, not all social conservatives are Christian or Muslim.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, many conservatives are either of other religions, or not religious at all.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Their socially conservative views, while deep-seated, are not religious in nature.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I also hope that our engagements going forward will be in the real world, offline.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Not in social media where certain narratives get amplified much more than others.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Social media creates echo chambers and not equally.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Some chambers may be small, but their echoes are especially loud and reverberate well beyond the realms of the chambers themselves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We have Singaporeans who are concerned about how and what social media is buffeting us with, and I think, rightly so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need safe spaces, in the real world, where all views can come forth and be heard equally, where we can get a good sense of the real balance of views amongst all of us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in these safe spaces, no one should have to labour under the fear of name-calling or being cancelled, especially by bad actors under the guise of anonymity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The separation of powers is a deeply rooted principle in our parliamentary tradition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parliament makes the laws, the Executive administers the laws and the Judiciary interprets and applies the laws when disputes are brought before the Courts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this House, regardless of personal beliefs, we are duty-bound to represent the different voices of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a responsibility that I do not take lightly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others have shared that removing criminality from homosexuality is long overdue, given that the law was introduced back in 1938.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some have also questioned if there is actually a real possibility of 377A being struck out by the Courts, while others have also worried about the wider ripples of this repeal, whether this has potential to change the way that marriage is defined in Singapore or how sexuality education will be taught to their children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have also heard stories of gay youths facing discrimination in their friend groups or struggling to find acceptance among peers who do not have the capacity or vocabulary to understand them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And also of youths who hold more conservative beliefs who have been called out in schools.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, these disagreements occur online, hidden under the cloak of anonymity which emboldens individuals to speak carelessly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But loud does not always mean right and some may feel pressured into adopting a view.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When issues are contentious, tribes are built and positions are entrenched and conversations quickly start from an adversarial place.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This environment, if left unchecked, do not allow for people to build the capacity to discuss and debate with respect and reconcile even internal incongruence between faith, heart and mind before coming to their own considered position.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it may be just one section of law – and about consensual acts in private, no less – section 377A has come to represent much more for many over the years, concerning fundamental values of individuals in a visceral way.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As elected representatives, we value every perspective shared with us.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, this matter which has been debated in both public and private spaces for many years, even before the 2022 National Day Rally, belongs here in this House after years of consultation and engagement in both public and private spaces – not in the Courts, where judges must make decisions based on the information and facts presented before them, resulting in a binary decision.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Laws and policies must be guided by a careful balancing of the scales, not having the scales tipped to one side or the other through judicial activism or driven by individuals with the resources to litigate.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will not belabour this point as it has been raised by hon colleagues such as Mr Murali Pillai yesterday.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This process of a judiciary intervening actively in social issues may also signal an unwillingness of elected politicians to deal with such issues ourselves and leave such decisions to the Courts so that we do not have to assume responsibility for them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In some countries, judicial activism has deepened polarisation in societies – for example, over immigration matters in Australia and abortion rights in the US.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This also results in judicial appointments in themselves becoming politicised affairs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should not foster this culture in Singapore and so I agree with the hon Minister for Social and Family Development on the approach of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appreciate that we are dealing with this now.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The decision made in 2007 to accept the legal untidiness and ambiguity of keeping the law on the books was the compromise struck by society at the time.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Former Attorneys-General Walter Woon and VK Rajah also separately said it was not desirable for the Government and Parliament to direct the Attorney-General not to prosecute offences under section 377A.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Following these comments, Attorney-General Lucien Wong clarified that the Public Prosecutor retains independence in deciding whether to pursue a case under section 377A.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He shared that "while the Public Prosecutor is entitled to consider public policies in exercising his discretion, these do not fetter the exercise of prosecutorial discretion." In all the feedback I have received, many of our people, regardless of race, language or religion, agree that acts of intimacy between two consenting men do not make them criminals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have also generally not seen public interest or organised groups for the active enforcement of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the hon Minister for Social and Family Development has elaborated on why such an approach is not the right one for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Singapore I grew up in is different from the one of my parents and I can also appreciate that the Singapore which my children one day may grow up in could be unrecognisable from my lived experiences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To do this, while we may choose to educate and guide our families based on our own personal values, we ought to avoid passing down entrenched positions to future generations, especially in our secular shared space.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Ever since Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong made an announcement about section 377A during National Day Rally 2022, many have been discussing this issue and expressed their support as well as their opposition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our Malay/Muslim community is not a monolithic community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each generation has different views, backgrounds, and experiences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my discussions with organisations and different individuals, I have heard different perspectives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also had the opportunity to meet leaders, staff, and volunteers from our various Malay/Muslim organisations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some shared their concerns about their ability to manage and support conversations between family members about Section 377A.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Others shared their personal struggles to reconcile their faith, mindset and society so that they could impart values to their children that are aligned with their faith and the way they were brought up because it is something that they cherish.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The tolerance and diversity that we have in Singapore is something that we have nurtured and built over the years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It exists today because the generations before us as well as the current generation agree that it is important for us to seek a compromise in our public spaces where advocacy does not necessarily mean that we need to tear down each other.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): On that note, I would like to finish off my speech to ask not just the Members of this House but Singaporeans at large – where do we go from here, with not just dealing with this repeal but other issues that may divide us?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first sees us entrenched in our positions, unwilling to engage in constructive dialogue with others who may not see the world the way we do.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second sees us engaging in respectful conversation while remaining steadfast to our own values.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Path 1 leads to division and we have seen the damage this has done in fractured societies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Path 2 leads to understanding and in turn, peace and a more lasting prosperity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a path rarely paved and harder fought and uncharted territory for many of us.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In moments of crisis, we run the risk of deviating back to Path 1.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the context of section 377A, we move beyond talking about criminality in the same sentence as homosexuality and see people as individuals for who they are.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is easy to say that we must move beyond tolerance and towards understanding but harder to accept that we can no longer steer clear from speaking on contentious issues.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I ask that we endeavour to not invalidate the lived experiences of others and that we do not fall prey to living in echo chambers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is not in a special bubble which makes us immune to these risks and I do believe that our leaders understand that.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such sessions are an important part of setting up a two-way mode of engagement between the Government and people, where engaging in productive dialogue, varying points of view, becomes the new normal.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In closing, there are many ways to create change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, it requires us raising our voices; most times, it requires persistence and tough conversations; and always, it involves time, a big heart and the willingness to hear each other out.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, change should not be born out of or led by fear as fear will not protect us.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I echo my hon colleague Joan Pereira's sentiments – that we should come from a place of love – and, I will add, also of courage.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Knowing that there are diverse groups who feel strongly about this, I hope that we can continue to be brave, to have tough conversations with mutual respect for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Since then, this matter has been deeply debated by members of the public as well as Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Based on my interactions with my friends, colleagues, union leaders and members, I have gathered that there are sentiments of worry and unhappiness amongst Singaporeans on this topic, despite the many engagement sessions carried out earlier involving various groups of leaders and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We have heard today and yesterday from more than 20 Members of Parliament and Nominated Members of Parliament on this thorny and sensitive subject matter.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened by the passion and conviction of the various speeches by the Members of this house and their commitment to safeguard the natural institution of marriage and family structure, as reiterated by many.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, I am also comforted, knowing that we are according the necessary space to those who had previously felt oppressed by the existence of section 377A in our books.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, many in our society may not have known that prior to this announcement, there have been constitutional challenges filed in Court against section 377A on the basis that it violates the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: They, too, shared their concerns with me either in person, over calls, messages or even emails.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I have received emails from multiple individuals and groups calling for the retention of section 377A.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This view is commonly held by more conservative and/or religious groups as they are concerned with what the repeal of section 377A represents – that there would be an erosion of family values and the traditional definition that marriage is between a man and woman could be challenged.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There is also another view that the Government should not intervene nor police private and sexual behaviours between consenting adults.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, it should be removed from our books, especially if the Government would not actively enforce it.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With all being said, I hope the Government can enlighten laypersons like myself on the relevant processes for legislative and policy reforms.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Under what circumstances would the Court be empowered to strike down the laws passed by Parliament?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What can be done by Parliament to avoid the striking down of the laws?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Should the matter be canvassed before Parliament for Parliament to consider repealing the same first?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: What is the difference between these two processes?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Can an infographic illustrate these processes to make it easier for people out there to understand?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, I am glad that this issue is canvassed before us presently, as such a law which has far reaching implications on Singapore’s family structure and societal norms should be decided by Parliament, which has the people’s mandate, and not the Courts, which only interpret and apply the laws passed by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We hope that the existing measures, such as public housing policies and financial benefits for married couples, as well as education and media policies continue to promote and safeguard the institution of marriage.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, our discussions on the repeal of Section 377 and amendments to the National Constitution have gained the attention of our citizens, regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many have expressed their concerns about the impact on our way of life if Section 377 is repealed.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly, not many people have given equal attention to the Constitutional Amendment through the addition of Article 156 which clarifies and strengthens the definition of marriage and family.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many are asking whether the Government agrees with the actions of such groups to the point that it acknowledges and gives in to their demands.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are all aware of the emergence of such groups and it is a grave concern for our society, present and future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The repeal can be seen as a minor success for this group.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Is it possible that in the future they will continue to make more demands based on equal rights for all in society?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Government also support and allow the same thing, just as it does now?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There is nothing wrong with expressing concerns, but we must accept that the world belongs to all of creation including humans, fauna, mountains, flora and countless others.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This group of people are also human beings just like us.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We should rightfully share the vastness of this world with all of God's creations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not alienate them, just because of their sexual preferences.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us spread kindness to all humankind and recognise the challenges that they face.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: They never asked to be that way, but we who claim to be of sound mind and body should take up the role of advising and sharing with them the natural state of life.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us cultivate respect, instead of being judgmental, based on our own different opinions, positions, and beliefs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We must avoid spreading slanders that can divide our society.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The harmonious cohesion that we built over the years that is founded on mutual respect must be maintained and strengthened.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):   Over the past few months, the Government has consulted extensively with various groups on this important issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have met Malay/Muslim religious leaders, Malay/Muslim organisations, interfaith groups, youth groups, and healthcare professionals during those engagement sessions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The majority in our society, including the Malay/Muslim community, value and wish to uphold the traditional view of family, where marriage is between a man and a woman, with children raised in such a family setting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our position on marriage and family is clear, and this has consistently been reflected in our policies and legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Many of Singapore’s policies are based on that definition, including adoption, housing, education, and media.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This would ensure that any changes to the definition of marriage can only be debated and decided through Parliament, and not through the Courts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: If we look at the various challenges mounted against Section 377A over the years, we can expect similar challenges to the definition of marriage and laws and policies based on this definition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Such decisions should not be left to the Courts to decide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: During Prime Minister’s National Day Rally speech, he made it clear that judges have neither the expertise nor the mandate to address political questions, nor rule on social norms and values.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Minister Masagos had also earlier in his speech highlighted US and India as examples of why Court-led decisions could lead to undesirable, win-lose outcomes for society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: If we do not take action to protect the institution of marriage, and allow this to be left to the Courts, we risk damaging the bedrock of society which is the structure of family.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Where important social issues are concerned, Parliament is more suited to deal with them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Parliament can consult different groups, take in their feedback, and assess the best way forward while balancing wider societal considerations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In essence, the making of pro-family laws should be decided by Parliament; not by the Courts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have shared a gist of the above in my various engagements with the Malay/Muslim community and most of them understood and welcomed this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As Minister Shanmugam explained in his speech, we are also moving to repeal Section 377A.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: During my engagements, some, including those in the Malay/Muslim community, shared they were concerned that the repeal would signal a sea of change in other laws and policies, and result in a sudden shift of the tone of our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Some also shared their fears – that the repeal of Section 377A would open the floodgates for same-sex marriage and same-sex family formation, normalising LGBT discourse in our society, and lead to knock-on effects pertaining to sex education in schools, normalising the portrayal of LGBT relationships in the media, and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Similarly, policies relying on the current definition of marriage will remain unchanged.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This has also been echoed by the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong that this Government has no intention of changing the definition of marriage, nor the policies that rely on this definition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: You may ask, “why repeal Section 377A now?” Allow me to briefly explain why the Government has decided to repeal Section 377A and protect the definition of marriage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, repealing Section 377A is the right and principled thing to do.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Fundamentally, there are no law-and-order concerns arising from consensual, adult homosexual conduct in private.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Society has changed since Parliament last debated Section 377A in 2007.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In 2007, our society was not yet ready, but our engagements over the past few months have shown that most Singaporeans today accept that sex between men should not be a crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Even if we may be personally opposed to homosexual conduct, we should recognise that Section 377A as a law has been a marker of stigmatisation to those in the gay community, and experienced as a stark reminder of their rejection by the rest of society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Removing this source of psychological and physical distress from their lives is the right thing to do, so we can move forward as a society where our gay family, friends, and colleagues are treated with the same degree of respect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Second, as Minister Shanmugam has explained earlier, there is a significant risk of Section 377A being struck down by the Courts, on the grounds that it breaches the equal protection clause of the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Third, if Section 377A were to be struck down by the Courts, our definition of marriage and related laws and policies would be subjected to similar legal challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Earlier I mentioned some of the key concerns raised by the Malay/Muslim community with regards to the repeal of Section 377A and the possible implications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I also made clear that there will be no change to the various laws and policies related to marriage as it is not the Government's intention to cause a destabilising shift in our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, I understand that the Malay/Muslim community wishes to protect longstanding religious and family values.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Regarding this, I would like to refer to the Mufti's recent religious guidance concerning LGBT matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I agree this should continue to be protected and promoted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: At the same time, Mufti also acknowledged that we live in a diverse society where we ought to respect differences in worldviews and that we should continue to extend compassion to Muslims who identify as LGBT.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As Muslims, we must exercise kindness and empathy to our fellow Muslims who might have differences in opinions and views from us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Second, some are concerned that the push for LGBT rights would infringe on religious freedom.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The community should also take reference from Mufti's guidance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: More importantly, I would like to emphasise that religious freedom must be balanced with mutual accommodation, respect and compassion in our plural society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Where sensitive issues are concerned, people are free to disagree with one another, and we should have the space to air views and concerns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: But even so, as we navigate these differences in worldviews, we must remember to abide by principles of mutual, understanding, respect and accommodation in these interactions so that we are able to have constructive conversations on how we can move our society forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In an earlier interview, Mufti commented that the repeal of Section 377A was a complex social issue and a tough balancing act for everyone, including the Government and religious groups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As a community, we must continue to be guided by Islamic values and teachings in all that we say and do, even as laws change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have to be careful not to polarize debate on this issue and risk straining the communal ties that we have built up painstakingly over the years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As Muslim leaders, we should not focus on our own personal views and appeal to our own community only.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Instead, we should fully consider what is best for our community by considering and balancing the views of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This will ensure that we adopt a holistic view and approach to enable us to move forward together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As we move forward, I would like to call on everyone to keep calm and exercise moderation as we work out a consensus for the betterment of Singapore, as one united society, as we have always done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I would also like to thank our community leaders and colleagues for sharing their views and giving their support to the Government in this matter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We heard their views and opinions, and we will continue to work closely with them in this matter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and National Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am touched with their readiness to continue strengthening our nation-building ecosystem despite facing complex issues from time to time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The heated civic discourse and vigorous advocacy speaks to strongly held beliefs that many hold on this issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This has been an opportunity for Singaporeans to learn to disagree in a spirited but civil way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that such open debate is a sign of a healthy and functioning democracy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, in doing so we cannot lose sight of our shared humanity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can do no better than quote MUIS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In response to the repeal of section 377A, it said that Muslim law "places importance on human dignity, respect and peaceful relations".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It further said, "These values are crucial as we navigate complex socio-religious issues today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Muslims, we should treat everyone with full dignity and respect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Everyone, regardless of their sexual orientations, must feel safe in our society and institutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Muslims should uphold the best of character, charity and compassion, in dealing with others, even with whom we disagree".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe these statements apply not just to those of the Muslim faith but to all of us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we continue to engage on discrimination against the gay community and discrimination of any form, I hope we continue to treat each other with dignity, respect and kindness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, we cannot shy away from having conversations with people that we do not identify with.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to continue the dialogue on issues affecting the gay community with the intent of achieving progress for everyone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the gay community, the repeal of section 377A is the correct thing to do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is the correct thing to do not only because of the likelihood of success of any Court challenges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is the correct thing to do because gay Singaporeans deserve, like any other member of society, not to be criminalised for their private behaviour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The repeal of section 377A is a positive step towards making Singapore a more equal and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should recognise and thank the collective efforts of activists and organisations over the years to raise awareness about the challenges that the gay community faces and foster acceptance of gay individuals within our society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to continue to have conversations about these issues as our nation progresses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the treatment of prior convictions under section 377A.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In his National Day Rally speech, when he announced the intended repeal of section 377A, Prime Minister Lee said he believed that the repeal is the right thing to do and that it would provide relief to gay Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Shanmugam has also said that it would be wrong to continue criminalising the sexuality of gay Singaporeans and what they do in private.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nobody, he said, deserves to be stigmatised because of their sexual orientation, so repealing section 377A and removing their pain is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the continued stigmatisation of gay Singaporeans is wrong, then the continued stigmatisation of gay Singaporeans because of their record of conviction under section 377A must also be wrong.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An exception is if the person is disqualified from having their criminal record being spent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, this may mean that individuals with existing records of conviction under section 377A because the conviction was within a five-year period or because the individual is disqualified from having the record becoming spent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These individuals may, due to their records, remain stigmatised, even as we repeal section 377A.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about support provided to students of diverse genders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The repeal of section 377A sends a strong message against the discrimination of gay Singaporeans on the basis, again, of their private behaviour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister Shanmugam shared, this legislative step is a significant step in removing stigma on a legislative level and will also go some way in removing hurt.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, discrimination and stigma do not just exist in abstract policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many individuals of diverse genders face discrimination, stigma and hurt in their day-to-day interactions in the community and even with their closest loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These challenges can be especially daunting for young students who are just starting to build their identity and navigate their teenage years which can already be a stressful experience for anyone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many surveys, both local and international, show that many individuals of diverse genders experienced symptoms of generalised anxiety disorder.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many also experienced major depressive disorder and engage in self harm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our teachers in schools are a first line of defence in identifying students who may be struggling from such stressors and challenges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are also well placed to facilitate appropriate intervention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share what support has been or will be extended to such students?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, what role will teachers and schools play in identifying students of diverse genders who may be struggling and extending such support to them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is on the new Article 156(1) in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It enables the legislature and the Government to define, regulate, protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote the institution of marriage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the explanatory statement, examples of such activities included housing preferences and financial benefits for married persons, and education and media policies that promote and safeguard the institution of marriage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we encourage marriage, I hope we will not discriminate against single parents, whether they are unmarried, divorced or widowed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that Minister Masagos provided some assurances on this during his opening speech that single parents will not be left behind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is a lot more we can do.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am mindful that the subject concerns sensitive matters of religious beliefs, sexuality and identity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I stand to speak what I believe and beg the indulgence of everyone who may not necessarily hold the same view.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We all have friends and family who may hold the liberal view or conservative view when it comes to matters concerning sexuality and morality.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we all have friends and family who are LGBTQ+ persons.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The long public debate of the status of section 377A of the Penal Code has weighed heavily on all sides and has divided our society and even families.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To see the cup half full, I would say that during this time, especially since 2018, parties holding differing views have learnt more about one another's perspectives and engaged in dialogues with the Government, and directly or indirectly with one another.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that after today's debate and after this House has decided, we will move forward together as one Singapore, upholding our pledge to be one united people, respecting one another's dignity as human persons and upholding the Singapore family built on marriage between a man and a woman, and the children they will birth and raise, to be the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I declare I am a Catholic and have been brought up knowing that my Creator is a loving God and he loves everyone.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The catechism of the Catholic Church teaches Catholics that the men and women who have deep-seated homosexual tendencies must be accepted with respect, compassion and sensitivity, even as they are called to chastity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Pope Francis, in his encyclical, Amoris Laetitia – The Joy of Love, wrote, and I quote, "We would like before all else to reaffirm that every person, regardless of sexual orientation, ought to be respected in his or her dignity and treated with consideration, while 'every sign of unjust discrimination' is to be carefully avoided, particularly any form of aggression and violence." The Catholic Church's position is clear – homosexual acts are sinful, but homosexual orientation is not.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Archbishop of Singapore, His Eminence, Cardinal William Goh, in a statement in August 2022 after the Prime Minister's National Day Rally speech on this matter of repealing section 377A, has come out to say that the Church is against the criminalisation of LGBTQ+ people and, so, supporting the repeal of section 377A is not the issue.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, the issue is with regard to the rights as a Catholic Church, to teach and practise our beliefs and regard the family and marriage as defined between a man and a woman, according to natural law.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As we have all heard over these two days in Parliament, his concerns on this issue matter to more segments than just the Catholic Church.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Several hon Members of Parliament have referred to the Youth Survey conducted in September by the news media, Today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Here is an excerpt from the news report: "The demographically representative survey, which polled 1,000 respondents aged between 18 and 35, was carried out between 5 and 16 September.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: First, that Singaporeans are sympathetic towards decriminalising gay sex; two, Singaporeans are divided on the acceptance of same-sex relations; and three, the majority of Singaporeans, both young and old, believe that it is important to uphold and safeguard the definition of marriage as that between a man and a woman.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: After much prayer, research and listening to many, including my own daughters, repealing section 377A is the right thing to do, and doing so will send a statement to the LGBTQ+ community that they are safe being who they are, even if their behaviour may not be accepted by the mainstream community in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As many in the House have said, the removal of anti-gay sex laws in some countries saw the issue of same-sex marriage falling under the spotlight and there are large segments in Singapore who care deeply about marriage as defined currently between a man and a woman, as well as family norms, such as how children are brought up and what is taught in school.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Most people have come to accept that gay sex is a matter of private individual choice.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Same-sex marriage, however, is effectively changing a social institution, contrary to what most Singaporeans believe and are ready to accept.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For me, marriage is a sacred bond between a man and a woman, committing fidelity to each other, so long as they both shall live, and bringing forth children to form a family and fulfil the natural order of the transmission of life.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, this Parliament has declared 2022 as the Year of Singapore Families.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore families want to be confident that, in Singapore, we will be able to freely guide our children on what we believe to be right and wrong.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, for us Catholics, the Catholic Church needs to be confident that their rights to preach and to teach in the parishes and Catholic schools, according to Catholic beliefs, will be protected.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What are those circumstances and how will the Government deal with such circumstances?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Cardinal William Goh has spoken of his concerns that we may be drawn into a situation as in the West, where we cannot even say that a same-sex relationship is wrong.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the Catholic Church, this would not be acceptable as the Church must have freedom to continue to teach in the Catholic schools and from the pulpit what we believe, and practise what we teach.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Bullying and cancel culture must not take root in our educational institutions and our society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, we should not allow a culture where people of religion are ostracised, attacked for espousing their views or their disagreements with LGBTQ+ viewpoints and vice versa.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has worked hard to create inter-religious harmony in our society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Government protect and safeguard this precious strength and asset of our country?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We will work together to prevent cancel culture to take root in our educational institutions, our workplaces and our society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And we will not disregard the importance and essential need to have the holistic family as the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And finally, we will continue to dialogue, to listen with compassion and kindness, to one another.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For too long, the law has remained in our statutes, explicitly stating that sex between adult men is a crime, even if it is consensual and done in private.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Despite the Government having said multiple times in the past that it will not enforce the colonial era law, and with the Court of Appeal ruling earlier this year that section 377A was unenforceable in its entirety, its existence has very real repercussions that affect many of our fellow Singaporeans, their families and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The topic of this debate is a complex and multi-faceted one, with individuals, including Members of Parliament, holding deep personal convictions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, beyond the Bills and clauses themselves, we must also be cognisant that the issues we are debating have far-reaching effects into the personal lives of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is on this note that I wish to touch on some aspects of the lived experience of our LGBTQ+ community in Singapore, which may be less apparent to those of us who are not from within the community.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am a young father, with a loving and happy family.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Section 377A never really bothered me in any way that I live my life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But over the years, I have gotten to know several members of the LGBTQ+ community, some of whom have become my close friends.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The daily struggles they face regarding their sexual orientation and gender identity are very real.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We all live in a largely heteronormative world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For my LGBTQ+ friends, that means they constantly face subtle judgement, discrimination, apathy and hatred, even towards them at home, at school, in the military and at work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Seemingly nondescript questions of "bring your girlfriend to drink next time" or "where is your husband?" or "do you plan to have kids" can come up suddenly at family gatherings or happy hour drinks at work and make them squirm.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Think about those awkward Chinese New Year conversations that you have with distant relatives at various stages of your life, be it when you are single, married but without children, or even married with one child, and replicate it throughout the rest of the year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These questions become even more damaging, especially when they are unsure of how others will react to their true sexual orientation or gender identity, and potentially affect their opportunities at work and in society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, some choose to hide their true selves and avoid talking about who they are dating or their hopes and dreams to lead a stable life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some choose to be public about it but fear the risk of being punished for their choices by not being considered for promotion at work or being bullied at school.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In some form or another, individuals who identify as LGBTQ+ have to cope with additional mental and emotional stress and, in some cases, physical abuse, just for being someone they were born as.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some suffer from internalised homophobia, where they loathe themselves over a sexual orientation or gender identity that they had no choice over.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Schools and companies may think twice about setting up official LGBTQ+ groups, or at least show overt support in counselling and supporting these individuals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us not forget the unfortunate incident from earlier this year, where a school counsellor himself presented content discriminating against the LGBTQ+ community, before being suspended from all duties pending investigations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The fact that there remains a legal route for prosecuting LGBTQ+ persons has a specific state-sanctioned chilling effect on the community.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Retaining 377A also makes Singapore look anachronistic, especially in light of our Asian financial hub status.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hong Kong's Legislative Council passed legislation decriminalising homosexual acts in 1991.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Japan briefly made homosexuality illegal and then repealed the law during the Meiji era.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Homosexual acts were never a legal issue in Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: India, which also shares similar colonial roots as Singapore, struck the law down in 2018.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The LGBTQ+ community's joy of seeing section 377A repealed would have been even greater if not for the fact that the move merely puts Singapore more in line with other cosmopolitan, open and inclusive societies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition, retaining a law that is not actively enforced or cannot be enforced sends a confusing signal on how one should comprehend Singapore's legal system.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some will know that my colleague and fellow Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Assoc Prof Jamus Lim attended a Pink Dot rally this past June in his personal capacity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As shared in a media release for Pink Dot 14, "We are living in an increasingly divided world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am glad to see that society is, indeed, ready to move on and repeal section 377A.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But repealing section 377A does not mean discrimination towards the LGBTQ+ community disappears overnight.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Discrimination against such individuals still exists in Hong Kong, China, Japan, India and many other jurisdictions where gay sex is not illegal per se.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For the geographies that I mentioned earlier that have repealed discriminatory same-sex laws, that discrimination still exists is a reminder to us that social acceptance is crucial to any landmark legal or constitutional changes, to maintain harmony and stability in society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: MOE said that the education curriculum will still be focused on what the majority of society supports, which is family, between a man and a woman.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But at the same time, we need to be conscious of LGBTQ+ individuals being invisible in our curriculums.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It will take time for society to come together and, as shared by Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh, "create conditions for all Singaporeans to succeed and certainly not to feel marginalised", "where we are tolerant of Singaporeans who are different in as far as the law allows." But it is all the more important for us to understand one another's viewpoints, stay civil and respectful as we engage all members of society as Singapore becomes more inclusive and open.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I had the privilege of hearing from one of our LGBTQ+ advocates recently and she is a household name who needs no introduction, Ms Theresa Goh.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: She shared her incredible journey as a child born with spina bifida, to becoming our first female swimmer at the 2004 Athens Paralympic Games, winning Gold at the 2006 IPC World Swimming Championships and Bronze at the 2016 Paralympic Games.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More recently, she has also been elected as one of 10 members of the Singapore National Olympic Council Athletes' Commission.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we know her for her extraordinary achievements, what is less well known were the struggles she and her family had to go through as a disabled person and a queer woman here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What was particularly heart-wrenching to me was hearing her speak so casually about the difficulties her parents had in searching for a kindergarten for her back in the 1990s, as they faced repeated rejections the moment the kindergartens found out that she had a disability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: She shared that there was even one day when she was not feeling well and threw up after lunch, yet her teacher did not help to clean her up.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But she felt that had she been any other normal child, her teachers would have cleaned her up before her parents came to pick her.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is upsetting to hear of such experiences, but I also take comfort in that such behaviour would be completely unacceptable and unthinkable in today's circumstances and we, as a society, have moved to become more accepting of the disabled since the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, however, LGBTQ+ inclusivity remains a frowned-upon topic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As late as 2017, when Theresa shared about how she decided to "come out" in an interview with The Straits Times, she was particularly afraid of how other people would see her and how they would react.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At home, she was worried that her parents, in particular, would take this news badly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, they reassured her that all they want is for her to find somebody who would take care of her, whether that person is a boy or a girl.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While Theresa's story has a happy ending, another close friend of mine is still facing challenges in broaching this topic with his parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As an only son, he has been extremely filial to his parents and shares a very special bond with them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A number of years ago, he felt that he no longer wanted to hide his sexuality from his parents and wanted to be completely honest with them as he has been with every other aspect of his life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
