text: This was not taken very well unfortunately, with his mother feeling distraught that there was something wrong with her son and even prays at the temple regularly with the hope that, one day, he will be "normal" again.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I pray that, one day, his parents will accept him fully for who he is.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many financial institutions encourage their employees to bring their true selves to work, because they believe that only then can they truly be engaged in what they do and fully develop their passions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many banks see being open about being who you are can make for a more productive workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They have clear DEI – or diversity, equity and inclusion – talent policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Incorporating DEI into business operations has proven to benefit companies' performance because it encourages a wider range of views and opinions among staff.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All these have clear, measurable impact and should equally apply to our country and economy, too, where we place a very strong emphasis on developing everyone's potential.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Only then can Singapore be truly a global, cosmopolitan, harmonious home that we can all be proud of.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have a male friend who married his partner of seven years just before the pandemic in New York.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The two men are in a loving relationship but there is just one snag – my friend is an only son.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When he is old and bedridden, he wants to know that he can trust someone to make difficult medical and legal decisions for him.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All they hoped for is that there is at least a jurisdiction out there that can give them societal and legal guarantees that straight couples enjoy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since the proposed repeal of section 377A was mentioned in the media and the public, I have received several written appeals from my Jalan Kayu residents to urge the Government not to do so.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These residents are mostly parents of young children and youths.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a mother, I can relate to their concerns.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In October 2007 when the Parliament undertook a comprehensive review of our Penal Code since its major amendments in 1984, the public feedback on section 377A was emotional.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Cabinet, after extensive public consultations and discussions, concluded at the end of the debate that Singapore society remained conservative and the majority preferred to uphold a stable society with traditional, heterosexual family values while giving homosexuals the space to live their lives and contribute to society.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As one who has been brought up in a traditional Asian family, I understand Singaporeans who uphold the construct of a family formed by marriage between a man and a woman.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is an important cornerstone of any society since the start and for the continuation of human history.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why then the need to repeal section 377A now?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Minister for Home Affairs, Mr Shanmugam, gave a detailed explanation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Looking at the recent developments in other jurisdictions like India, India's Supreme Court struck down part of the section 377 of their Indian Penal Code, which also criminalised gay sex.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It went further to redefine marriage and familial relationships.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As recent as in August this year, India's Supreme Court widened the definition of the family institution and ruled that familial relationships, "can also take the form of domestic, unmarried partnerships and queer relationships." To me, what happened in India gives a glimpse of the implications on societal norms when the judiciary branch of the government, which is the courts, instead of the legislative branch of the government, which is the parliament, began to interpret what are social norms, because the legislative branch, that is, the Parliament, avoided dealing with the matter.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As I am not a trained lawyer, I will not dwell further into the legality of this case, which Minister Shanmugam has also explained yesterday.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I have also taken careful note, as a community leader, of the wider views, especially among our younger generation, whose views must also be valued.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will not repeat the studies and surveys that several of my fellow hon Parliamentarians have mentioned about the attitudes towards the repeal of section 377A among our younger generation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will share that, in a Youth Network dialogue session, which I attended shortly after the National Day Rally this year, almost the full hall of youth audience between the ages of 15 and 35, raised their hands in support of the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On further dialogue, I learned that most youths are of the view that a law that will not be enforced is better off removed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But what touched me most in that session were a few young adults, who shared that they regretted being too quick to judge and being insensitive in their teenage years when some peers struggled with their sexual identity in their puberty years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more maturity now, they felt that they could have been more supportive.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One even contacted me for opportunities in social service agencies to serve as a counsellor for the homosexual individuals who may be in need, like how we would have helped any other individuals who are in need in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a trusted friend of a few homosexual individuals, some of whom I have known since school days, I have heard their stories of life's challenges, of loss and of regaining of hopes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What they taught me as a friend is the need for human kindness, compassion and love to prevail over judgement and stigmatisation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we propose the repeal of section 377A in our Penal Code and amend our Constitution for the Parliament of the day to be able to reflect our majority electorate's values on the definition of families in Singapore, let us do so with always a care for our fellow Singaporeans at heart, no matter how diverse we are.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the end, it was the reconciliation of my mind, of the duty I have as a Parliamentarian, and my heart, which holds respect and care for people, that I accept the need for the repeal and the important amendments to our Constitution, which will leave space for us as a people to continue to forge understanding, reconciliation and a future together.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given proactive steps taken by the Government on stakeholder engagements, including the Minister's explanation yesterday on the historical context of relevant laws, I fully understand the implications of the Court's rulings and judgments.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the Government's clear explanation of the legal risk that the colonial-era 377A faces and the potential domino impact on other parts of our legislation and related policies.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I accept Minister Shanmugam's interpretation on this issue.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I also fully agree that it is the responsibility of our Government and this House to address this issue head on.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot cop out and pass this uncomfortable duty to the judiciary.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Both Minister Masagos and Minister Shanmugam spoke of the perils of court-led decisions, where the US Supreme Court controversially reversed 50 years of federal abortion rights.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The US media noted the chaos brought about by the court judgment to a great nation already split by deep political divide.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As the debate on this topic can be divisive, I am glad that our Government has taken accountability and has taken steps to help us navigate this complex matter in an inclusive and transparent way, where views from different segments of our society are heard.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I, too, can attest to this process, where after the National Day Rally Speech, we discussed this issue at Nee Soon's events with our grassroots leaders, residents and religious organisations.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We did so in a cool-headed manner and I have to say, the discussions we had with a lot of understanding and empathy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It was way calmer than I earlier expected as this issue is an especially difficult one for all of us to speak on.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This topic affects many in the community who are our friends, relatives and colleagues from both gay and traditional families.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this point, it is my hope that on this basis, our Government will continue to find ways to further strengthen the structure of marriage and family in our current policies.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As the premise for the repeal of section 377A is that what happens in private should not be criminalised, the concern of the community is that this could be incorrectly viewed as a signal for stronger public advocacy of gay relationships.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We need to remember that the debate will not make this issue any less divisive.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We should expect diverse and passionate views from different stakeholders in society to carry on after today.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, we will need to continue to ensure a safe space for healthy and civil conversations, just as we did over the last many months so that our society evolves peacefully.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, can the Minister explain his thoughts on further mechanisms that the Government will put in place to promote genuine, healthy engagements?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Will surveys be done regularly and discussed over national conversations?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In some ways, this can guide the discourse moving forward, monitor fault lines and potentially reduce harassment or discrimination of pro-gay groups or those who do not agree with them, especially in secular spaces such as schools and workplaces.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, some multinational companies offer family benefits to their gay staff, like those for traditional couples.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, with regards to section 377A, over the past few months, we have held discussions with grassroots leaders, residents and religious groups at some of our activities in Nee Soon.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I have covered their questions in my English speech and look forward to the answers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: More importantly, from the national conversations, we can see that Singapore has gained maturity to discuss sensitive issues and find a balance.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I think this is the unique Singapore spirit.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that we can continue to seek common ground while preserving differences and make better decisions for our society.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Sir, in our Singapore Pledge, we committed ourselves to build a democratic society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For me, this process of stakeholder engagements leading to this debate has, I believe, enabled all of us to better understand what our pledge really means.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our Government has demonstrated its even-handed approach and the two Bills placed before us are well-balanced and are steps forward in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It recognises that there is a place for everyone, factoring majority preferences and protecting the dignity of our gay community.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has always prided itself as a melting pot of cultures, races and religions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I support in support of these two Bills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The announcement of the repeal of section 377A has elicited much response from the ground.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many in this House shared and agreed that this has been a divisive topic.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Over the past four months, I have received emails and messages, met in person with residents and members of the public across age groups who are supportive as well as those who are against the repeal.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While most have been respectful in sharing their opinions, I have come to learn of the hostilities some groups carried against those who do not share their views.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The vitriol in some manners of speech is of concern to me.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore understands the value of diplomacy and keeping peace with other nations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We do not have the option of being careless with our words or relationships.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Diplomacy has been and continues to be key to our progress.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, it would be futile to work hard on external relationships if our internal relations are weak.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A House divided against itself will not stand.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore cannot afford a society fractured by toxicity, with one group severing ties with the other simply because we hold different values and opinions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As Singapore progresses and continues to expose ourselves to global issues and movements, there will only be more opportunities for diverging options to arise in our society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must work towards a society that can hold difficult conversations where we make room for disagreements and do not force people into a corner of hate.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We need to allow many rooms for disagreement but not disharmony.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For this reason, Mr Speaker, I wish to focus my speech on how we can shape Singapore conversations on contentious issues such as the repeal, with a heart set on peace-making, to close the space between us and find the way forward.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Peace by domination and subjugation is not peace.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One side prevailing at the expense of the other will break the social compact that is vital for us to be able to live in harmony.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Once the compact is broken, repealing section 377A will not be the only divisive issue.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some view the repeal as rending the moral fabric of society and vice versa.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What we need to recognise is that the moral and social fabrics of any society are intricately intertwined.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One risks being torn as a consequence of the rending of the other.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As such, I commend our Government for seeking to protect both the moral and social fabrics of this nation through the proposed Bills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: After all, problems are solved in the middle, not at the extremes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Finding a way forward does mean that people or groups that fall outside the norms of a traditional family are still to be embraced and supported, whether the single parents, singles, widows, widowers or homosexual family members and friends.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As a Member of Parliament, I represent the aspirations of residents from traditional and non-traditional family units and also the rights of my constituents, regardless of their sexual orientation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I hope the decriminalisation of gay sex will bring relief to those who have experienced discrimination.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, those who are heterosexual should also not have to live in fear or be discriminated in their workplaces, schools and communities because they stand neutral or express pro-traditional family views.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It has brought distress to some parents to hear that terms ranging from "cancel them", "bigots" to homophobic, derogatory names are being used in our classrooms against students who do not share the same views on this topic, forcing others into silence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: No one should attack the other and no one should fear being cancelled for holding or expressing pro-homosexual, pro-traditional family views or neutral views.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We cannot allow coercion to infringe upon an individual's right to decide on matters of conscience and conviction.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is a right that we must protect through legislation as an open, multi-religious and multi-ethnic society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Wisdom is found in the ability to get along with others.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Just as family members differ from one another, yet still share our lives together, can we, as Singaporeans, define our relational compact to be one of a wider brother- or sisterhood?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We can remain honouring of others while disagreeing, respectful without conforming.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore has worked hard to create and build models that have worked well for us – economically, socially and religiously – precisely because we are a pluralistic society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This has been our strength, not a weakness.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am hopeful that we can do the same in the space of affirming heterosexual marriage and family culture, while creating safe social spaces for gay persons.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: On the personal front, my feet are firmly rooted in my faith and my arms are wide open.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Wide open especially to people who believe differently from me.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is this rootedness that allows me to love and walk alongside those different from me, and to stay interested in their lanes and their realities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.01 pm until 4.25 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Most have expressed support for the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will deal with questions raised by Members on: (a) our approach towards cancel culture; (b) past section 377A convictions; (c) keeping sex identification in NRICs and passports; (d) Article 156; and one or two other issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked for any update on the Government’s plans to deal with "cancel culture" and whether there will be any consultation and feedback process.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My Ministry – MinLaw – is looking at measures to deal with the harm caused by cancel campaigns online.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People really ought to be free to stand by their beliefs and express their views, with due respect for the feelings of others without fearing being "cancelled".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many religious groups and organisations, in particular, are very concerned about this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Their experience is that when they express their views, they are shouted down and they feel bullied.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have said that we will try and do something about this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are consulting different groups as part of our review.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We want to try and strike the right balance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not an easy area to deal with or legislate on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will give more details when we get a sense of what is doable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether there are any individuals with existing conviction records under section 377A and how these records will be dealt with.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are some individuals with convictions under 377A.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Most of these cases involved non-consenting victims or acts against minors, or sexual acts committed in public.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These acts continue to be offences, even after any repeal of section 377A.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do take a serious view of them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Criminal records for offences are dealt with under the framework in the Registration of Criminals Act.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And within that framework, people can apply to have their convictions rendered spent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of these offences have become automatically spent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Automatic expiry takes place after a period of time for specific offences and where the criteria are met.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Persons who are disqualified from having their conviction automatically spent, can apply to the Police for the record to be considered spent or rendered spent.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan said that he hopes that the Government will not allow individuals to remove their registered sex from their NRIC or passport.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim suggested that there is no real need for Article 156(1) and (2) since the Constitution already vests legislative power in the legislature and the executive authority in the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us take section 377A as an example.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a law made in the exercise of legislative power by the Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 377A has been challenged as being in breach of the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim agrees that section 377A could be unconstitutional.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The presence of Article 38 in the Constitution will not help if section 377A is in fact unconstitutional.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To put it another way, the fact that the Parliament can pass laws and that Article 38 gives that power, does not automatically mean that all such laws cannot be challenged.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can be challenged, for example, if they are contrary to the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, Articles 156(1) and (2) have been drafted in to give effect to this principle, to protect the laws and policies, based on that definition and to make it clear that passing laws and having policies based on the current definition of marriage are constitutionally valid.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They give context to Articles 156(3) and (4).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have been advised by AGC that Articles 156(1) and (2) could be relevant if there are questions raised as to whether regulating marriage and so on are constitutionally valid purposes and considerations for action by the legislature and Government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, Articles 156(1) and (2) have been enacted to make it clear that the legislature can exercise its legislative power to define, regulate, protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Similarly, the Government and public bodies can exercise their executive authority to achieve these ends.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked why is it necessary for Articles 156(3) and (4) to exclude the whole of Part 4 instead of just a few Articles.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This protects the heterosexual definition of marriage itself from invalidation by Part 4.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need to exclude the whole of Part 4 because we cannot predict what possible arguments might be made against this definition in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With section 377A, we have seen how the arguments in our Courts progressed from equal protection under Article 12 to asserting that sexual conduct is a form of liberty protected by Article 9 or a form of expression protected by Article 14.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of these alternative arguments have been accepted by courts in other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is possible that additional creative arguments could be made about the heterosexual definition of marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, could marriage be a form of association that is protected by Article 14?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is because just as we have been clear about repealing section 377A – we took a clear position – we are equally clear; this Government is very clear – that we will protect the heterosexual marriage as a key institution in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is why the Constitution is being amended.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But let me digress and say, as we say all this, as we listen to the speeches by Members on families, let us also not forget, let us also acknowledge that LGBT persons also have and come from families.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have parents, siblings, grandparents, nieces, nephews, aunties, uncles, close friends and much more.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, families are not exclusive to non-LGBT persons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us remember and acknowledge that these things are not binary.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Parliament tries to enact, say, for example, apartheid marriage laws or impose other outlandish definitions of marriage, those laws would not be protected.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because if you look at Articles 156(3)(b) and (4), the operating provisions, they protect the ability of the Parliament and the Government to make the laws and policies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The protection, the shield is strong, but what is shielded, we have sought to make it quite precise.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Government tries to give benefits to married couples, for example, say, with the surname Tan, Article 156 will only protect the part of the policy that relates to married couples.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government will still have to justify why giving benefits to only people with a certain surname	is a relevant consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think lawyers will understand; it will not be accepted as a relevant consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Nor will the Government be able to take measures that are absolutely prohibited under Part 4, for example, slavery.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If such a measure is taken, the challenge will not be that it is based on the heterosexual definition of marriage or some other basis, it will be that these measures are not allowed on any basis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will be a nice constitutional question if, for example, a same-sex couple were to argue that since Singapore does not recognise same-sex marriages, they had no choice but to emigrate and that is effectively a banishment, and that this Government's policy in not recognising same-sex marriages is therefore in breach of Article 13, which precludes banishment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you can see that a careful person will want to think about the different possibilities of arguments and then make sure that the drafting covers the different possibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not believe that the Government's policies and laws are in breach of Article 13 or for that matter any other Article in the Constitution, but Members can see that creative arguments can be made.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if you want to clear that we want to protect marriage and keep it within the province of the Parliament, then you need to make sure that your drafting is accurate.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is why we have had to draft Article 156 in the way it has been worded.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the case of executive actions, common law judicial review under administrative law principles will generally still apply.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The application of those principles must, however, take Article 156 into account.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, with Article 156, acting to promote marriage would not be an unlawful purpose or an irrelevant consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But otherwise, administrative law principles can and will still apply.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Lim and Ms He Ting Ru say that judicial review under Part 4 should be fully available without restriction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government believes that this is necessary for the reasons I have explained.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Parliament and the elected Government should deal with these questions and try and strike the right balance on these complex and delicate social issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh, as Leader of the Opposition, says that the Workers' Party does not take a position on the matter.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, as a party, the Workers' Party has no official position.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not support the repeal of section 377A.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also does not support the constitutional amendments to protect marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: From their speeches, Mr Pritam Singh and Ms Sylvia Lim, for example, support the repeal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: While Mr Singh supports the constitutional amendments, Ms Lim and Ms He Ting Ru do not support the constitutional amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Gerald Giam are against the repeal but support the constitutional amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Leon Perera is for the repeal, somewhat more enthusiastically than his Leader, and as for the constitutional amendments, he takes a divergent position from his Chairman, Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the Workers' Party had a debate among themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They debated and discussed but did not decide on a party position.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The question is – if this is how one decides, how will such a team function if they are in charge?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh said his lifting the whip on Workers' Party Members of Parliament (MPs) was democratic so as to allow for a full and honest representation of all views.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it does no credit to this House to say these things.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The WP MPs could have made all the speeches they made, even with the whip in place.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MPs are always entitled to state their honest views.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You can express your views, whatever they are, without having to lift the whip.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The whip does not, and has not, prevented MPs from speaking their minds.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MPs have always been free to express what they and their constituents think.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The whip is relevant for voting, not speaking; and the whip sets out the party's position.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In moving the Bills, Minister Masagos and I took pains to lay out both sides of the issue.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The PAP MPs speaking on the issue, too, have reflected the concerns, the fears and pain of the many individuals they have spoken with.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These include views of Singaporeans from different religious groups, LGBT groups and others.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Views on all sides can, have been and must be fully ventilated and they have been ventilated by PAP MPs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I said earlier, the whip is imposed to set out the party's position as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In our Westminster parliamentary system, parties must have a view on the important questions that come before the Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They need to be honest in this House, say what they think is good for Singapore and be accountable to the electorate for their decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The real point is that the Workers' Party as a party does not want to take a stand on this matter.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not want to be seen as supporting the repeal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, it also does not want to be seen as opposing the repeal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That way, it hopes to be all things to all men, and not too much of anything to anyone.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members may know the second line was said in respect of a well-known person.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In my remarks yesterday, I reminded Members there are two reasons for repealing section 377A.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, it is the right thing to do because there are no public concerns that justify private consensual sex between men being a crime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They think that the law should be retained as a matter of conscience.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are seriously held views by honest, sincere people, including in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have thought about it, have decided that for reasons of conscience and often of personal faith	they cannot agree to the repeal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I also outlined a second reason to repeal section 377A – the significant legal risk of it being struck down by the Courts if we were to leave section 377A alone and the significant negative and disruptive consequences for Singaporeans and Singapore if that were to happen.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is a policy question – a question that requires us to consider what is in Singapore's interests.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: From the debate, the following points are clear and are not in question, and the WP does not question them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: No one has questioned these risks in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The WP understands this; there are four lawyers among them in this House, including Ms Lim who has agreed that the legal risks with section 377A, exist.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Given that, then what does the WP has a party propose, if you do not want to repeal section 377A and also do not want to support strengthening marriage which we have proposed?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The position with section 377A is like a train approaching.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The question is whether we have the courage to act or rather dive for cover to protect yourselves and leave society to face the train wreck.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Given the risks, we have a responsibility to do our duty as Parliamentarians, to take a position, to deal squarely with the problem and not abdicate our duty.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To say the party has no position allows the WP MPs to make speeches supporting all sides without having to make a decision and be held responsible for that decision.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is better described as wanting to speak without taking responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the context of our debate, their position will mean that they would leave the decision to the Courts and let Singaporeans face the negative consequences, including perpetuating differences and polarising our society further; if we leave this matter to the Courts, because the Courts can only make binary decisions, as we have seen happen elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the WP truly believes that these sensitive matters ought to be decided by the Court, never mind the consequences, including further dividing us in endless rounds of litigation, then they should be honest and say so in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you stand up and speak at length about the pain and suffering of the LGBT community, then I think one can ask, “Why don’t you take a clear stand and support the repeal?” Or if you believe otherwise, take a stand, oppose the repeal, as a party.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I say this, Sir, let me tell Members, the issue of conscience which is real, is quite different from the issue of policy.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In this House, Members have reflected the complexity of the issue and the diversity of our stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Members have shown why Parliament, rather than the Courts, is the right forum to debate difficult social issues.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have explained clearly why we must act without delay.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many Members touched on this in their speeches.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Some have voiced the concern of Singapore going down a slippery slope after the repeal.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Some touched on support for families with single parents.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Others asked about the posture in educational institutions and expressed concerns on religious freedom.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Alex Yam, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Abdul Samad have asked for assurance that the repeal would not result in a change in social norms.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I explained in my speech yesterday, the many different practices and policies that support society’s notion of children within a marriage between a man and a woman.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: On surveys, while they can help facilitate conversations and potentially reduce discrimination, we recognise that a single or a series of questions would not fully capture such a complex and emotive matter.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It also depends on the survey’s sampling method, whether it is representative and when it was conducted.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There are ongoing efforts to facilitate conversations and civil dialogue.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Mark Chay and Mr Louis Ng said there should be support for other families such as single unwed parents.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We make a distinction between incentives and support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Janet Ang and Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman have asked about sexuality education in public and private schools and the madrasahs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam said students should be taught based on evidence.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Henry Kwek commented that school leaders should take a clear objective stance.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Mark Chay asked how we prepare students to be more understanding and empathetic.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also asked about international schools that compel staff or students to participate in gay community projects even if they do not subscribe to the same lifestyle.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I explained in my opening speech that our education policies and curriculum remain anchored on Singapore's prevailing family values and social norms, which most Singaporeans want to uphold.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These include the family as the cornerstone of our social fabric, and marriage between a man and a woman.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In our schools, all students learn and practise values such as mutual understanding, respect and empathy for everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They will also understand that issues can have multiple perspectives and are taught to listen to each other’s points of view, understand the perspective of others and learn to interact and engage respectfully with each other, even if their views differ.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Sexuality Education Curriculum in MOE schools respects the primary role of parents and reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family as the basic unit of society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The curriculum remains secular and based on research and evidence.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is focused on age appropriateness and the developmental needs of the child when touching on topics such as homosexuality.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In madrasahs, sexuality education is part of their education curriculum and included in specially curated programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Madrasahs are also equipped with trained asatizah and teachers to address sexuality issues.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Counsellors are available should students need further advice and support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MUIS is in regular consultation and collaboration with the madrasahs to further enhance the sexuality education curriculum for students.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Teachers will also be equipped and updated on the current discourse on the matter, to advise and guide students on matters related to sexuality, according to the teachings and traditions of the religion.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For international schools, MOE does not regulate the curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: That said, as the schools operate in Singapore, they should respect our social norms and values.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They must also be careful not to cross the line into advocacy on issues in Singapore that could be socially divisive, such as how sexual orientation, are handled in laws and public policy.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These are matters for Singaporeans to discuss and decide.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how LGBT students struggling with family and mental health issues are supported.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim also asked how teachers and educators are supported.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our schools have a system of support for students with issues concerning their well-being, including on sexuality.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Teachers will listen to students objectively to facilitate support, and not discount, disregard or judge their views.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They assure confidentiality but explain to students that the disclosed information has to be shared with the appropriate key school personnel to assist students in managing their concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Teachers also consult the School Leader and Lead School Counsellor who will further manage these cases, with the school counsellor providing targeted support for the student’s concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Where required, schools, will, with parents’ consent, refer students to professionals and relevant authorities to provide counselling support and appropriate intervention.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Schools must remain a common and safe space for all students, regardless of their background.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have a duty to care to every student.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For students with sexuality issues, our focus is likewise to provide them with a conducive learning environment and the necessary support to ensure their overall well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As sexuality issues are complex, schools work with these students and their families sensitively.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked where families can seek help.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Family Service Centres offer family counselling and can also assist if family relations are strained because one of them has sexuality concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Lastly, Members Mr Christopher De Souza, Mr Zhulkarnain, Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman, Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Darryl David, Ms Janet Ang and Mr Alex Yam have spoken about religious freedom.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Second, religious freedom is protected in Article 15 of the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Every person has the right to profess, propagate and practise his or her own religion, subject to public order, health and morality.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Every religious group has the right to manage its own religious affairs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One can still preach on the pulpit their beliefs about homosexuality or family, even if others might disagree.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But no one should incite violence or hate towards others.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is against the law and is not the society we want to become.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is regardless of whether the comments are made in public, online, or in your private space.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There is no law which prohibits them from treating same-sex couples differently from opposite-sex couples when exercising such rights.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Religious organisations may support those who are struggling or have issues with their sexuality, including through prayers and counselling, as long as consent is obtained and criminal thresholds of harm are not crossed.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Third, in exercising religious freedom, we must understand that we are also members of a plural society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must graciously accommodate those who have different values from us.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Gay people are members of our society and have access to the same opportunities and social support as other Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Social Service Agencies (SSAs) provide secular services to the community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Some SSAs are set up by, or affiliated to, religious organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: All SSAs, regardless of their religious affiliations, serve all clients, including gay persons.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Social service professionals are continuously trained to be sensitive to the diverse needs of clients.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We do not tolerate discrimination at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Employees are protected against discrimination under the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP).

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These guidelines require employers to make employment decisions based on merit and not factors irrelevant to the job.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For religious organisations, understandably, the potential employee's religion and values would be a relevant consideration for certain roles.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Derrick Goh enquired about staff benefits offered by companies to gay couples.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Government, generally, does not interfere in how a private business operates.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, private businesses must respect that their own staff have a right to their personal beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They also cannot cross the line into advocacy on issues in Singapore that are socially divisive, which include issues on homosexuality.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These are matters only for Singaporeans to discuss and decide.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At our workplaces, employees should not feel compelled to support causes or participate in activities that do not align with their beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: TGFEP is clear that an employee's support or non-support of causes, if not relevant to job performance, cannot be used in employment decisions and performance evaluation.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Lastly, we should keep the marketplace free from the polarising contestation of values.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In a free and open economy, with an abundance of choice, businesses can decide what events are allowed on their premises.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, while businesses make their own commercial judgement with regard to their prospective customers, they should do so in a sensitive and respectful manner.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Nonetheless, I urge everyone not to use commerce as a platform to display the conviction of their beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the spirit of mutual respect, I hope businesses and prospective customers can strive to be gracious and adopt the approach of "live and let live".

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And while each of us, as individuals, may have our religious convictions, we take care to ensure that when we make decisions for the whole country, we apply secular, universal values and not individual religious beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Dennis Tan, Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Faisal Manap indicated they will not support the repeal because of their religious values.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Yet, they do not offer any solution on how we can keep society united and cohesive if section 377A is found to be unconstitutional.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Is it their solution to accept a decision by the Courts?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: If so, then why not vote for the repeal now?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Hazel Poa says that the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) wants the definition of marriage to be decided by national referendum rather than by Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Government has explained why we are not proposing to hold a referendum on this issue.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The PSP says that we should not allow Parliament to decide but, instead, let the definition of marriage be decided by national referendum.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But let us call it what it is.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is an attempt to avoid taking a position, as Parliamentarians, as elected representatives of the people.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even if a referendum is held, which side will the PSP be on?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Would the PSP try to bring people together or stay silent on where it stands on heterosexual marriage, as it is doing in this debate?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Also, would a referendum settle this issue once and for all?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Brexit was eventually approved, in a referendum, with the slimmest of margins, and people continued to campaign for a second referendum.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the process, the credibility of the British government was severely damaged.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Despite being in government, the Tories were split on Brexit.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The leadership, rather than uniting around a single position, allowed their members of parliaments and even their ministers to take different views.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Let us not look for politically easy options and cite referendum as an easy solution, just so that a decision does not have to be made in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In any case, even if the PSP wants a referendum, does it or does it not support the constitutional amendments?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It then leaves the Courts to decide on heterosexual marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I have explained why that is not ideal.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In any case, PSP seems to be against the constitutional amendment.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I have explained why that is not good for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We should especially not adopt positions just because it coincides with our own religious beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, everyone in Singapore cannot expect their maximalist position to be realised because Singapore is a vastly diverse society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Singapore has progressed because everyone understands this and has been accommodating of one another.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To be able to faithfully discharge our duties as leaders, we cannot make decisions that affect our fellow citizens based on personal religious beliefs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Instead, I hope we understand the principles of our religions, in making decisions that affect others.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: That is what our Malay/Muslim leaders we engaged were able to do after numerous engagements – they went beyond their own perspectives and assessed what is good for the community, Singapore and Singaporeans – and accepted why these changes need to be made.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I hope all Members of this House can do so, too, and support the repeal of section 377A, together with the proposed amendment to the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As a society, we cannot lose sight of mutual respect when we engage with one another and must endeavour to listen to those who disagree with us.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must not destroy their social or economic standing.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This applies to all sides in every debate.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We should consistently exercise responsibility, restraint and sensitivity to one another, both online and in person.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The work of staying united as one Singapore is what lies ahead of us, even as the debate on these two Bills concludes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is an example of Parliament stepping up to do its duty.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is a responsible Government that has balanced the views expressed by Members and stakeholders and has shown the viable way forward.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We did not deflect the matter to the Courts nor kick the can down the road.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is the strength of our system in Singapore when each branch – the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary – does its part to its fullest and does it well and does what is right for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is time to come together and move forward.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Preserve the peace and stability that our society has fought hard for, and forge ahead – united, not divided – so that we can achieve progress as a nation for many more years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the Minister – I refer to Minister Shanmugam – has mischaracterised my speech somewhat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What I said was specific to the party position in 2019 and here, there was a context.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The party position, as I mentioned, was varied and divided, with no consensus as to whether section 377A should be repealed – and as I said, somewhat similar to Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I lifted the whip and did not fetter the voting rights of Members of Parliament (MPs).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I did not fetter the voting rights of MPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What has been the result arising from this debate?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, in my view, they behaved like a loyal Opposition, not loyal to the PAP, but loyal to Singaporeans, knowing the position of Singaporeans outside of this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have two clarifications for the Minister, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first question pertains to an understanding of how and why the PAP chooses to lift the whip for some Bills and not others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I raise this because the Minister raised it in his closing address.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced that the PAP did not lift the whip for this debate because section 377A is a matter of public policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister, in his National Day address this year, said that not everyone is equally accepting of homosexuality and there were considerable reservations within certain religious groups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the Human Organ Transplant Bill of 2009, the PAP lifted the whip so that MPs could vote based on their religious and ethical beliefs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first generation of PAP leaders under Lee Kuan Yew did the same with the Abortion Bill of 1969, where Mr Lee Kuan Yew himself rose to deliver a speech but was absent when it came to voting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If I follow the Minister's reasoning, would it be correct to say Mr Lee Kuan Yew was abdicating his responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There would be compelling reasons to suggest that for both these Bills, public policy could have been deployed as a reason not to lift the whip – but the PAP lifted it anyway.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister please clarify the consistency or lack of consistency with regard to lifting the whip?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second question pertains to implications of the constitutional amendments for the LGBTQ+ community in the political context.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With these amendments, the effect would be that the Courts are not the correct forum to determine questions of housing policies and same-sex marriage, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the 2011 General Elections some 11 years ago, the sexual orientation of an Opposition candidate came into the spotlight with the PAP asking the Singapore Democratic Party to "come out of the closet" and the PAP statement on this issue pursued an innuendo that made an allusion to paedophilia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the speeches made by PAP MPs over the last two days and the call for any change on the definition of marriage to be a political question, can I confirm the PAP's position with regard to LGBTQ+ candidates standing in General Elections?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that in the pursuit of democracy, he will lift the whip.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he now says that is not so, then he can state that for the record.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, "We are more democratic, we lift the whip".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I just wanted to point out, let us just be accurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People can speak their minds even with the whip imposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And when Mr Singh says the whip will not be imposed on his MPs, he is referring to voting positions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is referring to a party position, that when he came into the Chamber here yesterday, the party did not have a position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And his MPs spoke on both sides; the party did not have a position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not a question of totalling up the numbers at the end of the day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a question of coming upfront and saying, "This is our position as a party even though individuals have their different views and they will speak about them".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is an abdication of responsibility as Parliamentarians.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But where it is purely matters of conscience and you do not quite see such a significant issue for society as a whole, where the very institution of marriage, all your housing policies and your education policies and your rules on the structure and basic content of society can change overnight and where societies get rent asunder by cultural wars, those are the risks we are talking about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we duck and say, "Well, you know, we do not have a position"?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Abortion is quite different in that it was a matter of individual conscience, at least at that point in time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think, today, the issue is well settled in Singapore at least, unlike in some other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But at that time, it was a matter that raised very serious personal concerns.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was not in the House at that point in time and I do not think we should draw conclusions from the fact that one or another Member was present or was not present.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I would be careful if I were Mr Singh to bring Mr Lee Kuan Yew into this and suggest that he had somehow acted dishonourably.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Mr Singh can remind me of his second question?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was about the LGBTQ question vis-à-vis the PAP's position as to whether the LGBTQ community would not be a victim of some personal attacks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think if a paedophile was standing for elections, I am surprised Mr Singh would advocate that cause.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But before that, sorry, the point of abdication and suggesting that I am saying Mr Lee Kuan Yew was dishonourable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I made the point in the context of the question that I put to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the issue of paedophilia, let me share the specific statement that the PAP made which led me to make that point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This was the statement that was released by the PAP. "What is its agenda?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A video has been posted on the Internet showing Vincent Wijeysingha participating at the forum which discussed the promotion of the gay cause in Singapore." I do not think there is a problem with that statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And thereafter it says, "The discussion at the forum also touched on sex with boys and whether the age of consent for boys should be 14 years of age." The innuendo I think is clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the video, Mr Wijeysingha was introduced as being from the SDP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In addition to other comments, Wijeysingha stated, "I think the gay community has to rally ourselves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Perhaps, one outcome of today's forum would be for those of us who are interested to come together to further consider how we can address the 377 issue as well as further rights issues in relation to gays and lesbians." I do not have any issue with the PAP coming up and saying, "Look, what is the political agenda of a candidate?" But what is the relevance of that point on sex with boys, if not to cast aspersions on the candidate himself and to suggest that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Was this a forum where this was the only issue that was discussed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh started out the second question by saying that paedophilia was talked about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is a candidate who is standing for elections, whether for the PAP – and I hope the PAP will never field such a candidate – or for the Workers' Party or SDP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if there is a suggestion of paedophilia, I will certainly speak about it and I am sure all right-thinking Singaporeans will speak about it and will say it is not acceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I do not quite know the precise context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I said in my speech, sexual offences against minors continue to remain serious offences and we take a very serious view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope Mr Singh is not suggesting that paedophiles stand for elections and we do not need to talk about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to whether there are broader innuendoes, I think let us get to the point, Mr Singh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the Workers' Party trooped into Parliament yesterday, there was one point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that point is: Mr Singh, Sir, as Leader of the Opposition, was not prepared for his party to take a position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is what we are talking about; not about an election held in 2011.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And whether we come here prepared to take a position or we are abdicating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Likewise, Mr Speaker, I think I have made my point with regard to what Minister has said.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the issue was not about paedophilia and I agree with him I do not think anybody in Singapore would be thrilled to have a person who is a paedophile standing for elections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the question I asked was: what is the PAP's position with regard to LGBTQ+ candidates standing in general elections?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think that question has been answered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It appears to me that, as usual, Mr Singh wants to move the goalpost and start an entirely new debate about who can and who will stand for elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not the Prime Minister or the Secretary-General of the party, but my personal view is that anyone who is not a criminal and who is of good character and of sound mind and who can work for the residents ought to be able to stand for elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In all of this, in a democracy, it also depends on how people are perceived and accepted in society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One has got to look at individual candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Mr Singh started out by talking about paedophilia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am sure the records, the Hansard, will show that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because I was shocked that he would even ask that question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Indeed, Mr Speaker, the record will show what the context was with regard to that point on paedophilia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I accept the Minister's reply to my second question.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wish to respond to Minister Masagos' comment earlier on PSP's position.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wish to clarify that our position on wanting the definition of marriage to be determined via a national referendum instead of Parliament is not a convenient way to avoid difficult decisions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A case in point would be the fact that we do have a position on section 377A which is also a difficult one.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are aware of the Government's position on what the criteria are for holding a referendum.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is just that we have a slightly different view on what are the issues that should go for a referendum.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this particular case on the issue of the definition of marriage, we feel that this is an issue that is important to many Singaporeans and there is a high level of interest from the public to have a say in this matter.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And since it is an area that does not require any specialised knowledge – which would otherwise make it unsuitable for participation from members of the public – and actually, marriage, as many Members have pointed out, is a matter of social norm, we feel that this is an area that is suitable for the public to participate.
