speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But I think the most important question is not the referendum.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is what is the PSP's position on the constitutional amendment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And, therefore, when the referendum, if held, are they for or against it?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, we know that they are going to support the repeal of section 377A, but they will not support that the amendment to the Constitution be made.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Their position means that while now there would be no further challenges to section 377A because it does not exist, there will now be new challenges that will be put up in Court on constitutional grounds that other institutions, like marriage and families, important to many Singaporeans, will now stand before the Court.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And then we are back to square one again.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They will wait for the train to crash on us.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish to make four points if I may, three are clarifications for the Minister for Home Affairs and one is a clarification on my position on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yesterday, during his Second Reading speech, he cited many Court challenges to the constitutionality of section 377A.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But I do not believe any of the Ministers cited any Court challenges to the heterosexual definition of marriage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask the Government, whether there has been any Court challenge to the heterosexual definition of marriage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And to that extent, would he not agree with me that his analogy of the oncoming train applies to section 377A, but does not quite apply to the heterosexual definition of marriage?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification, earlier he mentioned that the Government does not believe that their policies violate the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It serves the purpose of promoting procreation within a family unit under AMLA, under Women's Charter; and therefore, the Government is on much stronger footing on the constitutionality of the heterosexual definition of marriage, compared to section 377A.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And the reason I am abstaining is that I have concern about the role of the Courts having judicial oversight over the legality of Government actions and Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can the Member clarify or repeat the third clarification, please?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The third clarification is, I would like the Minister to confirm whether he accepts that the Courts have a constitutional role to ensure that Government actions, as well as Parliament's laws, do conform to the Constitution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, whether I agree that while there is a more immediate risk on section 377A, that those concerns do not quite apply to the current definition of marriage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the Government's concern about the current definition of marriage?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at what has happened in India.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The courts first said that their version, their section 377 was not unconstitutional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, within a few years, they said – well, it is unconstitutional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And now, earlier this year, they have said – the definition of marriage should be broader than a purely heterosexual marriage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a similar system and similar broad common law principles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One can say and one can discern that there are different approaches that the Singapore Courts take vis-à-vis the Indian courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think if you were to look at it as a lawyer, legal analysis and, particularly, if you are charged with a heavy responsibility to make sure that Singapore is looked after properly and that you care for Singapore and that your concern is for the well-being of Singaporeans, then you will not take these risks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will think them through, whether it is immediate or perhaps it is in the mid-term.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you think that there is a risk, then our duty is to go out there, explain the risks and then say how we would seek to put the laws in place to protect society, protect marriage, protect the institution of marriage and the structure of marriage, so that our society, successful as it has been, can continue to be successful, and so that the fundamental values of Singaporeans can be protected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fine legal analysis is necessary to identify whether there is a risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that does not lead to, "Well, we do not have to do anything about it".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is a risk to something as fundamental as marriage, you act – or at least this Government acts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, do I not believe that the Government can convince the Court that providing for a heterosexual definition of marriage, we can tell the Court it is reasonable to say it should be between a man and a woman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have seen the social policy changes in the United Kingdom, from which many of our laws come.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, there, the laws have been changed through parliament, but there are many countries where the laws have been changed through the courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I, for one, while I believe that our Courts have always taken the approach, the three great branches of the state, as I said yesterday – the Courts, the Judiciary, Parliament and the Executive – the system has worked well because each has respected the sphere of the other and our Judiciary is independent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I were asked, I would say there is a reasonably good likelihood that we will be able to persuade the Court today that there is a basis for making a distinction between same-sex marriages and heterosexual marriages, and that the current definition of marriage in the Woman's Charter should be maintained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if I were asked a different question, "Is there a risk that it could be struck out?", I think it would be either a stupid lawyer or a foolish lawyer who will say there is no risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you accept that there is a risk, then, what do you do?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, do I accept that the Courts have a constitutional role?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think if the question goes towards why do we then say that the Courts should not look at the definition of marriage, I think I have given a very extensive answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What should count as marriage should be decided here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should discuss it, we should decide it and we should take into account what society is ready for and what society needs and what strengthens society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even if we take a view which is different from the majority view, then it is our duty to go and convince society as to why we are taking that view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, any elected Government, by a simple majority, can decide on what a marriage ought to be like.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No Court can do what we did yesterday and today, which is to consider repealing section 377A, but at the same time, strengthening the institution of marriage and explaining the reasons, having it fully discussed, going out to the public and explaining – that is what is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We believe that a future discussion would require these sorts of discussions and it may require changes to more than one piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will decide on the question presented to them and strike out if they think it should be struck out.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a vote is taken to ascertain that the Second Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, which is 63 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I note that there are Members seated in the Speaker's Gallery.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For Members seated there, the Clerk will call your name to indicate your vote.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members seated within the Bar of the House will vote electronically.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: They are reminded to be seated at their designated seats.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will first call the names of Members seated in the Speaker's Gallery to indicate their votes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These Members are to verbally state their vote indication when their names are called by the Clerk in alphabetical order.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to record the votes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now proceed with the electronic voting for Members seated within the Bar of the House.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These Members should only start to vote when the voting buttons on their armrest start to blink.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members seated within the Bar of the House are advised to check that their names are registered according to their vote indication when the voting results are shown on the display screens.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These results do not include the votes taken manually from the Members seated in the Speaker's Gallery and the final results are subject to the addition of these votes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I proceed to declare the results of the vote, are there any Members who wish to claim that his or her vote has not been recorded correctly?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Now, Sir, I beg to move, "That the Bill be now read a Third time."

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the Bill be now read a Third time." Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a vote is taken to ascertain that the Third Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of Elected and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, which is 63 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to record the votes of the Members at the Speaker's Gallery.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now proceed with the electronic voting for Members seated within the Bar of the House.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Again, Members should only start to vote when the voting buttons on their armrest start to blink.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Once again, do remember to depress the vote button firmly to register your vote in the system.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are advised to check that their names are registered according to their vote indication when the voting results are shown on the display screens.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These results do not include the votes taken manually from the Members seated in the Speaker's Gallery and the final results are subject to the addition of these votes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I proceed to declare the results of the vote, are there any Members, apart from myself, who wish to claim that his or her vote has not been recorded correctly?
